by a permutation operator
T_{\pi}
and taking the trace, we obtain

\operatorname{tr}(\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(O)T_{\sigma})=\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}c_{\pi}(O)\operatorname{tr}(T_{\pi}T_{\sigma}).

(78)

From this expression, it is evident that
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is a symmetric matrix.
Using
Eq.

23
and the fact that
T_{\pi}\in\com(\mathcal{U}(2^{n})^{\otimes k})
, we observe that
\operatorname{tr}(\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(O)T_{\sigma})=\operatorname{tr}(OT_{\sigma}).

Now, defining the
k!\times k!
matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
with components
\Lambda_{\pi,\sigma}=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\pi}T_{\sigma})
, we can invert the above relation to solve for the coefficients
c_{\pi}(O)
, to get

c_{\pi}(O)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\sigma}\operatorname{tr}(T_{\sigma}O).

(79)

∎

The matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is invertible for
k\leq d
; otherwise, it is not. In such a case, it is still possible to employ the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. This can be seen because the permutation operators are linearly independent in the regime
k\leq d
, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
serves as the Gram matrix.

Hence, after obtaining the matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
—which is independent of the specific choice of operator
O
—fully characterizing the twirling channel as given in
Eq.

23
requires computing the
k!
coefficients
\tr(O T_{\sigma})
for every
\sigma\in S_{k}
.

Lastly, let us introduce the asymptotic behavior of the Weingarten functions (see
Lemma

21
) in the limit of large
d
and
k=o(d)
. In many cases–if not most–we are primarily interested in studying the asymptotic behavior of averaged quantities as
d
grows. Notably, Don Weingarten has been the first to analyze the asymptotic behavior of Weingarten functions in Ref.
Weingarten 1978
, and later, Collins
Collins and Śniady 2006
provided a general formula for integration over the unitary group
\mathcal{U}(2^{n})
.

Lemma 22

(Asymptotics of Weingarten functions
Weingarten 1978
)
.

Let
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
be the
k\times k
matrix with components
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\pi,\sigma}=\tr(T_{\pi}T_{\sigma})
. Then, in the limit of large
d
, the components of the inverse matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}
behave as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\pi}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d^{-k}+O(d^{-(k+2)}),

(80)

\displaystyle(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\sigma}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle O(d^{-(k+|\pi\sigma|)}),\quad\pi\neq\sigma.

The above asymptotics provide an extremely useful tool for applications (see also Ref.
Liu et al. 2018
).
In the following proposition, we present an example of a Haar average over the unitary group in the context of the orbit of a pure quantum state, which serves as a useful illustration for the subsequent discussion on averaging over the Clifford group. Additionally, in
Appendix

A.1
, we provide a user-friendly guide on how to perform such averages for relatively low values of
k
.

An example of particular interest arises when the operator
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})
in
Eq.

23
is chosen as
O=\outerproduct{\psi_0}{\psi_0}^{\otimes k}
, where we consider
k
identical copies of a state vector
\ket{\psi_0}
.

Proposition 23

(Haar orbit of pure states)
.

Let
d
and
k
be natural numbers. Consider a pure quantum state
\psi_{0}
. Throughout this manuscript, we denote the uniform (Haar) measure over pure states in the Hilbert space by
\de\psi
. Specifically, we have the expression

\displaystyle\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}\coloneqq\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(\psi_{0}^{\otimes k})=\int\de\psi\,\psi^{\otimes k}=\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}

(81)

for the Haar average,
where
\Pi_{\sym}\coloneqq\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi}T_{\pi}
, and

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym})=\binom{d+k-1}{d-1}=\frac{1}{k!}d(d+1)(d+2)\cdots(d+k-1).

(82)

Proof.

The Haar orbit of a pure state vector
\ket{\psi_0}
is independent of the chosen specific state, due to the invariance of the Haar measure. To determine the coefficients
c_{\pi}(\psi_{0}^{\otimes k})
in
Eq.

75
, we can make use of the symmetric property of
\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}
, which is invariant under left and right multiplication by permutation operators
\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}=T_{\pi}\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}=\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}T_{\pi}.

This symmetry implies that the coefficients
c_{\pi}(\psi_{0}^{\otimes k})
must be equal for all
\pi
, i.e.,
c_{\pi}(\psi_{0}^{\otimes k})=N^{-1},
where
N
is a normalization constant. Importantly, this step does not require the permutations to be linearly independent.
Thus, we can express
\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}
as
\Psi_{\operatorname{Haar}}=N^{-1}\sum_{\pi}T_{\pi}.

To determine the normalization constant
N
, we impose the condition
\tr(\Psi_{\haar})=1
, which gives us the final result. The dimension of the symmetric subspaces can be verified explicitly (see, e.g. Ref.
Harrow 2013
).
∎

IV
Characterization of the Clifford commutant from first principles

In this section, we present a rigorous construction of the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group from first principles. Our approach is based solely on the fundamental properties of Pauli operators, introduced in
Section

III
, ensuring a clear and self-contained derivation.

To this end, we begin by defining an equivalence class associated with a Pauli operator acting on multiple tensor copies of the system. This class is characterized by a
decomposition matrix

V
and the
anticommmutation graph

G
corresponding to the Pauli operators appearing in the decomposition.

Definition 24

(Equivalence class of Pauli operators)
.

Let
P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
be a Pauli operator. Let
P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}
algebraic independent Pauli and
V\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m}
with columns
V=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{m})
such that
P\propto P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}
. Let
G\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}
be the anticommmutation graph of
P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}
. We define the equivalence class of the pair
(V,G)
as

\displaystyle[V,G]\coloneqq\{(V^{\prime},G^{\prime})\mid\exists\,A\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\text{ such that }V^{\prime}=VA,\,G^{\prime}=A^{-1}GA^{-T}\},

(83)

where
A^{-T}
denotes the inverse transpose of
A
. Furthermore, we can define the map
\mathcal{M}:\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}\rightarrow\{[V,G]\}_{V,G}
which maps
P\mapsto[V,G]
.

We now verify that the above definition is well posed, i.e., the mapping
P\mapsto[V,G]
is consistent.

Proof.

By
Lemma

13
, any Pauli operator
P\propto P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}
is associated with a matrix
V\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m}
whose columns are
(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})
, and a matrix
B_{\boldsymbol{P}}
whose columns encode the bit string representation of the Pauli operators
\mathbf{P}\coloneqq(P_{1},\dots,P_{m})\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times k}
. Any other valid decomposition, say
(V^{\prime},B_{\boldsymbol{P}^{\prime}})
, must be related to
(V,B_{\boldsymbol{P}})
through an invertible transformation
A\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, such that
V^{\prime}=VA
and
B_{\boldsymbol{P}^{\prime}}=B_{\boldsymbol{P}}A^{-T}
(
Lemma

13
). Since the adjacency matrix of the anticommmutation graph associated with
\mathbf{P}
is
G\coloneqq B_{\boldsymbol{P}}^{T}(J+J^{T})B_{\boldsymbol{P}}
(By
Eq.

38
), it follows that under the transformation
B_{\boldsymbol{P}^{\prime}}=B_{\boldsymbol{P}}A^{-T}
, the corresponding adjacency matrix becomes
G^{\prime}=A^{-1}GA^{-T}
. This confirms that
[V,G]
is well defined.
∎

IV.1
An orthogonal basis for the commutant: the algebraic independent graph-based basis

We now present the first of our main results, namely an orthogonal basis for the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group for any
k
and
n
, denoting number of qubits. In subsequent sections, we will refer to this basis as
algebraically independent graph-based basis
(see
Definition

50
).

Theorem 25

(Orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant)
.

Let
\mathcal{M}\colon P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}\mapsto\mathcal{M}(P)=[V,G]
be the map from the Pauli operators
\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
to the equivalence class
[V,G]
, defined in
Definition

24
. Then, the set of operators

\mho_{I}([V,G])\coloneqq\frac{1}{|S_{[V,G]}|}\sum_{P\in S_{[V,G]}}\varphi(P)P

(84)

where
S_{[V,G]}=\{Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}|\mathcal{M}(Q)=[V,G]\}
,
\varphi(P)\coloneqq\tr(PT_{(k\cdots 21)})
with
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
with
\rank_{2}(G)\geq 2(m-n)
(which is equivalent to requiring that
\mho_{I}([V,G])\neq 0
), forms an orthogonal basis for
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
for any
n,k
.

Proof.

Our proof strategy is similar to that used in the proof of Lemma 4.8 in Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
, which exploits the fact that a basis of the commutant is given by the image of the twirling operator acting on Pauli operators.

In particular, we start by noticing that the image of the Clifford twirling super-operator
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\cdot)
defined in
Eq.

57
is precisely the commutant of the Clifford group.
So that we can consider the operator basis of Pauli operators
\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
and construct the commutant as

\displaystyle\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})=\operatorname{span}\{\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\,:\,P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}\}\,.

(85)

Using
Lemma

6
, we obtain

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{n}|}\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}C^{\otimes k}PC^{\dagger\otimes k}=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{orb}(P)|}\sum_{Q\in\mathrm{orb}(P)}Q\,,

(86)

where
\mathrm{orb}(P)\coloneqq\{Q\in\pm\mathbb{P}_{n}\mid\exists\,C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}:Q=C^{\otimes k}PC^{\dagger\otimes k}\}
is the orbit of
P
under the Clifford group which maps Pauli operators to Pauli operators up to phases.
We observe that if
-P\in\operatorname{orb}(P)
, then
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)=0
.
A sufficient condition for
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\neq 0
is given by

\displaystyle\varphi(P)=\frac{\tr(P T_{(k\cdots 2 1)})}{d}\neq 0\,.

(87)

To see this, it is sufficient to realize that
\varphi(P)
is Clifford invariant because
T_{(k\cdots 21)}\in\com(\mathcal{U}_{n}^{\otimes k})\supset\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, and thus
\varphi(P)=\varphi(\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P))
. Let us show that the condition in
Eq.

87
is also necessary. By virtue of
Lemma

13
, we can write
P=\phi P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}
with the associated matrices
V
and
B_{\boldsymbol{P}}
and phase
\phi
, and
G
being the anticommutation graph of the Pauli operators
\boldsymbol{P}=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{m})
. Then,

\varphi(P)=\frac{1}{d}\tr(PT_{(k\dots 2 1)})=\frac{1}{d}\phi\tr(\prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{\alpha=1}^{k}P_{i}^{(v_{i})_{\alpha}}),

(88)

since for any operators
O_{1},\ldots,O_{k}
then we have
\tr(O_1\otimes\cdots\otimes O_k T_{(kk-1\cdots 1)})=\tr(O_1\ldots O_k)
as it can be verified by
Eq.

69
. For
\varphi(P)\neq 0
, we need that the product of all the Pauli operators in the trace is proportional to the identity, meaning
0=\sum_{i,j}(v_{i})_{j}b(P_{i})\pmod{2}=\sum_{i}|v_{i}|b(P_{i})\pmod{2}
. This implies that either
|v_{i}|=0\pmod{2}
or that
b(P_{i})=0
for all
i
because
P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}
are algebraically independent (see
Lemma

13
).

Conversely, if there exists
i
such that
|v_{i}|=1\pmod{2}
and
b(P_{i})\neq 0
, then the Clifford operator that maps
P_{i}\mapsto-P_{i}
(and preserves
P_{j}
for
j\neq i
) also maps
P\mapsto-P
, meaning that
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)=0
. This proves that
Eq.

87
is a necessary and sufficient condition for
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\neq 0
. Moreover, the reasoning above shows that
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\neq 0
iff
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
.

Given the Pauli operator
P
written as
P=\phi P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}
, the Clifford action on
P
takes the following form

\displaystyle C^{\otimes k}PC^{\dagger\otimes k}=\phi C^{\otimes k}P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}C^{\dagger\otimes k}

\displaystyle=\phi C^{\otimes k}P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}C^{\dagger\otimes k}\cdots C^{\otimes k}P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}C^{\dagger\otimes k},

(89)

and, therefore, both
V
and
G
are preserved by the action of
C
. It, hence, follows that
\mathcal{M}(C^{\otimes k}PC^{\otimes k})=\mathcal{M}(P)
. Hence, by defining
S_{[V,G]}=\{Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}|\mathcal{M}(Q)=[V,G]\}
, we can identify the twirling operator of
P
as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)=\frac{\varphi^{*}(P)}{|S_{[V,G]}|}\sum_{Q\in S_{[V,G]}}\varphi(Q)Q,

(90)

where the relative
\pm
phase of Pauli operators belonging to
\operatorname{orb}(P)
is equal to
\varphi(P)/\varphi(Q)
. To see this, consider a Clifford
C
and
C^{\otimes k}PC^{{\dagger}\otimes k}=\theta Q
with
\theta=\pm 1
. Since
\phi(P)
is Clifford invariant, we have
\phi(P)=\phi(C^{\otimes k}PC^{{\dagger}\otimes k})=\theta\phi(Q)
, which implies
\theta=\phi(P)/\phi(Q)=\varphi(Q)/\varphi(P)=\varphi^{*}(P)\varphi(Q)
proving
Eq.

90
. We can, therefore, write

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)=\varphi^{*}(P)\mho_{I}([V,G])\quad\text{where}\quad[V,G]=\mathcal{M}(P).

(91)

Thus, we have established that the set of operators
\mho_{I}([V,G])
generates the commutant. Next, we demonstrate that these operators are orthogonal with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product,

\displaystyle\tr( \mho_I([V,G])^\dagger\mho_I([V',G']) )=0\quad\text{for}\quad[V,G]\neq[V^{\prime},G^{\prime}].

(92)

In fact, we have

\displaystyle\tr(\mho_I([V,G])\mho_I^\dagger([V',G']))=\frac{1}{|S_{[V,G]}||S_{[V^{\prime},G^{\prime}]}|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}P\in S_{[V,G]}\\
P^{\prime}\in S_{[V^{\prime},G^{\prime}]}\end{subarray}}\varphi(P)\varphi^{-1}(P^{\prime})\tr(PP'^\dag)=\frac{d^{k}\delta_{[V,G],[V^{\prime},G^{\prime}]}}{|S_{[V,G]}|},

(93)

which follows since
P
and
P^{\prime}
need to be in the
same orbit,
(i.e.,
[V,G]=[V^{\prime},G^{\prime}]
).
This result demonstrates that the operators
\mho_{I}([V,G])
are linearly independent, provided that
\mho_{I}([V,G])\neq 0
. Since
P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
serves as an operator basis, it follows that the set of non-zero, independent graph-based monomials forms a basis of the commutant for any
n
and
k
.

The remainder of the proof is now devoted to determining the conditions on
V,G
under which
\mho_{I}([V,G])
is non-zero, which is the case if and only if the set
S_{[V,G]}
is not empty.
First we note, that this property is independent of
V
, as long as
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
.
As such, it reduces to asking whether a matrix
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
can represent a valid anticommmutation graph of Pauli operators on
n
qubits. By
Lemma

14
, we can take a
representant of
[V,G]
, where

\displaystyle G\coloneq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus 0_{m-2r,m-2r}

(94)

and where
r\coloneqq\mathrm{rank}_{2}(G)/2
. Naturally, we can construct a set of Pauli operators that satisfy the anticommmutation graph by choosing the set
\{X_{i},Z_{i}\}_{i\leq r}\cup\{Z_{i}\}_{r+1\leq i\leq m}
. This requires
n\geq m-r
many qubits.
If instead
n\leq m-r
, we have that
S_{[V,G]}
must be the empty set, as it must contain
m-r
algebraically independent and commuting Pauli operators, which requires at least
m-r
many qubits.
As such,
r\geq m-n
needs to be satisfied for
\mho_{I}([V,G])
to not vanish. This concludes the proof.
∎

IV.2
Dimension of the Clifford commutant

Theorem

25
provides a basis for the commutant for any
k,n
, by leveraging the fact that the image of the Clifford twirling on the Pauli group
\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
yields an orthogonal basis of the commutant. The crucial element of the proof is the identification of nonzero orbits through the equivalence classes
[V,G]
into which each Pauli operator
P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
falls. Specifically, the vector space
V
and the anticommutation graph
G
associated with
P
correspond to the only invariants of the Clifford orbit of
P
. By establishing a necessary and sufficient condition for
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\neq 0
through the equivalence class
[V,G]
, we can directly determine the dimension of the commutant, as stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 26

(Dimension of the Clifford group commutant)
.

The dimension of the Clifford group commutant for any
n
and
k
is given by the expression

\displaystyle\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))

\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{r=\max(m-n,0)}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{(k-1+2r-m-1)m-r-2r^{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1-2^{-k+j}}{1-2^{-j}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{(1-2^{-m+i-1})(1-2^{-m+r+i-1})}{1-2^{2i}}

(95)

\displaystyle\simeq\begin{cases}2^{\frac{k^{2}-3k}{2}}&2n\geq k-1,\\
2^{2kn-2n^{2}-3n}&2n<k-1,\end{cases}

where ‘
\simeq
’ means ‘up to factors’ bounded with constants from above and below in the subsequent proof. In particular, if
n\geq k-1
, the dimension is independent of
n
, and is equal to
\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))=\prod_{i=0}^{k-2}(2^{i}+1)
.

Proof.

Using
Theorem

25
, to determine the dimension of the commutant it is sufficient to count the number of equivalence classes
[V,G]
corresponding to an operator
\mho_{I}([V,G])\neq 0
. First, the number of binary vector subspaces of
\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}
spanned by
m
vectors with even Hamming weight is given by the Gaussian Binomial coefficient
\binom{k-1}{m}_{2}
, see
Lemma

2
, which we can rewrite as

\displaystyle\binom{k-1}{m}_{2}=2^{km-m^{2}-m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1-2^{-k+j}}{1-2^{-j}}\,.

(96)

for future convenience. This determines the number of matrices
V
, up to the linear transformation
A\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, see
Definition

24
. We are now left to count the number of allowed anticommmutation graphs
G
on
n
qubits. The requirement for this is computed in
Lemma

27
, namely
n\geq m-r
, where
2r=\mathrm{rank}_{2}(G)
.
The number
N_{0}(m,r)
of
m
-dimensional symmetric matrices with zero diagonal with a given even binary rank
2r
is given by
Lemma

1
:

\displaystyle N_{0}(m,r)

\displaystyle=2^{2mr-r-2r^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{(1-2^{-m+i-1})(1-2^{-m+r+i-1})}{1-2^{-2i}}

(97)

which exactly counts the number of graphs.
Therefore, to determine the dimension of the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group, we use that this corresponds to the number of all even Hamming weight vector spaces of dimension
m
times the number different anticommmutation graphs of
m
Pauli operators allowed on
n
qubits. Hence:

\displaystyle\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))

\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{r=\max(m-n,0)}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\binom{k-1}{m}_{2}N_{0}(m,r)

(98)

\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{r=\max(m-n,0)}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{(k+2r-m-1)m-r-2r^{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1-2^{-k+j}}{1-2^{-j}}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{(1-2^{-m+i-1})(1-2^{-m+r+i-1})}{1-2^{-2i}}

\displaystyle\eqqcolon\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{r=\max(m-n,0)}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}(\#\mho_{I})(k,m,r)

where

\displaystyle(\#\mho_{I})(k,m,r)=c_{k,m,r}\times 2^{(k+2r-m-1)m-r-2r^{2}},

(99)

and
c_{k,m,r}
is the factor arising from the product terms in
Eq.

98
. In
Eq.

98
, we remark that whenever
m-n\leq\lfloor\frac{m}{2}\rfloor
, then
(\#\mho_{I})(k,m,r)\neq 0
. This condition is equivalent to requiring that
m\leq 2n
. Hence, overall
m\leq\max\{k-1,2n\}
. We now determine simplified lower and upper bounds.
By setting
r=\lfloor m/2\rfloor-x

and defining
m_{0}=\min(k-1,2n)
to choose
m=m_{0}-y
, we arrive at the following expression:

\displaystyle(\#\mho_{I})(k,m\!=\!m_{0}-y,r\!=\!\lfloor m/2\rfloor-x)

\displaystyle=2^{(k-3/2)m_{0}-m_{0}^{2}/2}\!\times\!2^{(m_{0}-k+3/2)y-y^{2}/2}\!\times\!2^{(-1)^{m_{0}-y}x-2x^{2}}\!\times\!c_{k,m_{0}-y,\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor-x}.

(100)

As can be seen, the number of elements drops exponentially in
x
and
y
. This allows us to bound the overall size of the commutant by computing the prefactor explicitly

\displaystyle\sum_{y=0}^{m_{0}}2^{(m_{0}-k+3/2)y-y^{2}/2}\sum_{x=0}^{\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor}2^{(-1)^{m_{0}-y}x-2x^{2}}c_{k,m_{0}-y,\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor-x}

\displaystyle=\sum_{y=0}^{m_{0}}2^{(m_{0}-k+3/2)y-y^{2}/2}\sum_{x=0}^{\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor}2^{(-1)^{m_{0}-y}x-2x^{2}}

\displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{m_{0}-y}\frac{1-2^{-k+j}}{1-2^{-j}}\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor-x}\frac{(1-2^{-m_{0}+y+i-1})(1-2^{-m_{0}+y+\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor+i-1-x})}{1-2^{-2i}}

(101)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(i)}}}}{{\leq}}\sum_{y=0}^{\infty}2^{y/2-y^{2}/2}\times\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}2^{x-2x^{2}}\times\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1-2^{-j}}\times\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1-2^{-2i}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(ii)}}}}{{\leq}}20.3.

In (i) we have used that
m_{0}\leq k-1
, hence
m_{0}-k+3/2\leq 1
and then we upper bounded
(1-2^{-m_{0}+y+i-1})(1-2^{-m_{0}+y+\lfloor(m_{0}-y)/2\rfloor+i-1-x})\leq 1
; further we noticed that the arguments of the products are increasing functions greater then
1
. In (ii) we have used a numerical solver.
Let us now turn to discussing the lower bound. We can use only the term when
y=x=0

\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{m_{0}}\frac{1-2^{-k+j}}{1-2^{-j}}\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor m_{0}/2\rfloor}\frac{(1-2^{-m_{0}+i-1})(1-2^{-m_{0}+\lfloor m_{0}/2\rfloor+i-1})}{1-2^{2i}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(i)}}}}{{\geq}}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{0}}\frac{1-2^{-m_{0}+j-1}}{1-2^{-j}}\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}(1-2^{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(ii)}}}}{{\geq}}0.28\,.

(102)

In (i) we have used the fact that
0\leq m_{0}\leq k-1
and in (ii) we have employed a numerical solver. This gives the following bounds

\displaystyle 0.28\times 2^{(k-3/2)m_{0}-m_{0}^{2}/2}\leq\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))\leq 20.3\times 2^{(k-3/2)m_{0}-m_{0}^{2}/2}\,.

(103)

We now discriminate two cases, namely
2n<k-1
and
2n\leq k-1
, to determine
m_{0}=\min\{2n,k-1\}
, leading to:

\displaystyle 0.56\times 2^{k^{2}/2-3k/2}

\displaystyle\leq\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))\leq 40.6\times 2^{k^{2}/2-3k/2}

\displaystyle 2n\geq k-1

\displaystyle 0.28\times 2^{2kn-2n^{2}-3n}

\displaystyle\leq\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))\leq 20.3\times 2^{2kn-2n^{2}-3n}

\displaystyle 2n<k-1\,.

(104)

In the case where
n\geq k-1
, all graphs are allowed, and thus there is no restriction on their rank. Consequently, the number of distinct basis elements
\mho_{I}
is solely a function of
k
and
m
. This results in a much simpler expression for the dimension of the commutant, given by

\dim(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{m}_{2}2^{\frac{m(m-1)}{2}}=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(2^{i}+1),\quad\text{if }n\geq k-1

(105)

using the Gaussian binomial theorem. We also observe that
Eq.

105
coincides with the dimension of the commutant derived in
Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
.

∎

IV.3
Properties of the orthogonal basis elements

The following lemma establishes some key properties of the operators
\mho_{I}
that provide a orthogonal basis for the Clifford group commutant for any
n,k
.

Lemma 27

(Properties of the operators
\mho_{I}
)
.

Let
\mho_{I}([V,G])
be the set of operators defined in
Theorem

25
, with
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
with
\rank_{2}(G)\geq 2(m-n)
. They obey the following properties:

(i)

\tr(\mho_I([V,G]))=0
for all
V\neq 0
;

(ii)

\|\mho_{I}([V,G])\|_{\infty}\leq 1
;

(iii)

i^{\mathrm{rank}_{2}(G)}\mho_{I}([V,G])
is Hermitian;

(iv)

For
S_{[V,G]}=\{Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}|\mathcal{M}(Q)=[V,G]\}
, it holds that

\displaystyle|S_{[V,G]}|=2^{2mn-m^{2}/2+m/2}\prod_{j=r-(m-n)+1}^{n}(1-4^{-j}).

(106)

(v)

\|\mho_{I}([V,G])\|_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{2^{nk}}{|S_{[V,G]}|}}=2^{(k/2-m)n-m/4+m^{2}/4}\times\prod_{i=0}^{m-r-1}\sqrt{1-2^{-2(n-i)}}
.

Proof.

Condition (i) and (ii) can be obtained by noticing that
\mho_{I}([V,G])=\varphi^{*}(P)\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)
with
\mathcal{M}(P)=[V,G]
. For condition (iii), we note that
\varphi(P)\mho_{I}([V,G])
is Hermitian, for
P\in S_{[V,G]}
.

Condition (v) follows from (iv) and
Eq.

93
. Indeed, computing the
2
-norm reduces to computing the size of the set
S_{[V,G]}=\{Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}\,|\,\mathcal{M}(Q)=[V,G]\}
. Note that by
Lemma

17
, the size of the set is equal to

\displaystyle|S_{[V,G]}|=|\{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times k}\,|\,\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\}|

(107)

we can use the invariance of the equivalence class under
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
and
Lemma

14
to rewrite
G\mapsto G^{\prime}=A^{-1}GA^{-T}
such that

G^{\prime}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus 0_{m-2r,m-2r}

(108)

with
\mathrm{rank}(G)=2r
. One particular set of Pauli operators that satisfies the anticommmutation graph
G
is consisting of
(Z_{i},X_{i})_{i\in[r]}
pairs, followed by
(Z_{r+i})_{i\in m-2r}
stabilizers. This consideration helps in computing
|\mathrm{orb}(P)|
. To count them, we first start by selecting the first anticommuting pair of
Z_{1}
-like and
X_{1}
-like operators. There are
(4^{n}-1)\times 4^{n}/2
many options. As any further selected Pauli operators need to commute with the previous ones to ensure algebraic independency. This restricts our choices effectively reducing the number of qubits by
1
each time. As such, we have that there are

\displaystyle\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^{2(n-i)}-1)\times 2^{2(n-i)-1}

(109)

many options to select algebraically independent pairs of
X
-like,
Z
-like operators. We now count the
Z
components.
Here we have effectively
m^{\prime}=m-2r
many
Z
type Pauli operators on
n^{\prime}=n-r
many qubits. This reduces the counting on selecting algebraically independent Pauli operators all commuting with the previous ones, giving

\displaystyle\prod_{i=0}^{m^{\prime}-1}(2^{2n^{\prime}-i}-2^{i}).

(110)

Multiplying
Eqs.

109
and
110
gives the desired result.
∎

V
A natural and easy-to-manipulate basis for the Clifford commutant: Pauli monomials

While in
Section

IV
we derived the commutant of the Clifford group for any
n,k
, here we aim to develop a framework that allows us to handle the commutant in a more direct and simplified manner. In particular, this section introduces a fundamental concept of our work: Pauli monomials. These are constructed as products of isotropic sums of Pauli operators. In the following, we familiarize the reader with various types of Pauli monomials, which will serve as a key tool for constructing a simple basis for the commutant of the Clifford group.

The underlying intuition is that, since the Clifford group leaves invariant the set of Pauli operators, all operators that commute with every Clifford element must be constructed as isotropic sums over Pauli operators.

To begin with, we introduce the simplest and most intuitive type of Pauli monomials, referred to as
primitive Pauli monomials
. These monomials encapsulate many essential properties of the full commutant and, as we demonstrate in
Theorem

55
, generate the entire commutant.

Definition 28

(Primitive Pauli monomials)
.

Let
v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}
be a vector satisfying
|v|\in 2\mathbb{N}
. Define the operator

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega(v)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes v}.

(111)

The primitive Pauli monomials satisfy the following properties.

Lemma 29

(Properties of primitive Pauli monomials)
.

The primitive Pauli monomials satisfy the following properties:

A)

If
|v|/2=0\pmod{2}
(
v
is even), then
d^{-1}\Omega(v)
is a projector of rank
d^{k-2}
.

B)

If
|v|/2=1\pmod{2}
(
v
is odd), then
\Omega(v)
is a Hermitian unitary operator.

C)

If
v,w\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}
satisfy
v\cdot w=0\pmod{2}
, then
[\Omega(v),\Omega(w)]=0
.

Proof.

That
\Omega(v)
is Hermitian follows directly from the Pauli operators being Hermitian. We can compute

\displaystyle\Omega(v)^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}(PQ)^{\otimes v}=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\chi(P,R)}}R\big)^{\otimes v},

(112)

where we have defined
R\coloneqq\sqrt{\chi(P,Q)}PQ
and we have used that
\chi(P,Q)=\chi(P,R)
(because of
Lemma

18
).
Thus, we have

\displaystyle\Omega(v)^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\chi(P,R)^{|v|/2}R^{\otimes v}

(113)

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}R^{\otimes v}=\sum_{R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}R^{\otimes v}=d\Omega(v),&|v|\in 4\mathbb{N},\\
\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\bigg(\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\chi(P,R)\bigg)R^{\otimes v}=\sum_{R\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\delta_{R,\mathbb{1}}R^{\otimes v}=\mathbb{1}&|v|\in 4\mathbb{N}+2,\end{cases}

where we have used that
\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\chi(P,R)=d^{2}\delta_{R,\mathbb{1}}
.
For this, property A) and property B) follow directly.
Property C) follows straightforwardly from

\displaystyle P^{\otimes v_{1}}Q^{\otimes v_{2}}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{v_{1}\cdot v_{2}}Q^{\otimes v_{2}}P^{\otimes v_{1}},

(114)

where the commutator vanishes for
v_{1}\cdot v_{2}=0\pmod{2}
.

∎

From now on, we classify Pauli monomials as
even
(projectors) or
odd
(unitaries) depending on whether
\frac{|v|}{2}
is even or odd, respectively. Importantly, this classification is based on the parity of
\frac{|v|}{2}
, rather than on whether
|v|
itself is even or odd.
We remark that a specific type of Pauli monomial is given by the swap operator, which corresponds to an even vector
v
; see
Eq.

74
.

We are now ready to introduce the
Pauli monomials
, which generalize the primitive Pauli monomials introduced in
Definition

28
and arise from their products, as rigorously shown in
Section

V
.

Definition 30

(Pauli monomials)
.

Let
k,m\in\mathbb{N}
,
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
. A Pauli monomial, denoted
\Omega(V,M)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})
, is defined as

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{m}}P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}P_{2}^{\otimes v_{2}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}\right),

(115)

where
\chi(P_{i},P_{j})
is defined in
Lemma

18
.

Thus, the primitive Pauli monomial
\Omega(v)
for
v\in\mathbb{F}^{k}_{2}
, as defined in
Definition

28
, can be written as
\Omega(v)=\Omega((v),0)
, where
(v)
is the single-column matrix containing
v
as its column. Consequently, this structure hints at the role of the primitive Pauli monomials as fundamental building blocks of the set of Pauli monomials. Given a Pauli monomial, we refer to the linear combination of Pauli monomials as a
Pauli polynomial
.

An intriguing characteristic of Pauli monomials is that, while they are expressed as a sum of tensor products of Pauli operators, they can still be decomposed into a tensor product over individual qubits, as stated by the following lemma.

Lemma 31

(Tensor product structure of Pauli monomials)
.

Pauli monomials factorize as tensor products over qubits. Specifically, for any
\Omega(V,M)
, we have

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)

\displaystyle=\big(\omega(V,M)\big)^{\otimes n},

(116)

\displaystyle\omega(V,M)

\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{2^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{1}^{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}P_{i}^{\otimes v_{i}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}},

(117)

Proof.

We have

\displaystyle\big(\omega(V,M)\big)^{\otimes n}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2^{n})^{m}}\bigotimes_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{P}_{1}^{m}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{(l)\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi(P_{i}^{(l)},P_{j}^{(l)})^{M_{i,j}}\right)

(118)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2^{n})^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{P}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{P}_{1}^{m}}\bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}\left(\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{(l)\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi(P_{i}^{(l)},P_{j}^{(l)})^{M_{i,j}}\right)

(119)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2^{n})^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{P}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{P}_{1}^{m}}\left(\prod_{l=1}^{n}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi(P_{i}^{(l)},P_{j}^{(k)})^{M_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{b=1}^{m}\bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}P_{b}^{(l)\otimes v_{b}}.

Using the property
\chi(P_{1},Q_{1})\chi(P_{2},Q_{2})=\chi(P_{1}\otimes P_{2},Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2})
valid for Pauli operators
P_{1},P_{2},Q_{1},Q_{2}
, we get

\displaystyle\big(\omega(V,M)\big)^{\otimes n}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2^{n})^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{P}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{P}_{1}^{m}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi\left(\bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}P_{i}^{(l)},\bigotimes_{k=1}^{n}P_{j}^{(l)}\right)^{M_{i,j}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}\bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}P_{b}^{(l)\otimes v_{b}}

(120)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2^{n})^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}},

where in the last step we collected the sums into a single sum over
\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}=\big(\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}\big)^{\times m}
.
This matches the definition of
\Omega(V,M)
, concluding the proof.
∎

We now show that Pauli monomials belong to the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group.

Lemma 32

(Pauli monomials belong to the Clifford commutant)
.

Every Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
belongs to the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group.

Proof.

For all
C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}
, we have

\displaystyle C^{\dagger\otimes k}\Omega(V,M)C^{\otimes k}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}(C^{\dagger}P_{1}C)^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots(C^{\dagger}P_{m}C)^{\otimes v_{m}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}\right)

(121)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize\text{(i)}}}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{Q}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}Q_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots Q_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(C^{\dagger}Q_{i}C,C^{\dagger}Q_{j}C)^{M_{i,j}}\right)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize\text{(ii)}}}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{Q}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}Q_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots Q_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(Q_{i},Q_{j})^{M_{i,j}}\right)

\displaystyle=\Omega(V,M),

where in step
(i)
we have used that
C^{\dagger}P_{j}C=\pm Q_{j}
for each
j\in[m]
, and since
|v_{j}|=0\pmod{2}
, it follows that
(C^{\dagger}P_{j}C)^{\otimes v_{j}}=Q_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}.

In step
(ii)
, we have used the fact that if two matrices commute, their adjoint actions with respect to any unitary also commute.
∎

V.1
Graphical calculus to manipulate Pauli monomials

As a useful tool to enhance the reader’s understanding of Pauli monomials, we introduce a graphical representation that simplifies their manipulation.
This graphical calculus has applications beyond our focus on the Clifford commutant’s basis elements, proving useful in any context involving products of isotropic sums over tensor products of Pauli operators.

V.1.1
Pauli monomial diagrams

A Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
can be identified from the columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
of the binary matrix
V
, along with the matrix
M
, which encodes the ‘phase’ information, see
Definition

30
. To facilitate this identification, we now introduce in the following definition a graphical representation for keeping track of the columns of
V
and for the entries of
M
. For rapid understanding, refer to the example immediately following.

Definition 33

(Pauli monomial diagram)
.

Let
\Omega(V,M)
denote a Pauli monomial, where
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
, and
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
. The graphical representation is defined as

•

The columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
are depicted sequentially, where each column is represented as a vector of black and white dots corresponding to entries 1 and 0, respectively (see the following example for clarity).

•

Each off-diagonal element
M_{i,j}
of the matrix
M
is represented by a line (denoted
phase
) connecting the
i
-th and
j
-th columns if
M_{i,j}=1
, with no line drawn if
M_{i,j}=0
(again, see the next example).

Example 1
.

Consider
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, where
k=6
and
m=3
, and their corresponding Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
, as follows:

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)

\displaystyle=\Omega\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&0\\

\Omega(V,M)
can be written explicitly as

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}P_{2}^{\otimes v_{2}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,l\in[m]\\
j<l\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{j},P_{l})^{M_{j,l}}

(123)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{3}}\sum_{P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes(1,1,1,1,0,0)}P_{2}^{\otimes(1,1,1,1,1,1)}P_{3}^{\otimes(0,0,0,0,1,1)}\right)\chi(P_{1},P_{3})\chi(P_{2},P_{3})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{3}}\sum_{P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}}P_{1}P_{2}\otimes P_{1}P_{2}\otimes P_{1}P_{2}\otimes P_{1}P_{2}\otimes P_{2}P_{3}\otimes P_{2}P_{3}\times\chi(P_{1},P_{2})\chi(P_{2},P_{3})\quad.

Utilizing this diagrammatic representation, as we will see, will facilitate the execution of operations on Pauli monomials.

V.1.2
Substitution rules

Given a Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
, it is useful to establish rules for manipulating the matrices
V
and
M
in such a way that the Pauli monomial remains invariant. In particular, we focus on the case where Gaussian column operations (such as adding and swapping columns) are applied to
V
. Indeed, as we will see in full generality in
Theorem

37
,
\Omega(V,M)=\Omega(VA,M(A))
for any
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, where
M(A)
denotes a suitable transformation of the matrix
M
. At the level of
V
, this transformation corresponds to performing Gaussian column operations.

To start, we investigate the case where two nearest-neighbor columns of
V
are added, and we explore how the matrix
M
must be adjusted to maintain the invariance of the Pauli monomial under this transformation. Throughout, we will label a vector (
v
) odd or even based on the halved Hamming weight
\frac{|v|}{2}
.

Theorem 34

(Equivalence rule for adding columns in Pauli monomials)
.

Let
a_{\pm}\in[m]
denote either
a+1
or
a-1
, where
a
is a fixed index.
Let
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
be a matrix with columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
, where each
|v_{j}|=0\pmod{2}
, and let
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
be a symmetric matrix with a zero diagonal.

Define
V^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
, a matrix with columns
\{v^{\prime}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
, identical to those of
V
, except for the column
v^{\prime}_{a_{\pm}}
, which is defined as

v^{\prime}_{a_{\pm}}=v_{a}+v_{a_{\pm}},

(124)

where the addition is taken modulo 2.

Let
M^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
be a symmetric matrix with a zero diagonal, whose elements are identical to those of
M
, except for the following modifications:

\displaystyle M^{\prime}_{a,a_{\pm}}

\displaystyle=M_{a,a_{\pm}}+\frac{|v_{a}|}{2},

(125)

\displaystyle M^{\prime}_{j,a_{\pm}}

\displaystyle=M_{j,a_{\pm}}+M_{j,a},\quad\text{for any }j\in[m]\text{ such that }j\notin\{a,a_{\pm}\},

(126)

and their corresponding symmetric entries, ensuring that
M^{\prime}
remains symmetric.
The substitution
(V,M)\mapsto(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
leaves the corresponding Pauli monomial invariant, i.e.,

\Omega(V,M)=\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime}).

(127)

Proof.

Let us analyze the case in which
a_{\pm}=a+1
; the case
a_{\pm}=a-1
follows analogously.
We recall the definition of a Pauli monomial:

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\left(P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}P_{2}^{\otimes v_{2}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,l\in[m]\\
j<l\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{j},P_{l})^{M_{j,l}}.

(128)

Focusing on terms relevant to the substitution, we isolate the summation over
P_{a}
and
P_{a+1}
, to get

\displaystyle\sum_{P_{a},P_{a+1}}P_{a}^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes v_{a+1}}\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})^{M_{a,a+1}}\prod_{j\notin\{a,a+1\}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a})^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a+1,j}}.

(129)

Define the operator
R
as

\displaystyle R=P_{a}P_{a+1}\sqrt{\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})},

(130)

which belongs to the Pauli basis up to a
\pm 1
phase (see
Lemma

18
, Property 3).
Inverting the definition of
R
, we can rewrite
P_{a}
(up to a
\pm 1
phase) as

\displaystyle P_{a}\propto\sqrt{\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})}RP_{a+1}=\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})}RP_{a+1},

(131)

where, in the last step, we have used Property 3 of
Lemma

18
.

Substituting this expression for
P_{a}
into
Eq.

129
, recognizing that the global
\pm 1
phase does not affect the result since
|v_{a}|=0\pmod{2}
, and summing over
R
instead of
P_{a}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\sum_{R,P_{a+1}}\!\left(RP_{a+1}\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})}\right)^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes v_{a+1}}\chi(R,P_{a+1})^{M_{a,a+1}}\!\times\!\!\!\prod_{j\notin\{a,a+1\}}\!\!\!\chi(P_{j},RP_{a+1}\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})})^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a+1,j}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(i)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{R,P_{a+1}}\chi(R,P_{a+1})^{|v_{a}|/2+M_{a,a+1}}R^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes(v_{a}+v_{a+1})}\times\prod_{j\notin\{a,a+1\}}\chi(P_{j},RP_{a+1}\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})})^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a+1,j}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(ii)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{R,P_{a+1}}\chi(R,P_{a+1})^{|v_{a}|/2+M_{a,a+1}}R^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes(v_{a}+v_{a+1})}\times\prod_{j\notin\{a,a+1\}}\chi(P_{j},R)^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a+1,j}+M_{a,j}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(iii)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{P_{a},P_{a+1}}P_{a}^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes(v_{a}+v_{a+1})}\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})^{|v_{a}|/2+M_{a,a+1}}\times\prod_{j\notin\{a,a+1\}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a})^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a+1,j}+M_{a,j}},

where in step (i) we have used the identity

\displaystyle\left(\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})}\right)^{|v_{a}|}=\chi(R,P_{a+1})^{|v_{a}|/2},

(132)

and the fact that
P_{a+1}^{\otimes v_{a}}P_{a+1}^{\otimes v_{a+1}}=P_{a+1}^{\otimes(v_{a}+v_{a+1})}
.
In step (ii), we
have used the property

\displaystyle\chi(P_{j},RP_{a+1}\sqrt{\chi(R,P_{a+1})})^{M_{a,j}}=\chi(P_{j},RP_{a+1})^{M_{a,j}}=\chi(P_{j},R)^{M_{a,j}}\chi(P_{j},P_{a+1})^{M_{a,j}},

(133)

where, in the last step, we applied
\chi(P,QR)=\chi(P,Q)\chi(P,R)
(see
Lemma

18
, Property 2). In step (iii), we just renamed the variable from
R
to
P_{a}
.
∎

After introducing the notion of the sum between columns, it is useful to establish a rule that determines the parity of the sum of two columns based on the parity (even or odd) of the individual columns.

Lemma 35

(Parity of the sum of two columns)
.

Let
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
be two columns as defined above. The following relation holds:

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}|v_{1}+v_{2}|=\frac{1}{2}|v_{1}|+\frac{1}{2}|v_{2}|+v_{1}\cdot v_{2}\pmod{2}.

(134)

This relation leads to the following rules:

•

If
v_{1}\cdot v_{2}=0\pmod{2}
, then
v_{1}+v_{2}
is odd if exactly one of
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
is odd; otherwise, it is even.

•

If
v_{1}\cdot v_{2}=1\pmod{2}
, then
v_{1}+v_{2}
is even if exactly one of
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
is even; otherwise, it is odd.

Proof.

The quantity
|v_{1}+v_{2}|
counts the number of dots in
v_{1}+v_{2}
, that is the sum of dots in which
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
do not overlap.
That is, the number of dots in
v_{1}+v_{2}
is

\displaystyle|v_{1}+v_{2}|=|v_{1}|+|v_{2}|-2v_{1}\cdot v_{2},

(135)

from which the claim follows.
∎

From now on, we say that two columns
v_{1}
,
v_{2}
commute if
v_{1}\cdot v_{2}=0\pmod{2}
(which also implies that the respective Pauli monomials commute, see
Lemma

29
).

The rules introduced in
Theorem

34
provide the moves on such diagrams that leave the Pauli monomial invariant. Here we illustrate the graphical implementation of this rule.

(136)

We now demonstrate how the equivalence relation shown in
Theorem

34
can be implemented graphically. Specifically,
Theorem

34
describes how the matrix
M
should change when we add nearest-neighbor columns of
V
, to ensure that the Pauli monomial remains invariant.

If we add the first column to the second, the following ‘phases addition’ applies:

•

Add a phase if the vector being added is odd
: A phase is added between the first and second columns if
|v_{1}|=2\pmod{4}
, as dictated By
Eq.

125
of
Theorem

34
. (Note that if a phase already exists between these columns, it is removed, since
1+1=0\pmod{2}
.)

•

Add shared phases between columns
: Phases are added between the second column and any other column that shares a phase with the first column, as dictated by
Eq.

126
of
Theorem

34
.

Hence, the resulting equivalent diagram obtained by adding the first column to the second is

(138)

Let us now consider the case where two nearest-neighbor columns of
V
are swapped and investigate how the matrix
M
must be adjusted to ensure the invariance of the Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
. Although this rule can be derived from the previous one (e.g., by sequentially adding the first column to the second, then the second to the first, and again the first to the second), we provide a direct proof here for simplicity and clarity.

Theorem 36

(Swapping columns in Pauli monomials)
.

Let
a\in[m-1]
.
Let
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
have columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
, where
|v_{j}|=0\pmod{2}
, and let
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
be a symmetric matrix with a null diagonal.

Define
V^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m}
with the columns
\{v^{\prime}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
identical to those of
V
, except that columns
a
and
a+1
are swapped, i.e.,

v^{\prime}_{a}=v_{a+1}\quad\text{and}\quad v^{\prime}_{a+1}=v_{a}.

(139)

Define
M^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, a symmetric matrix with a null diagonal, whose elements are defined as those of
M
, apart from the element:

\displaystyle M^{\prime}_{a,a+1}

\displaystyle=M_{a,a+1}+v_{a}\cdot v_{a+1},

(140)

\displaystyle M^{\prime}_{j,a+1}

\displaystyle=M_{j,a}\quad\text{and}\quad M^{\prime}_{j,a}=M_{j,a+1}\quad\text{for any }j\in[m]\text{ such that }j\notin\{a,a+1\},

(141)

and its corresponding symmetric entries.

Then the substitution
(V,M)\mapsto(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
leaves the corresponding Pauli monomial invariant

\Omega(V,M)=\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime}).

(142)

Proof.

The invariance of the Pauli monomial follows directly from the fact that:

P^{\otimes v_{a}}_{a}P^{\otimes v_{a+1}}_{a+1}=\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})^{(v_{a}\cdot v_{a+1})}P^{\otimes v_{a+1}}_{a+1}P^{\otimes v_{a}}_{a},

(143)

where
\chi(P_{a},P_{a+1})
is the phase factor arising from the commutation relation between
P_{a}
and
P_{a+1}
.
Thus, swapping
v_{a}
and
v_{a+1}
in
V
introduces the phase adjustment
v_{a}\cdot v_{a+1}
into the matrix
M^{\prime}
.
∎

(Graphical implementation of
Theorem

36
)
.

Theorem

36
, which deals with the operation of swapping two nearest-neighbor columns.

Eq.

140

v_{2}
and
v_{3}
), an additional phase is introduced between these two columns if their overlap is one modulo 2 (i.e.,
v_{2}\cdot v_{3}=1\pmod{2}
), and each of these columns retains its previous phases when they are swapped.

(144)

With these two theorems in hand, we are now confident that arbitrary Gaussian-like column operations (i.e., addition and swapping of arbitrary columns) can be performed on the matrix
V
, with corresponding modifications to the matrix
M
, which can be derived by iteratively applying the previous two rules. Alternatively, general Gaussian operations can be tracked explicitly through the following result:

Theorem 37

(Arbitrary Gaussian-like column operations)
.

Let
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, and let
\Omega(V,M)
denote the corresponding Pauli monomial. Then, for any matrix
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, it holds that

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)=\Omega(VA,M(A))\,,

(145)

where
M(A)\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
is a function of the matrix
A
, determined as follows. Define

\displaystyle H

\displaystyle\coloneqq V^{T}V,

(146)

\displaystyle w_{i}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{|v_{i}|}{2},

(147)

\displaystyle\Lambda_{i,j}

\displaystyle\coloneqq M_{i,j}+w_{i}\delta_{i,j}+H_{i,j}\delta_{i<j},

(148)

where all operations are
\pmod{2}
. Then, for any
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, we obtain the transformations

\displaystyle\Lambda(A)

\displaystyle=A^{T}\Lambda A,

(149)

\displaystyle H(A)

\displaystyle=\Lambda(A)+\Lambda(A)^{T},

(150)

\displaystyle w_{i}(A)

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{i,i}(A),

(151)

\displaystyle M_{i,j}(A)

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{i,j}(A)\delta_{i>j}+\Lambda_{j,i}(A)\delta_{j>i}.

(152)

Proof.

First we note that the transformation
(w,M,H)\leftrightarrow\Lambda
is bijective, meaning we can transfer between them arbitrarily. Next, we note the action of
A
is decomposable
B^{T}\Lambda(A)B=\Lambda(AB)
. We can also use that every
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
can be decomposed into
A=\prod_{\alpha}(\mathbb{1}+E_{i_{\alpha},i_{\alpha}+(-1)^{s_{\alpha}}})
for some lists of integers and signs
(i_{\alpha},s_{\alpha})
, where
E_{i,j}
is the canonical matrix basis. Using the argument above it suffices to show that the generating transformation

\displaystyle(\mathbb{1}+E_{i\pm 1,i})\Lambda(\mathbb{1}+E_{i,i\pm 1})

\displaystyle=\Lambda+E_{i\pm 1,i}\Lambda+\Lambda E_{i,i\pm 1}+E_{i\pm 1,i}\Lambda E_{i,i\pm 1}

(153)

correctly preserves
(w,M,H)
. This corresponds to the elementary transformation of adding the
i
-th column vector to the
i\pm 1
-th. For
w
, we have

\displaystyle w_{j}\mapsto(A^{T}\Lambda A)_{j,j}=\Lambda_{j,j}+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}(\Lambda_{i,j}+\Lambda_{j,i}+\Lambda_{i,i})=w_{j}+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}(H_{i,j}+w_{i})

(155)

meaning that
w_{j}
is unchanged, unless the
j
-th column vector is added onto the
(j\pm 1)
-th, where it changes if the one added is an odd weight or the two primitives do not commute, as it is the requirement, see
Theorem

34
.
For
M
, we have for
j>k

\displaystyle M_{jk}

\displaystyle\mapsto M_{jk}+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}\Lambda_{i,k}+\delta_{k,i\pm 1}\Lambda_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}\delta_{k,i\pm 1}\Lambda_{i,i}

(156)

\displaystyle=M_{jk}+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}(\delta_{i,k}w_{i}+\delta_{i>k}M_{ik})+\delta_{k,i\pm 1}(\delta_{j,i}w_{i}+\delta_{j>i}M_{j,i})

(157)

\displaystyle=M_{jk}+w_{i}(\delta_{j,i\pm 1}\delta_{i,k}+\delta_{k,i\pm 1}\delta_{j,i})+\delta_{j,i\pm 1}M_{i,k}+\delta_{k,i\pm 1}M_{j,i}

(158)

which corresponds to adding the phases onto the
i\pm 1
-th column and row as well as changing the phase between
i\pm 1
if the respective
w_{i}
odd weight primitive as required. Finally, for
H
, we already know that
H(A)=A^{T}V^{T}VA=A^{T}(\Lambda+\Lambda^{T})A
transforms adjointly meaning that
H
and
\Lambda+\Lambda^{T}
transform identically.
∎

The above theorem establishes that a Pauli monomial remains invariant under column transformations
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
when applied appropriately and explicitly describes how these operations affect the matrix
M
.
Therefore, following the same approach as in
Definition

24
, we can define an equivalence relation for Pauli monomials. In fact, the substitution rules discussed above correspond precisely to exploring the equivalence class of a Pauli monomial.

We now present a theorem that encompasses several important properties derived from the aforementioned basic rules. These properties serve as the foundation for establishing the following key fact: primitive Pauli monomials generate the full commutant of the Clifford group, see
Section

IV
.

Theorem 38

(Graphical moves for Pauli monomials)
.

Consider a Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
, where
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
has columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
. The following properties hold:

(1)

Arbitrary Gaussian-elimination operations can be performed on the columns of the Pauli monomial diagram, by appropriately adjusting the phases.

(2)

If there exists an ‘odd’ column
v
(i.e.,
|v|=2\pmod{4}
) in the diagram, then it is possible to remove all phases attached to
v
and reposition
v
to any desired position by suitably modifying the remaining columns of
V
and
M
.

(3)

If we have linear dependence between the columns, by performing Gaussian-elimination operations on these columns, we can reduce
\Omega(V,M)
to
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
, which satisfies one of the following two cases:

•

There is a column
v=0
with no phase attached to it in the transformed diagram
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
. In this case, we can further reduce it to

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})=d\,\Omega(V_{r},M_{r}),

(159)

where
V_{r}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m-1}
and
M_{r}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m-1\times m-1}
are the matrices obtained by removing the respective column (and its associated rows) corresponding to
v
.

•

There is a column
v=0
with one or more phases attached to it in the transformed diagram
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
. In this case, we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})=\Omega(V_{r},M_{r}),

(160)

where
V_{r}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m-2}
and
M_{r}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m-2\times m-2}
are the matrices obtained by removing both the zero column
v
and the column connected to it through the phase (and their associated rows).

(4)

If there are two even non-identical columns that share a phase and commute (i.e., overlap in an even number of dots), they can be transformed into four odd columns without a phase. More specifically, the matrix
V
containing two even, commuting columns that share a phase can be converted into a new matrix
V^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times(m+2)}
, where these columns are replaced by four odd commuting columns that do not share any phases.

Proof.

We prove the properties one by one:

(1)

This is a restating of
Theorem

37
in diagram terminology, where Gaussian elimination on the columns of the diagram corresponds to permissible transformations that preserve the Pauli monomial structure, up to phases.

(2)

Assume there is an odd column
v
in the diagram, possibly with some phases attached. Begin by swapping this column to the leftmost position. During this process, additional phases may appear, but these are inconsequential for the argument.

Once
v
is in the first position, swap it with the second column. If a phase exists between the first and second columns after this swap, add the second column
v
to the first. Since
v
is odd (
|v|=2\pmod{4}
), this operation generates a new phase between the first and second columns, which cancels the pre-existing phase.

Repeat this process by swapping
v
from the second position to the third, and so on, always adding the now-swapped
v
to the left column if a phase exists between them. By continuing this procedure all the way to the rightmost position,
v
will have no attached phases and will occupy the far-right position.

To move
v
to any desired position, reverse the process: bring
v
leftward, adding to the right to removing phases as necessary to ensure that no phases remain attached to
v
at each step. This completes the proof of the second property.

Below is an example of such a procedure. Without loss of generality, assume that the column is already positioned on the leftmost side and we position it on the rightmost side without phases attached to it:

(161)

(3)

If there is linear dependence between the columns, we can, by virtue of property 1, perform Gaussian-elimination moves to transform the diagram into an equivalent form
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
, where at least one column is
v=0
.

There are three possible cases to consider: the column
v=0
has no phases attached to it, exactly one phase, or more than one phase. We analyze these cases one by one and explicitly show that the last case can always be reduced to one of the first two.
This will conclude the proof.

•

No attached phases: If a column
v=0
has no connected phases, it corresponds to a free sum contributing only a global factor. By
Definition

30
, this implies:

\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})=d\,\Omega(V_{r},M_{r}),

(162)

where
V_{r}
and
M_{r}
are obtained by removing the respective columns and rows of
v
. The factor
d
arises from the
d^{2}
-element sum, normalized by
1/d
.

•

One attached phase: If a column
v=0
has exactly one connected phase, the relation

\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}\chi(P,Q)=d\,\delta_{Q,\mathbb{1}}

(163)

ensures that the sum associated to the connected column vanishes. Consequently, we have

\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})=\Omega(V_{r},M_{r}),

(164)

where
V_{r}
excludes both the column
v=0
and the column associated with the phase.

•

Multiple attached phases: Without loss of generality, assume the first column is
v=0
, and subsequent columns have phases attached to it in order, followed by the columns that do not share any phase with the first zero column. This can be achieved without loss of generality through Gaussian elimination moves (column swaps). We will focus only on the phases interacting with the first zero column and disregard those between other columns.

For example, consider the following configuration:

(168)

At this stage, the system has effectively reduced to the case of a single attached phase, which we have already addressed.

(4)

If there are two even terms that share a phase and commute (overlap in an even number of dots modulo two), we can transform them into
4
odd commuting columns with no phase between them.

Let us explain the reason why. First, we can assume these terms to be nearest neighbors (due to Gaussian elimination moves). We can ‘add for free’ two identical two-dot columns with no phase next to these columns. This follows because it corresponds to applying two identical swap operators consecutively, which is equivalent to multiplying the monomial by the identity.

We are free to place such two-dot columns in any position, and the following argument remains essentially unchanged, provided that the added columns commute with both commuting primitives. In the example below, we place them where the two original columns both have dots. Such a position exists because the columns are assumed to overlap in an even number of points (i.e., at least two).

Next, we add the second column (now odd) to the first column (even). Since these two columns still overlap in an even number of dots (modulo two), the first column becomes odd after this transformation (By

(171)

At this point, we have four (commuting) odd columns, all commuting, but we still need to remove the introduced phases.

To remove the phases, recall that there is now a phase between the first column and the third, and between the second column and the third.
We begin by adding the second column (odd) to the third (odd). Since they commute, the third column becomes even after this addition (By
Lemma

35
), and we remove the phase (because adding an odd column add an additional phase).

In the example, this yields

(172)

Now, we are left with only the phase between the first and the second columns, but the third column is now even. To address this, we swap the first column to the second position. Since the columns commute, this introduces no additional phase.
Finally, we add the second column (odd) to the third (even), removing the remaining phase. After this, the third column becomes odd (By
Lemma

35
), and we achieve the desired configuration with no phases. We also observe that all columns commute, as the operations of swapping and summing even columns preserve the fact that they commute.
