V.2
Properties of Pauli monomials: reduction, normal form and inner product

Having outlined the substitution rules for Pauli monomials, we now use them to establish their fundamental properties.

We begin by introducing the notion of
reduced Pauli monomials
.

Definition 39

(Reduced Pauli monomial)
.

Let
\Omega(V,M)
be a Pauli monomial with
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
. We say that
\Omega(V,M)
is a reduced Pauli monomial if and only if
\rank(V)=m
, i.e., the column vectors of
V
are linearly independent.

At this point, one might question the reasoning behind introducing an extra set of Pauli monomials; however, this is justified by the following lemma.

Lemma 40

(Pauli monomial reduction)
.

Every Pauli monomial is proportional to a reduced Pauli monomial. More precisely, for any
\Omega(V,M)
with
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
, there exists a reduced Pauli monomial
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
with
V^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m^{\prime}})
with
m^{\prime}\leq m
, such that

\Omega(V,M)=d^{\alpha}\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime}),

(174)

where
\alpha\in\mathbb{N}
is a natural number such that
\alpha\leq m-m^{\prime}
.

Proof.

The statement descends from graphical rule (3) of
Theorem

38
. Specifically, in the presence of linear dependencies, we can perform Gaussian elimination to produce zero columns, which, without loss of generality, can be positioned at the beginning of the matrix. By then applying rule (3) from
Theorem

38
, we can further reduce the number of columns, repeating this process until no linear dependencies remain. This yields the desired result.
∎

Lemma

40
is crucial because it implies the existence of an essential set of Pauli monomials, to which all other monomials are proportional to, thereby allowing us to focus our analysis exclusively on the set of reduced Pauli monomials.

It is evident that reduced Pauli monomials differ based on the number of independent column vectors. Consequently, we can classify Pauli monomials according to the rank of the associated reduced Pauli monomials, leading to the concept of
order
.

Definition 41

(Order of Pauli monomials)
.

Let
\Omega(V,M)
be a Pauli monomial. Let
\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
be the reduced Pauli monomial corresponding to
\Omega
, i.e., there exists
\alpha
such that
\Omega(V,M)=d^{\alpha}\Omega(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
. The order of
\Omega
, hereby denoted as
m(\Omega)
, is defined as
m(\Omega)\coloneqq\rank(V')
.

Definition 42

(Set of reduced Pauli monomials)
.

We define the set of reduced Pauli monomials as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{P}\coloneqq\{\Omega(V,M)\,|\,V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})\,:\,\rank(V)=m\,,\,M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\,,\,m\in[k-1]\}\,.

(175)

Remark 43

(Representative Pauli monomials)
.

Two remarks about
Definition

42
are in order. First, by the definition of the set, only a single representative of the equivalence class
[V,M]\coloneqq\{(VA,M(A))\,:\,A\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\}
is sufficient to specify
\mathcal{P}
, similarly to
Definition

24
. Here,
M(A)
is defined in
Theorem

37
. Second, since we require
\operatorname{rank}(V)=m
, the corresponding Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
is reduced, as all the column vectors in
V
are linearly independent.

The following lemma determines the value of the trace of a general Pauli monomial.

Lemma 44

(Trace of Pauli monomials)
.

Let
\Omega
be a Pauli monomial with
\beta
many linear dependencies, corresponding to
m
many column vectors. It holds that

\displaystyle\tr(\Omega)=d^{k-m+2\beta}.

(176)

Proof.

Let us first assume that
\beta=0
, i.e., the Pauli monomial is reduced. For every
\Omega
there exists a transformation that puts
\Omega
in a pivotal structure, i.e.,
(V,M)\mapsto(V^{\prime},M^{\prime})
, where
V^{\prime}
contains pivotal vectors with no linear dependencies. As such, we can perform the trace starting from the first column of
V
. Since
(v_{1})_{1}=1
and
(v_{i})_{1}=0
for
i\neq 1
, this sets
P_{1}
to the identity, since
\tr(P)=d^{k}\delta_{I,P}
and there are no linear dependencies. Hence, the only term contributing is the all identity term. As
\tr(\mathbb{1})=d^{k}
, then we have
\tr(\Omega)=d^{k-m}
. Now, let us assume that
\beta>0
. By
Lemma

40
, every Pauli monomial can be reduced as
\Omega=d^{\alpha}\Omega_{R}
, with
\Omega_{R}\in\mathcal{P}
. Then,
\tr(\Omega)=d^{\alpha}\tr(\Omega_{R})=d^{k-(m(\Omega)-\alpha)}
, where
m(\Omega)
denotes the order of
\Omega
according to
Definition

41
. Iterating rule 3
Theorem

38
for
\beta
many linear dependencies, we know that
m(\Omega)-\alpha=m-2\beta
. Therefore, the result follows.
∎

After defining the concept of Pauli monomials and their reduction to a more compact set of components, comprehending their features remains crucial. To this end, let us introduce the notion of unitary and projective Pauli monomials.

Lemma 45

(Unitary and projective Pauli monomials)
.

Let
\Omega(V,0)\in\mathcal{P}
be a reduced Pauli monomial, where
V\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m}
with columns
\{v_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}
. The following hold:

•

If
V
consists exclusively of even column vectors satisfying
v_{i}\cdot v_{j}=0\pmod{2}
for
i\neq j
, then
\Omega(V,0)
, called
projective Pauli monomial
and denoted
\Omega_{P}(V)\coloneqq\Omega(V,0)
, satisfies
\Omega_{P}(V)/d^{m}
is a projector of rank
d^{k-2m}
.

•

If
V
consists exclusively of odd column vectors, then
\Omega(V,0)
, called
unitary Pauli monomial
and denoted
\Omega_{U}(V)\coloneqq\Omega(V,0)
, is a unitary operator.

We denote the set of reduced Pauli monomials which are unitary as
\mathcal{P}_{U}
, and reduced Pauli monomials which are projectors as
\mathcal{P}_{P}
.

Proof.

We can express
\Omega(V,0)
as

\displaystyle\Omega(V,0)=\Omega(v_{1})\cdots\Omega(v_{m}),

(177)

where
\{v_{j}\}^{m}_{j=1}
are the columns of
V
.
If the vectors
\{v_{j}\}^{m}_{j=1}
are all even, then, by
Lemma

29
, each
d^{-1}\Omega(v_{j})
is a projector (property A of
Lemma

29
). Additionally, since
v_{i}\cdot v_{j}=0\pmod{2}
for
i\neq j
, these projectors commute with each other (property C of
Lemma

29
). Since the product of commuting projectors is itself a projector, we can conclude that
\Omega(V,0)/d^{m}
is a projector. The rank of this projector is given by its trace:

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d^{m}}\tr(\Omega(V, 0))

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr(P_1^{\otimes v_1} P_2^{\otimes v_2} \cdots P_m^{\otimes v_m})

(178)

\displaystyle=d^{k-2m},

where the only non-zero contribution arises when
P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}P_{2}^{\otimes v_{2}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}
equals the identity. This occurs only when all Pauli matrices
P_{1},\dots,P_{m}
are themselves identities, which follows from the linear independence of
v_{1},\dots,v_{m}
(
Lemma

13
).

If the vectors
\{v_{j}\}^{m}_{j=1}
are all odd, then, by
Lemma

29
(property B), each
d^{-1}\Omega(v_{j})
is a unitary. Since the product of unitaries is also a unitary,
\Omega(V,0)
is a unitary operator.
∎

It is clear that when
V=(v)
, this notion reduces to what is shown in
Lemma

29
for primitive Pauli monomials.

Given this characterization of the Pauli monomials, we can provide a general decomposition for every Pauli monomial, which we refer to as
normal form
. For the sake of simplicity, we restrict ourselves to the case of reduced Pauli monomials (
Definition

39
), although it also holds for general Pauli monomials due to
Lemma

40
.

Lemma 46

(Normal form)
.

Let
\Omega(V,M)\in\mathcal{P}
be any reduced Pauli monomial. It can be decomposed as a product of a projective Pauli monomial and a unitary Pauli monomial as introduced in
Lemma

45
. Specifically:

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)=\Omega_{P}(V^{\prime})\times\Omega_{U}(V^{\prime\prime}),

(179)

where
\Omega_{P}(V^{\prime})
and
\Omega_{U}(V^{\prime\prime})
denote a projective and a unitary Pauli monomial, respectively.

Proof.

We consider a general reduced Pauli monomial
\Omega(V,M)
along with its associated Pauli diagram. The goal is to partition
V
into a left part (
V^{\prime}
), representing the
projective
component, and a right part (
V^{\prime\prime}
), representing the
unitary
component. The left part will consist of even commuting columns with no phases, while the right part will contain odd columns with no phases. The procedure is as follows:

•

Step 1: Move odd columns to the rightmost positions.

Examine the columns of
V
. For each odd column
(|v|=2\pmod{4})
, move it to the rightmost position among the remaining columns, ensuring no phase is attached, as guaranteed by rule
(2)
of
Theorem

38
. Fix this column in place, mark it as settled, and exclude it from further consideration. Continue this process until no odd columns remain in
V
.

This process terminates in at most
m
iterations, where
m
is the total number of columns in
V
. If all columns are moved to the right, then
\Omega(V,M)
is a unitary Pauli monomial, i.e.,
V^{\prime}=0
.

•

Step 2: Ensure the left part contains only even commuting columns.

After Step 1, the remaining columns on the left are even
(|v|=0\pmod{4})
. If any of these columns do not commute, add one to another as prescribed By
Lemma

35
. By doing so, any odd column resulting from the sum can be moved to the rightmost position without a phase, as in Step 1. Repeat this process until all remaining columns on the left are even and commute with each other.

•

Step 3: Eliminate phases between even commuting columns.

If the left part contains even commuting columns with non-zero phases, proceed as follows (otherwise, we can conclude the proof). First, bring the two columns with a phase between them close to each other and position such column pairs in the rightmost part of the left part.
Next, apply rule (4) of
Theorem

38
to transform the two even commuting columns into four commuting odd columns with no phases between them. These four odd columns may share phases with other columns in the left part. To remove these phases, take each of the four odd columns in turn and use rule (1) of
Theorem

38
to eliminate the phase, keeping the column fixed in its position. Since these columns commute with each other, they can then be moved to the right part as part of the
unitary
component.

After this process, the left part loses two columns, while the right part gains four odd columns. Any odd columns created in the left part during this process are moved to the rightmost positions as in Step 1. Repeat this procedure until the left part contains only even commuting columns with no phases.

This iterative procedure ensures that
V^{\prime}
and
V^{\prime\prime}
are properly partitioned into the projective and unitary components, respectively, satisfying the conditions of the lemma. The process terminates in a finite number of steps, as each iteration strictly reduces the number of columns of the left part.
This concludes the proof.
∎

Therefore, any reduced Pauli monomial
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}
can be expressed as
\Omega=\Omega_{P}\Omega_{U}
, where
\Omega_{P}\in\mathcal{P}_{P}
and
\Omega_{U}\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
. The following proposition determines the order of these respective monomials (see
Definition

41
).

Proposition 47
.

Let
\Omega
be a reduced Pauli monomial, reading
\Omega=\Omega_{P}\Omega_{U}
in normal form, where
\Omega_{P}
(resp.
\Omega_{U}
) are the corresponding projective (resp. unitary) Pauli monomials. Then,
their order satisfies (cf.
Definition

41
)

\displaystyle m(\Omega_{P})

\displaystyle=\dim(\mathrm{kern}(\Lambda(\Omega)),

(180)

\displaystyle m(\Omega_{U})

\displaystyle=\dim(\Lambda)-\dim(\mathrm{kern}(\Lambda(\Omega))=\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda),

(181)

where
\Lambda(\Omega)
is defined in
Theorem

37
.

Proof.

In
Lemma

46
, we showed that any reduced monomial
\Omega
can be expressed as the product of a projective and a unitary monomial,
\Omega=\Omega_{P}\Omega_{U}
. In particular,
\Omega_{P}
is reduced, whereas
\Omega_{U}
may not be.

We observe that for step 3 of
Lemma

46
to succeed, it suffices to add two new permutations commuting with any other primitive. This eliminates the phase from the even commuting columns, effectively rendering them unitary. A convenient strategy is to introduce two additional registers (i.e., increasing the number of copies from
k
to
k+2
) and place the new permutations there. By construction, these columns commute with all others. In this setting, we can write
\Lambda\mapsto\Lambda\oplus\mathbb{1}_{2}
.

Now, by
Lemma

46
, there exists a matrix
A\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
such that the transformation
\Lambda\oplus\mathbb{1}_{2}\mapsto A^{T}(\Lambda\oplus\mathbb{1}_{2})A
yields an upper triangular matrix. In the unitary part of the normal form, the unitary primitives have a
1
on the diagonal, implying that the corresponding columns are linearly independent. In contrast, the projectors have a
0
on the diagonal and commute with one another. Consequently, the corresponding columns are all-zero columns, meaning that all and only the projective primitives contribute to the kernel dimension. Hence,
m(\Omega_{P})=\dim\ker\left(A^{T}(\Lambda\oplus\mathbb{1}_{2})A\right)=\dim\ker(\Lambda\oplus\mathbb{1}_{2})=\dim\ker(\Lambda)
. Therefore, we have
m(\Omega_{U})=m(\Omega)-m(\Omega_{P})=m-\dim\left(\ker(\Lambda)\right)
, which proves the statement.
∎

As a consequence, we have the following corollary about the Hilbert-Schmidt product between Pauli monomials.

Corollary 48

(Hilbert-Schmidt inner product between Pauli monomials)
.

Let
\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}
be two reduced Pauli monomials. Their Hilbert-Schmidt inner product obeys

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(\Omega^\dagger\Omega')=\begin{cases}d^{k},\quad\Omega=\Omega^{\prime},\\
\leq\min\{d^{k-m(\Omega)-m(\Omega^{\prime})+2\min\{m(\Omega),m(\Omega^{\prime})\}},d^{k-2}\},\quad\Omega\neq\Omega^{\prime}.\end{cases}

(182)

Further, notice that
k-m(\Omega)-m(\Omega^{\prime})+2\min\{m(\Omega),m(\Omega^{\prime})\}\leq k-1
. Moreover,
\tr(\Omega^\dagger\Omega')\geq 1
.

Proof.

To show that
\tr(\Omega^\dagger\Omega)=d^{k}
, we make use of
Lemma

46
, i.e., that any reduced Pauli monomials
\Omega(V,M)
can be expressed in
normal form
as
\Omega=\Omega_{P}\Omega_{U}
. We have

\displaystyle\tr(\Omega^\dagger\Omega)=\tr(\Omega_U^\dagger\Omega_P^\dagger\Omega_P\Omega_U)=\tr(\Omega_P^\dagger\Omega_P)=\tr(\Omega_P^2)=d^{m(\Omega_{P})}\tr(\Omega_P)=d^{m(\Omega_{P})}d^{k-m(\Omega_{P})}=d^{k}\,.

(183)

where we have used that
\Omega_{P}
is Hermitian. Now, let us tackle the case
\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')
for which
\Omega\neq\Omega^{\prime}
. It is evident that
\Omega^{{\dagger}}\Omega^{\prime}
is a, potentially not reduced, Pauli monomial with
m(\Omega)+m(\Omega^{\prime})
many columns. Denoting
\beta
the number of linear dependencies of the monomial
\Omega^{{\dagger}}\Omega^{\prime}
, by
Lemma

44
, we know that
\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')=d^{k-(m(\Omega)+m(\Omega^{\prime})+2\beta}
. The number of linear dependencies obeys to
\beta\leq\min(m(\Omega),m(\Omega^{\prime}))
if
m(\Omega)\neq m(\Omega^{\prime})
. Otherwise,
\beta\leq m(\Omega)-1
.
∎

V.3
Alternative basis for the commutant: Graph and algebraically independent Pauli monomials

In this section, we define two alternative representations of Pauli polynomials, namely graph-based Pauli monomials and algebraically independent Pauli monomials (which we already introduced in
Section

IV
). Here, instead of summing over all Pauli operators, we restrict the sum to only consider Pauli operators with a certain anticommmutation relation and/or Pauli operators that are algebraically independent (i.e., cannot be written as products of each other). These representations have the advantage that they form Hilbert-Schmidt orthogonal operators, which is a useful property for twirling and the Weingarten calculus. They also have drawbacks, most notably, they do not factorize on qubits, meaning that the structure is way more dependent on the number of qubits. In this section, first, we define the different representations and show that they can be bijectively transformed into each other.

V.3.1
Definition of alternative basis

Let us start by introducing the definition of Graph-based Pauli monomial. We note that we use different scaling conventions here, as this allows for a better relation between various bases of the commutant.

Definition 49

(Graph-based Pauli monomials)
.

Let
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
, and
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
. The graph-based Pauli monomials is defined as

\mho(V,G)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}\\
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\end{subarray}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}},

(184)

where
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})
denotes the adjacency matrix of the anticommmutation graph (as defined in
Definition

12
) associated with the set
\{P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}\}
. We denote the set of graph-based Pauli monomials as
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
, to reflect the fact that the two sets are connected by a binary Fourier transform, as we will show later in
Lemma

51
.

An equivalent formulation of
\mho(V,G)
is

\displaystyle\mho(V,G)=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})}{2}\right)

(185)

which can be verified as the latter term gives
\delta_{\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G}
.
We conclude our set of definitions on graph-based Pauli monomials, by introducing the notion of algebraically independent graph-based Pauli monomials.

Definition 50

(Independent graph-based Pauli monomials)
.

Let
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
be a symmetric binary matrix, and
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
. We define independent graph-based Pauli monomials as

\displaystyle\mho_{I}(V,G)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S_{[V,G]}|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\\
\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{P})=G,\\
\mathbf{P}\textrm{ alg ind. }\end{subarray}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}

(186)

i.e., the sum runs over the set of algebraically independent Pauli operators
P=(P_{1},\ldots,P_{m})
.
Notice that
\mho_{I}(V,G)\propto\mho_{I}([V,G])
holds, introduced in
Section

IV
. In particular, the proportionality factor is a phase
\{\pm 1,\pm i\}
that is uniquely determined by a choice of the representative
V
.

V.3.2
Transformations of different Pauli monomials

Thus far, we have introduced various notions of Pauli monomials. Since the set of monomials remains the same, a transformation between these definitions must exist. In the following lemmas, we show that such transformations do exist.

Lemma 51

(Linear transformation between Pauli and graph-based monomials)
.

Let
\Omega(V,M)
denote a Pauli monomial (
Definition

30
) and
\mho(V,G)
a graph-based Pauli monomial (
Definition

49
). The following ‘Fourier transform’ expresses the linear transformation between these two representations:

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}\mho(V,G),

(187)

\displaystyle\mho(V,G)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\binom{k}{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}\Omega(V,M).

(188)

Here, the summation in both equations runs over all symmetric
m\times m
matrices
M
or
G
with zero diagonal entries.

Proof.

To prove the lemma, we verify the validity of the transformations. We first confirm
Eq.

187
as

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}):\\
\mathrm{diag}(G)=0\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}\mho(V,G)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(i)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\end{subarray}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})}{2}(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

(189)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\end{subarray}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})}{2}(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(ii)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\end{subarray}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{1+\chi(P_{i},P_{j})+(-1)^{M_{i,j}}(1-\chi(P_{i},P_{j}))}{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{\mbox{\scriptsize(iii)}}}}{{=}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\end{subarray}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle=\Omega(V,M).

In step (i), we have used
Eq.

185
. In step (ii), we
have employed the identity

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}):\\
\mathrm{diag}(G)=0\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\left(1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\sum_{G_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}}\left(1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

(190)

\displaystyle=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\left(\left(1+\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)+\left(1-\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)(-1)^{M_{i,j}}\right).

Finally, in step (iii), we have used the case distinction

\displaystyle\left(1+\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)+\left(1-\chi(P_{i},P_{j})\right)(-1)^{M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}2&\text{if }M_{i,j}=0,\\
2\chi(P_{i},P_{j})&\text{if }M_{i,j}=1,\end{cases}

(191)

\displaystyle=2\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}.

(192)

Similarly, we verify
Eq.

188

as

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\binom{k}{2}}\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}):\\
\mathrm{diag}(M)=0\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\Omega(V,M)\times(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\binom{k}{2}}\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}):\\
\mathrm{diag}(M)=0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}

(193)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m}):\\
\mathrm{diag}(M)=0\end{subarray}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}(-1)^{G_{i,j}M_{i,j}}}{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\end{subarray}}\prod_{b=1}^{m}P_{b}^{\otimes v_{b}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\frac{1+(-1)^{G_{i,j}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})}{2}

\displaystyle=\mho(V,G),

where in the final step, we have again used
Eq.

185
. This completes the proof.
∎

Lemma 52
.

There exists a bijective transformation between the sets of operators
\mho_{I}(V,M)
and
\mho(V,M)
.

Proof.

First, we observe that the definition of graph-based monomials in
Definition

49
and the definition of independent graph-based monomials in
Definition

50
are identical (up to a constant), except for the additional requirement in the latter that the set of Pauli operators must be linearly independent. Consequently, starting from
\mho(V,G)
, we can write

\displaystyle\mho(V,G)=\frac{|S_{[V,G]}|}{d^{m}}\mho_{I}(V,G)+\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\\
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\\
\boldsymbol{P}\text{ not linear ind.}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in[m]}P_{i}^{\otimes v_{i}}.

(194)

Let us analyze the second term. If the set of Pauli operators
\boldsymbol{P}
is not algebraically independent, there exists at least one linear relation within the set
\boldsymbol{P}
. As such, we can express
P_{k}=\theta\prod_{i\neq k}P_{i}^{a_{i}}
, where
\theta\in\{\pm i,\pm 1\}
. Notably,
\theta^{2}
depends only on the anticommutation graph
G
(as we show in
Lemma

18
) of
\boldsymbol{P}
and, since
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
, only
\theta^{2}
appears. We can, therefore, rewrite

\displaystyle\prod_{i\in[m]}P_{i}^{\otimes v_{i}}=\phi(G)\prod_{i\in[m]\backslash k}P_{i}^{\otimes(v_{i}+a_{i}v_{k})}

(195)

where the proportionality factor depends on the anticommmutation graph
G
originating from permuting the Pauli operators in the product to the correct spot. We can reiterate the argument in the presence of more than one algebraic relations. We can, therefore, write

\displaystyle\mho(V,G)=\frac{\Phi_{V}|S_{[V,G]}|}{d^{m}}\mho_{I}(V,G)+\sum_{a\in\text{lin relations}}\frac{\phi_{a}(G)|S_{[V_{a},G_{a}]}|}{d^{m}}\mho_{I}(V_{a},G_{a})

(196)

where
m_{a}<m
and
\phi_{a}(G)
only depends on the anticommmutation graph
G
.
Eq.

196
proves that there exists a map
\{\mho_{I}(V,G)\}\rightarrow\{\mho(V,G)\}
. This map is also bijective. To prove it, we note that for
m=0
, we have that
\mho_{I}(0,0)=\mho(0,0)=\mathbb{1}
. Then, by induction, we simply note that if one can generate all
\mho_{I}(V,G)
from
\mho(V,G)
for
m=m^{\prime}-1
, we can invert
Eq.

196
and get all the
\mho_{I}(V,M)
for
m=m^{\prime}
:

\displaystyle\frac{\Phi_{V}|S_{[V,G]}|}{d^{m}}\mho_{I}([V,G])=\mho(V,G)-\sum_{a}\frac{\phi_{a}(G)|S_{[V_{a},G_{a}]}|}{d^{m}}\mho_{I}(V_{a},G_{a}).

(197)

This shows that we can generate all the set
\{\mho_{I}(V,G)\}
from
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
, and, therefore, the map is bijective.
∎

Corollary 53
.

The sets
\mathcal{P}
,
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
,
\{\mho_{I}([V,G])\}_{[V,G]}
generate the same vector space, i.e.,

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{P})=\operatorname{span}(\hat{\mathcal{P}})=\operatorname{span}(\{\mho_{I}([V,G])\}_{[V,G]}).

(198)

Proof.

The proof follows from the fact that there exists a bijective correspondence between
\mathcal{P}
and
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
by
Lemma

51
, and similarly, a bijective correspondence between
\hat{\mathcal{P}}
and
\{\mho_{I}(V,G)\}
by
Lemma

52
. Moreover, we have that
\mho_{I}(V,G)=\Phi_{V}\mho_{I}([V,G])
for a choice of representative
V
.
∎

V.4
Pauli monomials form a basis of the commutant

In this section, building on the results of
Sections

V
and
IV
, we demonstrate that Pauli monomials form a basis for the Clifford commutant.

The next corollary shows that the set of reduced Pauli monomials as defined in
Definition

42
span all the commutant of the Clifford group, and are independent provided that
k\leq n+1
.

Corollary 54

(Reduced Pauli monomials form a basis of the commutant)
.

The span of set of reduced Pauli monomials
\mathcal{P}
is the commutant of the Clifford group

\displaystyle\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{P})=\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k});

(199)

moreover, if
k\leq n+1
, then
\mathcal{P}
contains linearly independent operators and thus
\mathcal{P}
provides a basis of
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
.

Proof.

Both claims follow directly from
Corollaries

53
and
25
, as together they establish a bijective transformation between the set of operators
\mho_{I}([V,G])
, which constitute a basis for
\rank_{2}(G)\geq 2(m-n)
trivially (verified for
k\leq n+1
).
∎

VI
The Clifford commutant is generated by permutations and three fundamental operators

VI.1
The Clifford commutant is generated by only three additional elements

In this section, building on the formalism of Pauli monomials introduced in
Section

V
, we state and prove one of the main results of this work. The following theorem shows that the
k
-th order Clifford group commutant is generated by only three additional elements compared to the commutant of the full unitary group, namely the primitives corresponding to
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 4}
,
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 6}
, and, if
k
is a multiple of
4
, also
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes k}
.
In this sense—as already observed for the specific case
k=4
in Ref.
Zhu et al. 2016a
, which showed that the Clifford group fails “gracefully” to be a unitary 4-design—we show that the Clifford group fails gracefully to be a unitary
k
-design for
any

k
, thereby providing a natural generalization of this result.

Theorem 55

(The
k
-th order Clifford group commutant is generated by only three additional elements)
.

Let
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
be the commutant of the Clifford group.

(i)

All Pauli monomials are generated by

\Omega_{4}\coloneqq\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes 4},\quad\Omega_{6}\coloneqq\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes 6},\quad\text{and, if $k$ is divisible by 4,}\quad\Omega_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes k},

(200)

and permutations.

(ii)

All unitary Pauli monomials are generated by
\Omega_{6}
and permutations.

(iii)

Every reduced Pauli monomial
\Omega
can be generated by the product of at most
\min(m(\Omega)+4,k+1)
many primitives.

Proof.

First of all, let us notice that, with
\Omega_{4},\Omega_{6}
and
\Omega_{k}
and permutations, we can generate every primitive
\Omega(v)
with
|v|=4,6,k
.
Then, thanks to the result of
Lemma

46
, we know that any reduced Pauli monomial
\Omega
can be written as
\Omega=\Omega_{P}\Omega_{U}
with
\Omega_{U}\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
and
\Omega_{P}\in\mathcal{P}_{P}
, a unitary and projective Pauli monomial, see
Lemma

45
. This result automatically implies that the commutant of the Clifford group is generated by products of primitives
\Omega(v)
with
|v|\in[k]
. We are therefore just left to show that we can generate every primitive Pauli monomial by
\Omega_{4}
and
\Omega_{6}
and permutations. First, we show that we can generate
\Omega(v^{\prime})
from
\Omega(v)
with
|v^{\prime}|=|v|+4
and two
\Omega_{6}
(up to the adjoint action of permutations), using one extra register, as the following diagrammatic calculation shows:

(201)

Since, in the above diagrammatic calculation, we only use the property that the middle primitive anticommmutes with the two
\Omega_{6}
, we can generate all
\Omega(v)
with
|v|=0\pmod{2}
from
\Omega_{4}
,
\Omega_{6}
, and permutations using one extra register. This only leaves
\Omega_{k}
if
k
is even, which cannot be generated by this method, because there is no extra register to be used, and it commutes with all other primitives.

Let us see how to generate
\Omega_{k}
. It turns out that there are two cases.

•

If
k=4\mathbb{N}
, then the primitive
\Omega_{k}
is a projector (see
Lemma

29
) and, as we show below, it cannot be generated by lower order primitives.
To proceed with the proof, let assume, towards contradiction, that we can create
\Omega_{v_{k}}
by lower primitives as

\displaystyle\Omega_{k}\propto\prod_{m}\Omega(v_{m})

(202)

where
|v_{m}|<k
, and the proportionality factor arises from the fact that the product of lower-order primitives may not be reducible (cf.
Definition

39
). Using
Theorem

38
, we then move all unitary primitives to the right and result in the following expression:

\displaystyle\Omega_{k}\propto\prod_{m}\Omega_{P}(v^{\prime}_{m})\times\prod_{m}\Omega_{U}(v^{\prime\prime}_{m})

(203)

where
\Omega_{P}(v_{m}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{P}
and
\Omega_{U}(v_{m}^{\prime\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
for every
m
. We note that this process cannot generate an
\Omega_{k}
primitive, since
\Omega_{k}
commutes with everything. Hence we have
|v_{m}^{\prime}|<k
for every
v_{m}^{\prime}
. Consequently, we have
\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{P}\times\Omega_{U}
, where
\Omega_{P}
is the product of commuting non-full-weight primitives. Notably,
\Omega_{P}
may be non-reduced, meaning that
\Omega_{P}=d^{\alpha}\Omega^{\prime}_{P}
, as stated in
Lemma

40
. Thus, we obtain

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega_{k}\propto\Omega_{P}^{\prime}\Omega_{U}.

(204)

Now, multiplying both sides by the conjugate—specifically,
\Omega_{k}
on the left and
(\Omega_{P}^{\prime}\Omega_{U})^{{\dagger}}
on the right—we arrive
at

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptd\Omega_{k}\propto d^{\alpha}\Omega_{P}^{\prime},

(205)

where we have used the fact that
\Omega_{U}
is a unitary operator. However,
since both
\Omega_{k}
and
\Omega_{P}^{\prime}
are reduced, it follows that
\Omega_{k}=\Omega_{P}^{\prime}
, which contradicts our initial assumption that
|v_{m}|<k
. This establishes the contradiction.

•

If
k=4\mathbb{N}+2
, then
\Omega_{k}
is unitary and can be generated as a product of lower-order primitives. Therefore, it lies in the algebra generated by,
\Omega_{4}
,
\Omega_{6}
, and permutations as shown by the diagrammatic calculation.

. The weight of the first primitive can be arbitrary, as long as it is unitary.

The above reasoning thus shows items (i) and (ii).

Let us prove item (iii). For the minimal number of terms, we proceed as in the normal form proof, see
Lemma

46
. Hence, we can write every monomial as

\displaystyle\Omega=\Omega_{P}\tilde{\Omega}\Omega_{U}

(207)

where
\Omega_{P}\in\mathcal{P}_{P}
, i.e., is a multiplication of even commuting primitives with no phase,
\Omega_{U}\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
i.e., is a product of odd primitives and
\tilde{\Omega}
is a monomial of commuting projective primitives, which share a phase. The form in
Eq.

207
is obtained right before Step 3 of the proof of
Lemma

46
. We note that, through
Theorem

38
, we can always write
\tilde{\Omega}
as products of
pairs
of commuting projective primitives with a phase. An example of this kind is provided below.

(208)

Crucially, to obtain the product form in
Eq.

207
, the number
r
of primitives is
r=m(\Omega)
, which corresponds to the order of the reduced monomial
\Omega
. Indeed, is only after Step 3 of
Lemma

46
that the number of primitives increases. Indeed, Step 3 consists of adding commuting permutations and then expanding the product of two even-commuting primitives sharing a phase into four unitaries. However, this approach is suboptimal in the present case, as our goal is to develop a strategy that minimizes the number of primitives. To address this, let us carefully analyze the problem. First, we identify two possible scenarios that may arise.

(a)

\Omega_{U}\neq\mathbb{1}
. First, we observe that if there exists a primitive
\Omega(u)
in the decomposition of
\Omega_{U}
that commutes with every element of every pair in
\tilde{\Omega}
, then, by Rule (4) of
Theorem

38
, we can decompose
\tilde{\Omega}
into a product of unitaries, resulting in
r=\tilde{m}
with no additional cost in terms of primitives.

We can then assume that there exists an
\Omega(u)
in the decomposition of
\Omega_{U}
that does not commute
with at least one element of some pairs in
\tilde{\Omega}
. Note that if
{\Omega}_{u}
does not commute with both elements of a given pair, we can sum the elements of the pair, ensuring that only one of them fails to commute with
\Omega(u)
. Suppose that there are at least two pairs whose elements do not commute with
\Omega(u)
, and, without loss of generality, consider the first element of each pair as the non-commuting one. In this case, summing the first elements of each pair together and the second elements of each pair together results in one completely commuting pair and one pair where only the first element does not commute. This implies that, without loss of generality, we can assume that in
\tilde{\Omega}
there is exactly one pair of even-commuting primitives sharing a phase that does not commute with
\Omega(u)
(or any other odd primitive in
\Omega_{U}
). If this holds, we simply apply Rule (4) of
Theorem

38
, adding two commuting permutations and generating four unitaries from the non-commuting pair, while using
\Omega(u)
to unfold all other pairs at no additional cost. Consequently, this case results in a total number of primitives
r=m(\Omega)+2
.

(b)

\Omega_{U}=\mathbb{1}
. In this case, we apply Rule (4) of
Theorem

38
, adding two permutations to unfold, without loss of generality, the first pair of even-commuting primitives in
\tilde{\Omega}
, thereby creating four unitaries in the process. At this stage,
\Omega_{U}\neq\mathbb{1}
, allowing us to proceed as in case (i). This procedure ultimately results in a total number of primitives
r=m(\Omega)+4
.

Let us then bound the total number of primitives by considering two distinct scenarios.

In the first scenario (A), in the worst case, we have
m(\Omega)=k-1
, and therefore the number of primitives satisfies
r\leq(k-1)+2=k+1
.

In the second scenario (B), since
\Omega_{U}=\mathbb{1}
from the outset, the worst case corresponds to having all commuting primitives contained in
\Omega_{P}
and
\tilde{\Omega}
. However, the maximum number of commuting primitives is
\frac{k}{2}
, and thus
r\leq\frac{k}{2}+4\leq k
for any
k\geq 8
. Item (iii) thus follows.

For the second scenario (B), we can also construct an example that cannot be generated using only
m(\Omega)+2
generators unless we extend
k\rightarrow k+2
. Such an example can be constructed for
k=8
to be
