(209)

Here, no unitary primitive commutes with all four operators. Consequently, constructing it requires the product of four additional primitives.
∎

Let us point out that, due to
Corollary

54
,
Theorem

55
provides not only a set of generators for the set of Pauli monomials but also a set of generators for the Clifford commutant.

VI.2
Equivalence of basis

In this section, building on
Theorem

55
, we provide a brief argument supporting the claim that the basis of Pauli monomials, introduced in
Definition

30
, precisely coincides with the basis found in Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
. Let us first recall the main result given in Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
.

Proposition 56

(Commutant basis of Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
)
.

Let
T\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}\times\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}
be a subspace. Labelling the elements of
T
as
(x,y)
for
x,y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}
,
T
is a Lagrangian subspace if the following conditions are met:

(i)

|x|=|y|\pmod{4}
for all
(x,y)\in T
;

(ii)

\dim(T)=k
;

(iii)

(1,1,\ldots,1)\in T
.

For every
n\geq k-1
, the following operators

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptR(T)=\left(\sum_{(x,y)\in T}\outerproduct{x}{y}\right)^{\otimes n}

(210)

form a basis of the Clifford commutant
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
.

In the next lemma, we show that the above mentioned basis corresponds to the basis of Pauli monomials.

Lemma 57

(Equivalence of basis)
.

The basis
\{R_{T}\}
corresponds to the set
\mathcal{P}
.

Proof.

To prove this result, we proceed in a few steps. First, in the proof of Lemma 4.25 of Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
, it has been established that the product of any two operators satisfies
R(T_{1})R(T_{2})\propto R(T)
for some Lagrangian subspace
T
.

Next, the primitive Pauli monomials
\Omega({v_{m}})
(see
Definition

28
) correspond to what the authors of Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
define as the
antiidentity

\bar{\mathbb{1}}_{m}
(see, e.g., Eq. (1.4) in Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
). Hence, we have the relation
R(\bar{\mathbb{1}}_{m})=\Omega({v_{m}})
. In
Theorem

55
, we showed that at most three fundamental primitive Pauli monomials (up to permutations), namely
\Omega_{4}
,
\Omega_{6}
, and
\Omega_{k}
, generate the set
\mathcal{P}
. Since the set
\{R(T)\}
is closed under multiplication, it follows that the above primitives generate a subset of
\{R(T)\}
. Therefore, we immediately obtain the inclusion
\mathcal{P}\subseteq\{R(T)\}
.

However, since the set
\mathcal{P}
contains linearly independent operators (for
n\geq k-1
) that span
\operatorname{Comm}(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, as shown in
Corollary

54
, and since the set
\{R(T)\}
also contains linearly independent operators (for
n\geq k-1
) that span
\operatorname{Comm}(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, we must conclude that
\mathcal{P}=\{R(T)\}
.

∎

VII
Applications and examples

This section explores several applications and examples based on the Clifford commutant. We begin by introducing the Haar average over the Clifford group in
Section

VII.1
. Next, we establish a connection between magic state resource theories and the Clifford commutant in
Section

VII.2
. We then demonstrate how the Clifford commutant serves as a useful tool to characterize the property testing of stabilizer states in
Section

VII.3
. Following this, we extend our discussion to group-symmetric states, where the group we consider is the Clifford group. Finally, we conclude with a few examples in
Section

VII.5
, considering the Clifford commutant for values of
k
ranging from 4 to 8.

VII.1
Haar average over the Clifford group

In this section, we provide the essential tools to compute the averages of the Clifford group, one of the key applications of the Clifford group commutant.

VII.1.1
Twirling over the Clifford group

Let us provide an explicit expression for the twirling operator (see
Eq.

23
) over the Clifford group, for any
n
and
k
, as a direct of
Theorem

25
.

Corollary 58

(Twirling operator over the Clifford group)
.

Let
n,k>0
. Consider the twirling operator, defined in
Eq.

57
, applied on
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})
. Then,
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)
belongs to
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, and can be expressed as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)=\sum_{\mho_{I}([V,G])}\frac{\tr[O\mho_{I}([V,G])]}{\|\mho_{I}([V,G])\|_{2}^{2}}\mho_{I}([V,G])\,,

(211)

where the
2
-norm of the operators
\mho_{I}([V,G])
is computed in
Lemma

27
.

Proof.

Given that the twirled operator
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)
belongs to the commutant of the Clifford group, it can be expressed as a linear combination of basis elements. In particular, we can use the orthogonal basis formed by the operators
\mho_{I}([V,G])
for
V\in\mathrm{Even}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times m})
and
G\in\mathrm{Sym}_{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m})
with
\rank_{2}(G)\geq 2(m-n)
, see
Theorem

25
. Therefore, we can express the twirled operator as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)=\sum_{\mho_{I}([V,G])}b_{\mho_{I}([V,G])}\mho_{I}([V,G])\,.

(212)

To determine the coefficients, one can multiply each side of the equation by
\mho_{I}([V^{\prime},G^{\prime}])
and use the orthogonality of the coefficients to obtain

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptb_{\mho_{I}([V^{\prime},G^{\prime}])}=\frac{\tr(\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)\mho_I([V',G']))}{\|\mho_{I}([V^{\prime},G^{\prime}])\|_{2}^{2}}\,;

(213)

noticing that
\tr(\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)\mho_I)=\tr(O\mho_I)
concludes the proof.
∎

VII.1.2
Clifford-Weingarten calculus

In
Corollary

58
, we introduced a decomposition of the twirling operator using the operator basis
\mho_{I}([V,G])
. Here, we express the twirling super-operators in terms of the simpler basis of Pauli monomials. Based on such a decomposition, we introduce the notion of Clifford-Weingarten calculus, which plays a key role in analytical calculations involving the twirling operator over the Clifford group—analogous to the role of Weingarten calculus for the full unitary group; see
Lemma

21
.

Consider the set of reduced Pauli monomials
\mathcal{P}
. We know that the twirling operator, because of
Lemma

5
, can be written as a linear combination of elements of
\mathcal{P}

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi^{(k)}_{\cl}(O)=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega}(O)\Omega,

(214)

where we drop the explicit dependence on the matrix
M
and the
m
-dimensional vector space
V
, introduced in
Definition

30
.

Lemma 59

(Clifford-Weingarten calculus)
.

Let
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)
be the
k
-fold twirling operator
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})
and let
\mathcal{P}
be the set of (reduced) Pauli monomials. Then it reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)=\sum_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\tr(O\Omega)\Omega^{\prime}

(215)

where we call the coefficients
(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}
Clifford-Weingarten functions, which can be obtained as the (pseudo-)inverse of the Gram-Schmidt matrix
\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\coloneqq\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')
.

Proof.

Similarly to what done in
Lemma

21
, we multiply both sides of
Eq.

214
with
\Omega^{{\dagger}}\in\mathcal{P}
and trace both sides:

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Phi^{(k)}_{\cl}(O))=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega^{\prime}}(O)\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega').

(216)

Noticing that the channel
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\cdot)
is self-adjoint and acts trivially on
\Omega^{{\dagger}}\in\mathcal{P}
, we can rewrite the coefficients
c_{\Omega}(O)
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptc_{\Omega^{\prime}}(O)=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\tr(\Omega^{\dag} O),

(217)

where we have defined the (symmetric) Gram-Schmidt matrix
\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\coloneqq\tr(\Omega\Omega^{\prime\dag})
.
∎

The Gram matrix is defined as the matrix generated by Hilbert-Schmidt inner products between the operators in the reduced Pauli monomial set
\mathcal{P}
. Therefore, the Gram matrix is invertible if and only if the operators in
\mathcal{P}
are linearly independent. This condition holds if and only if
k\leq n+1
, as established in
Corollary

54
.

The following lemma explores the properties of the matrix
\mathcal{W}
.

Lemma 60

(Properties of the Gram-Schmidt matrix
\mathcal{W}
)
.

Let
\mathcal{P}
be the set of reduced Pauli monomials and
|\mathcal{P}|=\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))
be the dimension of the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group. The matrix
\mathcal{W}
, with components
\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}=\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega^{\prime})
, obeys the following properties:

(i)

\mathcal{W}
is symmetric.

(ii)

1\leq\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\leq d^{k-1},\quad\Omega\neq\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}
.

(iii)

\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}=d^{k},\quad\Omega\in\mathcal{P}
.

(iv)

d^{k}-|\mathcal{P}|d^{k-1}\leq\lambda(\mathcal{W})\leq d^{k}+|\mathcal{P}|d^{k-1}
where
\lambda(\mathcal{W})
is any eigenvalue of
\mathcal{W}
.

(v)

\det(\diag\mathcal{W})\left(1-\frac{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)\leq\det(\mathcal{W})\leq\det(\diag\mathcal{W})\left(1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)
, if
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
.

Proof.

To prove item (i), it is sufficient to notice that
\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')
is real, hence
(\mathcal{W}^{T})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}=\mathcal{W}_{\Omega^{\prime}\Omega}=\tr(\Omega^{\prime\dag}\Omega)=\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')^{*}=\tr(\Omega^{\dag}\Omega')
. Item
(ii),(iii)
follows from
Corollary

48
.
From points
(ii)
and
(iii)
, we can lower and upper bound all the eigenvalues of
\mathcal{W}
. Denoting
\lambda(\mathcal{W})
any eigenvalue of
\mathcal{W}
, we have, through the Gershgorin circle theorem
Bhatia 1997

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\min_{\Omega}\Big(\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}-\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\neq\Omega}\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\Big)\leq\lambda(\mathcal{W})\leq\max_{\Omega}\Big(\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}+\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\neq\Omega}\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\Big)

(218)

bounding
\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\neq\Omega}\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\leq|\mathcal{P}|d^{k-1}
, item
(iv)
readily follows.

Let us show item
(v)
. Denoting
\operatorname{diag}(\mathcal{W})
the diagonal part of
\mathcal{W}
, and
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(\mathcal{W})^{-1}\mathcal{W}-I
, where
I
denotes the
|\mathcal{P}|\times|\mathcal{P}|
identity matrix. We can write
\det(\mathcal{W})=\det(\diag(\mathcal{W}))\det(I+\mathcal{W}')
. Let us bound the eigenvalues of
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}
by using the Gershgorin circle theorem. Denoting
\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})
any eigenvalue of
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}
, from item
(ii)
, it follows that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})|\leq\max_{\Omega}\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\neq\Omega}\frac{\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}}{\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}}\leq\frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{d}.

(219)

Using the Bhatia inequality (Theorem VI.7.1 in Ref.
Bhatia 1997
), we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt(1-|\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})|)^{|\mathcal{P}|}\leq\det(I+\mathcal{W}')\leq(1+|\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})|)^{|\mathcal{P}|}.

(220)

Let us now carefully upper and lower bound the two terms. We use
(1+x)^{C}\leq 1+2xC
, valid for
x\leq\frac{1}{2C}
, to get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt(1+|\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})|)^{|\mathcal{P}|}\leq 1+2|\lambda(\mathcal{W}^{\prime})||\mathcal{P}|\leq 1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d},\quad\text{if}\,\,2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}\leq d\,.

(221)

Similarly, we use
(1-x)^{C}\geq 1-Cx
valid for
x\geq-1
and
C>1
, and we get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\det(I+\mathcal{W}')\geq 1-\frac{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}.

(222)

Hence, overall, for the inequalities
Eq.

221
and
Eq.

222
to hold, we need to require
d\geq 2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}
, for which a sufficient condition is
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
(where we have used the results of
Theorem

26
. We are left to compute
\det(\diag\mathcal{W})=\prod_{\Omega}\tr(\Omega\Omega)=d^{k|\mathcal{P}|}
. Putting it all together, this implies item
(v)
.
∎

The following theorem, on the other hand, examines the properties of the inverse, specifically those of the Clifford-Weingarten functions.

Theorem 61

(Asymptotics of Clifford-Weingarten functions)
.

Let
\mathcal{W}
the Gram-Schmidt matrix, and let
\mathcal{W}^{-1}
be its inverse. Let
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
. Then the properties

\displaystyle\left|(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega}-\frac{1}{d^{k}}\right|

\displaystyle\leq\frac{6|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}}\,,

(223)

\displaystyle|(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}|

\displaystyle\leq\frac{5|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}},

(224)

hold true.

Proof.

By the definition of inverse,
(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega}=\frac{\det(\mathcal{W}^{/\Omega})}{\det(\mathcal{W})}
, where
\mathcal{W}^{/\Omega}
denotes the
(|\mathcal{P}|-1)\times(|\mathcal{P}|-1)
matrix obtained by
\mathcal{W}
by erasing the row and the column corresponding to
\Omega
. If
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
, and using the same proof as for item
(v)
of
Lemma

60
, it can be shown that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\det(\diag\mathcal{W}^{/i})\left(1-\frac{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)\leq\det(\mathcal{W}^{/i})\leq\det(\diag\mathcal{W}^{/i})\left(1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right).

(225)

Notice that
\det(\diag\mathcal{W}^{/i})=d^{k(|P^{(k)}|-1)}
. Let us use item
(v)
of
Lemma

60
, to upper and lower bound
(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega}
. First

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega}=\frac{\det(\mathcal{W}^{/\Omega})}{\det(\mathcal{W})}\leq\frac{\det(\diag\mathcal{W}^{/\Omega})}{\det(\diag\mathcal{W})}\frac{\left(1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)}{\left(1-\frac{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)}\leq\frac{1}{d^{k}}\left(1+\frac{6|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right),\quad\text{if}\,\,2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}\leq d,

(226)

where we have used the fact that
\frac{(1+x)}{(1-x/2)}\leq 1+3x
for
x\leq 1
. Similarly for the lower bound we get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}^{-1}=\frac{\det(\mathcal{W}^{/\Omega})}{\det(\mathcal{W})}\geq\frac{1}{d^{k}}\frac{\left(1-\frac{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)}{\left(1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right)}\geq\frac{1}{d^{k}}\left(1-\frac{4|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d}\right),\quad\text{if}\,\,2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}\leq d.

(227)

Notice that together
Eqs.

226
and
227
prove the first bound. To prove the second bound, we make use of

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|\mathcal{W}^{-1}_{i,j}|

\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}

(228)

\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}\|_{\infty}+\|\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}

\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\|\mathcal{W}\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-I\|_{\infty}+\|\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}

\displaystyle=\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\|\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+\|\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}

where, similarly to
Lemma

60
, we have defined
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathcal{W}\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-I
. Now, since
\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}(\mathcal{W})}
, we can exploit item
(iv)
of
Lemma

60
, to bound

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\|\mathcal{W}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{d^{k}}\left(1+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|}{d}\right),\quad\text{if}\,\,2|\mathcal{P}|\leq d.

(229)

From
Eq.

219
in the proof of
Lemma

60
, we know that
\|\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{d}
. We are left in upper bounding
\|\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}
. From point
(ii)
of
Lemma

60
and point (i) above, we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\|\diag(\mathcal{W})^{-1}-\diag(\mathcal{W}^{-1})\|_{\infty}=\max_{\Omega}\Big(\frac{1}{\mathcal{W}_{\Omega,\Omega}}-(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega}\Big)\leq\frac{4|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}}.

(230)

Putting it altogether, we finally have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|\mathcal{W}_{i,j}^{-1}|\leq\frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{d^{k+1}}+\frac{2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+2}}+\frac{4|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}}\leq\frac{5|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}},\quad\text{if}\,\,2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}\leq d\,.

(231)

To conclude the proof it is sufficient to note that
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
is sufficient to ensure
2|\mathcal{P}|^{2}\leq d
due to the dimension of the Clifford group
Theorem

26
.
∎

As an application of the asymptotics of Clifford-Weingarten functions, in the next lemma, we show that the only contributing terms are the ones coming from unitary Pauli monomials whenever we twirl an operator
O
with constant operator norm.

Lemma 62

(Unitary Pauli monomials dominate)
.

Fix
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
. Let
O
be an operator with
\|O\|_{\infty}\leq K
, and let
c_{\Omega}(O)
be the coefficients of the twirling operator
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(O)
for
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}
, then

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|c_{\Omega}(O)|\leq\frac{6K|\mathcal{P}|^{3}}{d},\quad\forall\Omega\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\mathcal{P}_{U}

(232)

i.e., for any non-unitary monomial
\Omega
, it holds that
|c_{\Omega}(O)|=O(2^{\frac{3}{2}k^{2}-n})
.

Proof.

The proof directly descends from
Theorem

61
. Indeed, we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|c_{\Omega}(O)|

\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}}(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\tr(\Omega O)\right|\leq|\tr(\Omega O)|\left(\frac{1}{d^{k}}+\frac{6|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{k+1}}\right)+\frac{5|\mathcal{P}|^{3}}{d^{k+1}}\max_{\Omega^{\prime}\neq\Omega}|\tr(\Omega'O)|.

(233)

Now notice that if
\Omega\not\in\mathcal{P}
, then
\|\Omega\|_{1}\leq d^{k-1}
. In fact, in normal form (see
Lemma

46
) we can write
\Omega=\Omega_{U}\Omega_{P}
then
\|\Omega\|_{1}=\|\Omega_{P}\|=\tr(\Omega_P)\leq d^{d-1}
, as proven in
Lemma

44
. However, if
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
, we have
\|\Omega_{U}\|_{1}=d^{k}
. Therefore, we can bound

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt|c_{\Omega}(O)|\leq\|O\|_{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{d}+\frac{6|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}{d^{2}}+\frac{5|\mathcal{P}|^{3}}{d}\right)

(234)

where we have bounded
|\tr(\Omega O)|\leq\|\Omega\|_{1}\|O\|_{\infty}
. Upper bounding
1+6|\mathcal{P}|^{2}/d\leq|\mathcal{P}|^{3}
, which holds for
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
.

∎

VII.1.3
Clifford orbit of quantum states

In
Proposition

23
, we analyzed the orbit of
k
-copies of a pure quantum state,
\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}^{\otimes k}
, under the action of the full unitary group. As anticipated, the orbit remains the same for any reference state vector
\ket{\psi}
and is proportional to the projector onto the symmetric subspace,
\Pi_{\sym}=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}T_{\pi}
. In contrast, the Clifford orbit of a pure quantum reference state
\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}^{\otimes k}
is more intricate and strongly depends on the choice of the reference state vector
\ket{\psi}
. However, the calculations for the Clifford orbit of pure quantum states are more tractable compared to those for general operators
O
.

Thanks to the symmetry
T_{\pi}\ket{\psi}^{\otimes k}=\ket{\psi}^{\otimes k}
of pure states under permutations, we can write the twirling operator applied on
\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}^{\otimes k}
in terms of Pauli monomials modulo the equivalence class given by permutations.

Lemma 63

(Clifford orbit of a pure quantum state)
.

Let
\ket{\psi}
be a quantum state vector and define
\psi=\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}
its density matrix. Define the following equivalence relation
\Omega\sim\Omega^{\prime}
if and only if there exists
\pi,\sigma\in S_{k}
such that
\Omega=T_{\pi}\Omega^{\prime}T_{\sigma}
. Define
\mathcal{P}/S_{k}
as the set of representative elements of the equivalence relation. The Clifford twirling operator
\Phi^{(k)}_{\cl}(\cdot)
, applied on
k
copies of
\psi
reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\psi^{\otimes k})=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}p_{\Omega}(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Omega\Pi_{\sym})}

(235)

where
p_{\Omega}(\psi)
are quasi-probabilities, i.e.,
\sum_{\Omega}p_{\Omega}(\psi)=1
, but in general they are not positive and
\Pi_{\sym}=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}\pi
. Moreover,

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptp_{\Omega}(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}(\mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\frac{\tr(\Omega'\psi^{\otimes k})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega')}

(236)

where
\mathcal{S}_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\coloneqq\frac{\tr(\Omega\Pi_{\sym}\Omega'\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega)\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega')}
.

Proof.

The proof of
Eq.

235
follows identically compared to the derivation of Clifford-Weingarten functions, see
Lemma

59
.
Let us show that
p_{\Omega}(\psi)
are only quasi-probabilities. The fact that they sum to
1
, simply follows from
\tr(\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\psi^{\otimes k}))=1
. It suffices to compute the average over a Haar random state of
p_{\Omega}(\psi)
:

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi p_{\Omega}(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}(\mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\int\de\psi\frac{\tr(\Omega'\psi^{\otimes k})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega')}=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}(\mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}.

(237)

Now, it is sufficient to note that
\mathcal{S}_{\Omega^{\prime},\mathbb{1}}=\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}
. Hence

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi p_{\Omega}(\psi)=\delta_{\Omega,\mathbb{1}}

(238)

This demonstrates that
p_{\Omega}(\psi)
is generally non-positive. Suppose, for contradiction, that
p_{\Omega}(\psi)\geq 0
for all states. Given that the average is zero, this would imply
p_{\Omega}(\psi)=0
for all
\Omega\neq\mathbb{1}
and for any state. Consequently, this would lead to
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\psi^{\otimes k})=\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(\psi^{\otimes k})
for any state
\psi
, meaning that the Clifford orbit—such as that of stabilizer states—forms a projective
k
-design for all
k
, which is clearly a contradiction. Therefore,
p_{\Omega}(\psi)
must be non-positive in general.
∎

Lemma 64

(Clifford orbit of a stabilizer state
Gross et al. 2021
)
.

While the Clifford orbit depends on the reference state, it attains a simple value for stabilizer states. It is possible to show that, for every
n,k\geq 1
, it holds that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}\left(\outerproduct{0}{0}^{\otimes k}\right)=\frac{1}{Z_{n}}\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}\Omega

(239)

with
Z_{n}=d\prod_{i=0}^{k-2}(d+2^{i})
.

Proof.

This lemma has been proven in Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
, which we include here for completeness. For this proof, we explicitly denote the dependence of
n
in the twirling operator as
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}\left(\outerproduct{0_n}{0_n}^{\otimes k}\right)
. For any
n^{\prime}<n
, uniformity over Clifford circuits implies that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\left\langle 0_{n-n^{\prime}}^{\otimes k}|\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}\left(\outerproduct{0_n}{0_n}^{\otimes k}\right)|0_{n-n^{\prime}}^{\otimes k}\right\rangle\propto\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}\left(\outerproduct{0_{n'}}{0_{n'}}^{\otimes k}\right).

(240)

Now, consider
n\geq k-1
. From
Lemma

59
, we know that we can express

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\outerproduct{0_n}{0_n}^{\otimes k})=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{n,\Omega}\Omega^{(n)},

(241)

here we introduced the notation
\Omega^{(n)}
to make explicit the dependence from the number of qubits of the system we are considering, and we use the fact that
\tr(\Omega^{(n)} \ketbra{0_n}^{\otimes k})=1
, which holds for any
k
-tensor copies of a stabilizer state. We also define
c_{n,\Omega}=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}}(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}
. Since
\langle 0_{n-n^{\prime}}^{\otimes k}|\Omega^{(n)}|0_{n-n^{\prime}}^{\otimes k}\rangle=\Omega^{(n^{\prime})}
due to the tensor product structure
\Omega^{(n)}=\omega^{\otimes n}
(see
Lemma

31
),
Eq.

240
implies that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{n,\Omega}\Omega^{(n)}\propto\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{n^{\prime},\Omega}\Omega^{(n^{\prime})}.

(242)

This necessarily implies that
c_{n,\Omega}=c_{n}c_{\Omega}
. Since this equation holds for any
n^{\prime}
, in particular for
n^{\prime}<k-1
, it must hold for all
n
. We can thus express the twirling operator for any
n
as

\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\outerproduct{0_n}{0_n}^{\otimes k})\propto\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega}\Omega^{(n)}.

(243)

Next, we show that the coefficients
c_{\Omega}
must be equal. Consider the expectation value of a Pauli monomial
\Omega^{\prime}
. On one hand, we have

\tr(\Omega^{'(n)} \Phi_{\cl}^{(n)}(\ketbra{0_n}^{\otimes k}))=\langle 0_{n}|\Omega^{{}^{\prime}(n)}|0_{n}\rangle=1.

(244)

On the other hand, we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt1=c_{n}\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega}\tr(\Omega^{'(n)} \Omega^{(n)})=c_{n}d^{k}c_{\Omega^{\prime}}+\sum_{\Omega\neq\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega}\tr(\Omega^{'(n)} \Omega^{(n)})=d^{k}c_{n}(c_{\Omega^{\prime}}+O(d^{-1}))\quad\forall\Omega^{\prime}.

(245)

Taking the limit of large
d
, it follows that all coefficients
c_{\Omega^{\prime}}
must be equal. However, since
c_{\Omega^{\prime}}
is independent of
n
, the result holds for every
n
. Thus for any
n
and
k
, we can write

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(\outerproduct{0}{0}^{\otimes k})=\frac{1}{Z_{n}}\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}\Omega,

(246)

where
Z_{n}=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}\tr(\Omega)
, which can be computed directly from
Lemma

44
, using the fact that
\tr(\Omega)=d^{k-m}
and similarly from
Theorem

26
one can obtain that the number of reduced Pauli monomials with order
m
is given by
\binom{k-1}{m}_{2}\times 2^{m(m-1)/2}
.

∎

VII.2
Magic-state resource theory

In this section, we apply the framework developed for the Clifford commutant to a closely related topic: magic-state resource theory. As in other resource theories, magic-state resource theory focuses on defining resource monotones, which are functions that do
not increase under Clifford operations
Veitch et al. 2014
;
Howard and Campbell 2017
;
Seddon and Campbell 2019
. In a broader context, Clifford operations encompass not only Clifford unitary transformations but also computational basis measurements, partial traces, and operations conditioned on measurement outcomes. The presence of these general operations significantly complicates the search for computable magic monotones. As a result, most magic monotones involve a minimization procedure over the entire set of stabilizer states
Liu and Winter 2022
;
Seddon and Campbell 2019
, rendering them fundamentally unmeasurable in experimental settings and analytically intractable
Heinrich and Gross 2019
. However, stabilizer entropy has emerged as the first magic monotone that is both experimentally measurable and analytically tractable
Leone et al. 2022
. Nevertheless, this experimental feasibility is largely limited to pure states. This limitation is not surprising, as it is a common feature across other resource theories, such as entanglement resource theory. For this reason, in the remainder of the section, we will primarily focus on magic-state resource theory as applied to pure states.

In the following, we will use the term
magic measures
to refer to quantities that are not necessarily magic monotones. The key distinction is that magic measures are required only to be resource non-increasing under Clifford unitaries, a necessary condition for being a magic monotone but not sufficient on its own, while magic monotones must exhibit monotonic behavior under a much broader class of stabilizer operations. In our terminology, every magic monotone is also a magic measure, but the converse is not true. For a more detailed discussion, see
Leone and Bittel 2024b
.

To begin, let us formally define the notion of
measurable
function in the context of quantum information.

Definition 65

(Measurement strategy)
.

A measurement strategy is a quantum algorithm
\mathcal{A}(\rho^{\otimes k})\mapsto[0,1]
with arbitrary classical processing. Any such strategy describes a statistical process from shot-noise statistics and potentially a randomized classical processing strategy. We assume that both the classical and quantum processing can have arbitrary circuit complexity and arbitrary auxiliary bits and qubits.

Definition 66

(Measurable function)
.

A measurable function
f
is the expectation value of a measurement strategy
f(\rho^{\otimes k})\coloneqq\langle\mathcal{A}(\rho^{\otimes k})\rangle
, where the expectation value
\langle\cdot\rangle
is over all possible measurement outcomes of the measurement strategy
\mathcal{A}.

Moving on to magic measures, let us introduce stabilizer entropies, which will serve as the central objects of our subsequent discussion.

Definition 67

(Stabilizer entropy
Leone et al. 2022
)
.

Let
\ket{\psi}
be a pure quantum state vector and
\psi=\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}
its density matrix. Then, the stabilizer entropies
M_{\alpha}(\psi)
are defined

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM_{\alpha}(\psi)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\Delta_{2\alpha}(\psi),\quad\Delta_{2\alpha}(\psi)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2\alpha}(P\psi)\,.

(247)

Upon closer examination, it becomes evident that the
\Delta_{2\alpha}(\psi)
in the definition of stabilizer entropy is, in fact, the expectation value of the primitive Pauli monomial (see
Definition

28
):

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega_{2\alpha}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes 2\alpha},\quad\Delta_{2\alpha}=\tr(\Omega_{2\alpha}\psi^{\otimes 2\alpha})\,.

(248)

This equivalence and the ordering of Rényi entropies
Leone et al. 2022
, allows us to write
\Delta_{2(\alpha+1)}\leq\Delta_{2\alpha}\leq\Delta_{2(\alpha+1)}^{1-1/\alpha}
.

This observation hints at a profound connection between magic-state resource theory and the commutant of the Clifford group. Specifically, in what follows, we prove that any measurable magic measure can be expressed as a Pauli polynomial, that is, a linear combination of Pauli monomials.

Before stating the main result, let us lay down the following lemma in the context of magic-state resource theory.

Lemma 68

(Invariance under unitary Clifford operations)
.

Let
M(\psi)
be any magic measure. Then
M(\psi)
is invariant under Clifford unitary operations, that is,
M(\psi)=M(C\psi C^{{\dagger}})
for every
C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}
.

Proof.

Due to their invertibility, the fact that a resource does not increase under Clifford unitaries implies that it remains invariant under Clifford unitaries.
∎

Lemma 69
.

Every measurable function
M(\rho^{\otimes k})
on
k
copies, which is invariant under Clifford unitary operations, is equal to an expectation value of a positive operator
\Pi\leq\mathbb{1}
that belongs to
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, i.e.,

\displaystyle M(\rho^{\otimes k})=\tr(\rho^{\otimes k} \Pi),\quad\Pi=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}\alpha_{\Omega}\Omega.

(249)

Proof.

Let us first show that any measurable function in the sense of
Definition

66
can be recast as an expectation value of a positive operator
\Pi
. Notice that every classical process can be described by a quantum circuit. Quantum measurements can be simulated using an auxiliary qubit and a CNOT gate. To turn the distribution of classical outcome estimates into an expectation value, the experimenter implements the state

\displaystyle\rho=\begin{pmatrix}r&0\\
0&1-r\end{pmatrix}

(250)

where
r
is the classical estimate. The final measurement is then
\pi=\outerproduct{0}{0}
. Therefore, supplying with
k^{\prime}
additional registers initiated in the state
\ket{0}
, any measurement strategy can be implemented. Since measurable functions are expectation values of measurement strategies, we can write

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM(\rho^{\otimes k})=\tr(\rho^{\otimes k}\otimes\ketbra{0}^{\otimes k'}U\Pi U^{\dag})

(251)

where
U
is a classical-quantum circuit and
\pi=\outerproduct{0}{0}
. Defining
\Pi\coloneqq\langle 0^{\otimes k^{\prime}}|U\pi U^{{\dagger}}|0^{\otimes k^{\prime}}\rangle
, we can thus write the measurable function
f(\rho^{\otimes k})=\tr(\Pi\rho^{\otimes k})
. Notice that since
\pi\leq\mathbb{1}
, so is
\Pi
. Now we just have to prove
\Pi\in\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
. Let us exploit the invariance under Clifford unitary operations

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM(C^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k}C^{{\dagger}\otimes k})=f(\rho^{\otimes k}),\quad\forall C,\rho\implies\tr(C^{\dag\otimes k} \Pi C^{\otimes k} \rho^{\otimes k})=\tr(\Pi\rho^{\otimes k}),\quad\forall C,\rho.

(252)

By the requirement that this equality holds for any state
\rho
, it follows that the operator
\Pi
must satisfy
\Pi=C^{{\dagger}\otimes k}\Pi C^{\otimes k}
for all
C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}
, implying that
\Pi\in\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
, and thus a Pauli polynomial. This concludes the proof.
∎

Lemma

69
says that any measurable function corresponding to a measurement strategy on
k
copies that is also invariant under Clifford operations belongs to the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group. This result suggests that measurable magic measures, which must be invariant under Clifford operations, see
Lemma

68
, are nothing more than Pauli polynomials. This result is formalized in the following theorem, the proof of which descends from the above lemma.

Theorem 70

(Measurable
magic measures as Pauli polynomials)
.

Any magic measures
M(\rho)
, for which there exists an unbiased estimator employing
k
copies of the state
\rho
, is a Pauli polynomial of degree
k
.

Proof.

Let
M(\rho)
be the magic measure and let
\hat{M}(\rho^{\otimes k})
be an unbiased estimator for
M(\rho)
. By definition of unbiased estimator, we have that
\langle\hat{M}(\rho^{\otimes k})\rangle=M(\rho)
, where the expectation value is over all the possible outcomes of the measurement strategy used on
k
copies. Hence,
M(\rho)
is a measurable function according to
Definition

66
. Moreover,
M(\rho)
must be invariant under the action of Clifford unitaries, as per
Lemma

68
. Hence, by virtue of
Lemma

69
, we can write
M(\rho)=\tr(\Pi\rho)
with
\Pi\in\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
being a Pauli polynomial of degree
k
.
∎

This result demonstrates that any experimentally measurable magic measure must be expressible as the expectation value of an operator in the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group, underscoring the strong connection between magic-state resource theory and the Clifford commutant. Moreover, the argument above also reveals that the minimal polynomial order for which a magic measure can exist is
k\geq 4
. For
k<4
, the Clifford commutant coincides with the commutant of the full unitary group and, therefore, cannot contain any useful information.

While the above general results apply to possibly mixed states, in the remainder of the section, we restrict our attention to pure states. In
Theorem

70
, we have shown that any measurable magic measure is equivalent to an expectation value of a positive Pauli polynomial. If we restrict to pure states, we can assume, without loss of generality, that such operator lives in the symmetric subspace with projector
\Pi_{\sym}
. As shown in
Lemma

63
, we can define the equivalence relation of Pauli monomials under left and right actions of permutations, and define the set
\mathcal{P}/S_{k}
as the set of independent Pauli monomials that are permutationally inequivalent. Consequently, without loss of generality, we can write any measurable magic measure restricted on pure states as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}c_{\Omega}\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k}),

(253)

i.e., the magic measure
M(\psi)
is simply a linear combination of independent, permutationally nonequivalent Pauli monomials, suggesting that these monomials represent more fundamental magic measures. This observation motivates the following definition.

Definition 71

(Generalized stabilizer purities)
.

Let
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}
, where
\mathcal{P}/S_{k}
is the set of reduced Pauli monomials up to permutations with representative elements Pauli monomials with the least possible order
m
. The
\Omega
-stabilizer purity is defined as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)\coloneqq\real(\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k})).

(254)

Notice that
\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)=1
for stabilizer states, and it is manifestly invariant under Clifford operations. Moreover, if
\Omega(v)
is a primitive Pauli monomial, we abbreviate it as
\Delta_{\Omega(v)}(\psi)=\Delta_{|v|}(\psi)
, consistently with
Definition

67
. The real part is used because not every
\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k})
is necessarily real. An alternative definition could also involve taking the absolute value of the expectation value.

In the context of qudits, Ref.
Turkeshi et al. 2025
introduced generalized stabilizer purity in the same fashion. In the next theorem, we show that generalized stabilizer purities attains their maximum values for stabilizer states.

Theorem 72

(Faithfulness of generalized stabilizer purities)
.

Let
\psi
be a pure quantum state, then for any
\Omega
-stabilizer purity, it holds that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)\leq 1

(255)

while
\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)=1
if
\psi
is a stabilizer state.

Proof.

We divide the proof into three cases:

(i)

If
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}
is a unitary Pauli monomial, the result follows directly from a simple Hölder inequality as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)\leq\|\Omega\|_{\infty}\|\psi\|_{1}^{k}\leq 1.

(256)

(ii)

If
\Omega(V,M)\in\mathcal{P}_{P}
is a projector, it corresponds to
a vector space
V
containing only even-weight primitives with no phases, i.e.,
M=0
. Let us now use the invariance under linear transformations, formally established in
Theorem

37
. There exists a transformation
V\mapsto VA
that performs Gaussian elimination on the column vectors of
V
, resulting in
VA
having a pivot structure. Since for projectors,
H=0\pmod{2}
, this linear operation ensures
M(A)=0
.

For the sake of clarity, after the transformation, we express
\Omega
as
\Omega=\Omega(v_{1})\Omega(v_{2})\cdots\Omega(v_{m})
,
with the property that
(v_{1})_{1}=1
, while
(v_{i})_{1}=0
for
i=2,\ldots,m
. Denoting
T_{1}
as the partial transpose on the first tensor copy, we use the invariance of the trace under partial transpose:

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)=\tr(\psi^{\otimes k} \Omega\psi^{\otimes k})=\tr(\psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)} \Omega(v_1)^{T_1} \Omega_{\text{rest}} \psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}),

(257)

where, crucially, the partial transpose does not affect the remaining terms, denoted as
\Omega_{\text{rest}}=\prod_{i=2}^{m}\Omega(v_{i})
, because of the pivot structure.

It is straightforward to verify that
\Omega(v_{1})^{T_{1}}
is a unitary operator, while
\Omega_{\text{rest}}
is proportional to a projector, i.e.,
\Omega_{\text{rest}}^{2}=d^{m-1}\Omega_{\text{rest}}
. We now bound
\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)
, to get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m-1}}\tr(\psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)} \Omega(v_1)^{T_1} \Omega_{\text{rest}} \Omega_{\text{rest}} \psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)})

(258)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d^{m-1}}\|\Omega_{\text{rest}}\psi^{T}\otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}\Omega(v_{1})^{T_{1}}\|_{2}\|\Omega_{\text{rest}}\psi^{T}\otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}\|_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m-1}}\|\Omega_{\text{rest}}\psi^{T}\otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}\|_{2}^{2},

where we applied Hölder inequality and, in the last step, used the unitary invariance of the
2
-norm to eliminate
\Omega(v_{1})^{T_{1}}
.

Thus, we obtain

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)\leq\frac{1}{d^{m-1}}\|\Omega_{\text{rest}}\psi^{T}\otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}\|_{2}^{2}=\tr(\Omega_{\text{rest}} \psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)} \psi^{T} \otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)})=\tr(\Omega_{\text{rest}}^{T_1} \psi\otimes\psi^{\otimes(k-1)}).

(259)

In the last step, we have used the pivot structure of
\Omega_{\text{rest}}
, which ensures that
\Omega_{\text{rest}}^{T_{1}}=\Omega_{\text{rest}}
. Iterating this argument
m-1
more times, we arrive at:
\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)\leq\Delta_{|v_{m}|}(\psi)
, where
\Delta_{|v_{m}|}
is a stabilizer purity corresponding to a primitive
\Omega(v_{m})
. Since it is known that
\Delta_{|v_{m}|}\leq 1

Leone et al. 2022
, the bound holds.

(iii)

When
\Omega=\Pi U
is a product of a projector
\Pi
and a unitary
U
, we can apply the same reasoning as above to obtain
\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k})\leq\tr(\Pi\psi^{\otimes k})
, which completes the proof.

∎

Before presenting explicit examples of generalized stabilizer purities, let us compute the average
\Omega
-stabilizer purity for Haar random states. This result will aid in establishing a hierarchy of generalized stabilizer purities based on their order
m(\Omega)
, as defined in
Definition

41
. Haar random states can be thought of as states with the maximal level of magic since they asymptotically (in the number of qubits
n
) saturate the bounds of all known magic monotones (see Refs.
Liu and Winter 2022
;
Leone et al. 2022
). Consequently, generalized stabilizer purities that achieve larger values for Haar random states are the most sensitive, as they would vary within a smaller range, making them more practical for experimental measurements.

Lemma 73

(Haar average of
\Omega
-stabilizer purity)
.

Let
\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)
be a
\Omega
-stabilizer purity with order
m(\Omega)
. The average value over Haar random state is

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)=\frac{c_{\Omega}}{d^{m(\Omega)}}+O\left(\frac{1}{d^{m(\Omega)+1}}\right)

(260)

where
c_{\Omega}\leq k!
.

Proof.

We know from
Section

VII.1
that the average
\Omega
-stabilizer purity is simply

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)=\tr(\Omega\Psi_{\haar}^{(k)})=\frac{k!}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}\tr(\Omega T_{\pi})=\frac{c_{\Omega}}{d^{m(\Omega)}}+\left(\frac{1}{d^{m(\Omega)+1}}\right)

(261)

where
c_{\Omega}\coloneqq|\{\Omega T_{\pi}\,:\,m(\Omega T_{\pi})=m(\Omega)\}|
is the number of permutations not increasing the order of the monomial
\Omega
. The above statement follows from
Lemma

44
, from the fact that
\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{k!}=d^{k}+O(d^{k-1})
, and from the fact that the
\Omega
-stabilizer purity is defined to be the one within the equivalence class with the smallest order
m(\Omega)
.
∎

Lemma

73
tells us that
\Omega
-stabilizer purities
vary
in a range depending on their order
m(\Omega)
, i.e.,
[O(d^{-m(\Omega)}),1]
. From a practical point of view, it is convenient to consider those with small
m(\Omega)
to reduce the number of measurement shots to measure magic in quantum states. This is particularly relevant for those stabilizer purities corresponding to the expectation value of unitary operators that can be efficiently measured in quantum experiments via a simple Hadamard test
Nielsen and Chuang 2000
.

Given that
\Omega
-stabilizer purities corresponding to unitary monomials are efficiently measurable magic measures, it is natural to expect that every measurable magic measure can be expressed as a linear combination of unitary generalized stabilizer purity. We prove this intuition to be true in the following lemma.

Lemma 74
.

Let
M(\psi)
be a measurable magic monotone, for which there exists an unbiased estimator on
k
copies of
\psi
. Then for any
n\geq k^{2}-3k+7
, it holds that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}}\alpha_{\Omega}\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)+O(2^{\frac{3}{2}k^{2}-n}).

(262)

Proof.

Thanks to
Theorem

70
, we can write
M(\psi)=\tr(\hat{M}\psi^{\otimes k})
. Since
\hat{M}
belongs to the commutant and, without loss of generality, lives in the symmetric subspace because
\psi
is pure, we can express it as
\hat{M}=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}}\alpha_{\Omega}(\hat{M})\Omega
with
\Omega
being Pauli monomials. Using
Lemma

62
, and using that
\|\hat{M}\|_{\infty}\leq 1
, we know

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\alpha_{\Omega}(\hat{M})\leq O(2^{\frac{3}{2}k^{2}-n})

(263)

Since
|\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)|\leq 1
(see
Theorem

72
), then it immediately follows that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptM(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}}\alpha_{\Omega}(\hat{M})\Delta_{\Omega}(\psi)+O(2^{2k^{2}-n})

(264)

From the condition of
M_{n}(\sigma)=1
for every stabilizer state and recalling that
\tr(\Omega\sigma^{\otimes k})=1
for every stabilizer state, one gets the condition
\sum_{\Omega}\alpha_{\Omega}=1
, from which it immediately follows that
\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}/S_{k}}\alpha_{\Omega}=1-O(2^{2k^{2}-n})
.
∎

VII.2.1
Examples of generalized stabilizer purities

Having defined generalized stabilizer purity and having drawn intuition of their hierarchy, let us discuss some practical examples.

In
Section

VII.5
, we identify all non-permutationally independent operators up to
k=8
. As previously noted, for
k<4
, no polynomial can capture the magic of pure quantum states. At
k=4
, the first magic measure is provided by the Pauli monomial
\Omega_{4}
, which corresponds to the
\alpha=2
stabilizer entropy. Thus, the
\alpha=2
stabilizer entropy represents
the minimal expectation value
capable of quantifying magic. Using the graphical calculus, this equivalence can be expressed as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{4}(\psi)=\tr( \Omega_4 \psi^{\otimes 4})=\tr(\monomialdiagram{4}{{1,2,3,4}}{}\,\,\,\, \psi^{\otimes 4})=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{4}(P\psi).

(265)

where for the sake of clarity we use the shorthand notation
\Delta_{x}=\Omega_{x}
.
For
\Delta_{4}(\psi)
, we can compute the leading order Haar average as done in
Lemma

73
. In fact, from
Section

VII.5
we know that
c_{\Omega}=4
, and therefore
\mathbb{E}_{\psi}[\Delta_{4}(\psi)]=4d^{-1}+O(d^{-2})
. Despite being the minimal stabilizer purity that can quantify magic and having an order
m(\Omega_{4})=1
, the second stabilizer entropy has a significant limitation. For large numbers of qubits, which are often the most common case of interest, it cannot be measured efficiently. Specifically, there is no known algorithm with non-exponential sample complexity in
n
that can measure
\Delta_{4}
to additive precision
Miller et al. 2024
. This inefficiency arises because the primitive
\Omega_{4}
is proportional to a projector with a proportionality factor of
d
, see
Lemma

29
. As a result, it has an exponential operator norm. Moreover, there are strong arguments suggesting that the efficiency of unbiased estimators for measuring the expectation values of observables depends on the operator norm of the observables. These facts motivate the search for magic measures corresponding to higher-order polynomials.

For
k=6
, two additional elements arise that correspond to Pauli monomials. The first is
\Omega_{6}
, which corresponds to the third stabilizer entropy:

\lxSVG@closescope {{{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\,\,\,\,\psi^{\otimes 6}\right)=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(P\psi)\tr^{2}(PQ\psi)\tr^{2}(Q\psi),

(267)

where we have used the shorthand
\Omega_{4,4}\coloneqq\Omega(1,1,1,1,0,0)\Omega(0,0,1,1,1,1)
(Note that we will use this shorthand notation from now on for all the
\Omega
s).

We can compute the Haar average of the two above explicitly, being
\mathbb{E}_{\psi}[\Delta_{6}(\psi)]=d^{-1}+O(d^{-2})
thanks to its unitarity, while
\mathbb{E}_{\psi}[\Delta(\psi)]=24d^{-2}+O(d^{-3})

While the latter is proportional to a projector, being the product of two operators proportional to projectors (see
Lemma

29
, and hence cannot be measured efficiently,
\Delta_{6}(\psi)
can be measured efficiently as it corresponds to a unitary operator. This observation motivates the introduction of a second criterion to give a hierarchy to the
\Omega
-stabilizer purities. Specifically, generalized stabilizer purities corresponding to Pauli monomials that are projectors are less appealing because of their inefficiency in measurements, whereas those corresponding to unitary Pauli monomials are more practical.

From the previous discussion, we know that for
k=6
, there exists a unitary Pauli monomial corresponding to the third stabilizer entropy. This fact makes the
\alpha=3
stabilizer entropy to be the minimal-order monomial that quantifies magic and can be experimentally measured efficiently. As we will see in
Section

VII.3
, this fact also has profound consequences for stabilizer property testing.

However, it is intriguing to explore whether higher-order polynomials give rise to other measures with similar properties.
Extending this to
k=8
, as further discussed in
Section

VII.5
, there is only one unitary Pauli monomial in addition to
\Omega_{6}
, that is,
\Omega_{6,6}\coloneqq\Omega(1,1,1,1,1,1,0,0)\Omega(0,0,1,1,1,1,1,1)
. Graphically, we find

(268)

However, since the Pauli monomial described above is the product of two primitives, we know that
m(\Omega_{6,6})=2
and, therefore, achieves a typical value, when averaged over Haar random states, of
d^{-2}+O(d^{-3})
.

Open Question 1
.

As noted above, invariance under Clifford operations alone is not sufficient for a quantity to qualify as a monotone. The generalized stabilizer purities defined in
Definition

71
have not yet been proven to be monotones for magic-state resource theory. Specifically, the question of whether
\Omega
-stabilizer purity for
\Omega
not being a primitive Pauli monomial (hence corresponding to stabilizer entropies) is non-decreasing under stabilizer operations remains an open question. See also Ref.
Turkeshi et al. 2025
.

VII.2.2
Stabilizer entropy and Bell magic

Bell magic is a magic measure, i.e., a quantity invariant under Clifford unitaries (though it is not known to be a magic monotone), introduced in Ref.
Haug and Kim 2023
. It has the property of being experimentally measurable via Bell difference sampling
Hangleiter and Gullans 2024
. In
Theorem

70
, we proved that any measure of this kind, denoted as
M(\psi)
, belongs to the
k
-th order commutant of the Clifford group, where
k
corresponds to the number of copies in the unbiased estimator. In this section, we first express Bell magic in terms of Pauli monomials and then show that it is tightly upper and lower bounded by stabilizer entropies.

Definition 75

(Bell magic
Haug and Kim 2023
)
.

Let
\psi
be a pure quantum state. The Bell magic is defined as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptB(\psi)=\sum_{P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\mathcal{Q}(P_{1})\mathcal{Q}(P_{2})\|[P_{1},P_{2}]\|_{\infty},\quad\mathcal{Q}(P_{1})\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(Q\psi)|\tr(PQ\psi)|^{2}

(269)

and it obeys 1)
B(\psi)=0
if and only if
\psi
is a stabilizer state and 2) it is invariant under Clifford unitaries.

Lemma 76

(Bell magic in terms of Pauli monomials)
.

The Bell magic can be expressed as an expectation value of the unitary Pauli monomial
\Omega_{6,6}
belonging to
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes 8})
. In particular, we find

(270)

Proof.

To prove the result, let us first observe that we can rewrite

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\|[P_{1},P_{2}]\|_{\infty}

\displaystyle=1-\chi(P_{1},P_{2})

(271)

\displaystyle|\tr(PQ\psi)|^{2}

\displaystyle=\tr^{2}(QP\psi)\chi(P,Q)

Hence, we can write the Bell magic as the following expression:

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptB(\psi)=1-\frac{1}{d^{4}}\sum_{P_{1},P_{2},Q_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(Q_{1}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{2}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{1}P_{1}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{2}P_{2}\psi)\chi(P_{2},Q_{2})\chi(P_{1},Q_{1})\chi(P_{1},P_{2})

(272)

This describes a Pauli polynomial, where the latter term can be expressed with the following diagrammatic representation

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\frac{1}{d^{4}}\sum_{P_{1},P_{2},Q_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(Q_{1}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{2}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{1}P_{1}\psi)\tr^{2}(Q_{2}P_{2}\psi)\chi(P_{2},Q_{2})\chi(P_{1},Q_{1})\chi(P_{1},P_{2})=\tr(\monomialdiagram{8}{{1,2,5,6},{5,6},{3,4,7,8},{7,8}}{0:1,2:3,1:3}\psi^{\otimes 8}).

(273)

To conclude the proof, it is sufficient to use the machinery developed in
Section

V.1
and manipulate this diagram

Section

VII.2

∎

As speculated in
Section

VII.2
, any computable magic measure can be recast as the expectation value of an operator residing in the commutant of the Clifford group. Since any operator in the commutant of the Clifford group is a linear combination of Pauli monomials, which, in
normal form
, can be expressed as products of primitive Pauli monomials, and since the expectation values of these primitives correspond to stabilizer entropies, it is natural to conjecture that any such computable monotone is equivalent to the stabilizer entropy. In the following theorem, we demonstrate that for Bell magic, this conjecture holds true: we establish upper and lower bounds for Bell magic in terms of the stabilizer entropy, thereby proving the universality of the stabilizer entropy in relation to Bell magic.

Theorem 77

(Stabilizer entropy upper and lower bounds Bell magic)
.

Let
B(\psi)
the Bell magic defined in
Definition

75
and let
M_{\alpha}=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\Delta_{2\alpha}(\psi)
be the stabilizer entropy defined in
Definition

67
. The bounds

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt1-\Delta_{4}^{2}(\psi)\leq B(\psi)\leq 1-\Delta_{6}^{2}(\psi)

(276)

hold true, which, in terms of stabilizer entropies and additive Bell magic defined in
Haug and Kim 2023

-\log(1-B(\psi))
, the above bounds can be expressed in terms of the stabilizer entropy as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt2M_{3}(\psi)\leq 2M_{2}(\psi)\leq-\log(1-B(\psi))\leq 4M_{3}(\psi).

(277)

Proof.

Using the result of
Lemma

76
, we can write Bell magic in terms of
\Omega_{6,6}
:

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptB(\psi)=1-\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(P\psi)\tr^{2}(Q\psi)\tr^{4}(PQ\psi).=1-\tr[\left(\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(P\psi)P^{\otimes 4}\psi^{\otimes 4}\right)^{2}]

(278)

Then, we have the following inequality between expectation values of Pauli monomials

(279)

where we used the fact that given a Hermitian operator
H

\tr(H^2\psi^{\otimes 4})\geq\tr^{2}(H\psi^{\otimes 4})
, this holds in our case because
\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{2}(P\psi)P^{\otimes 4}
is a Hermitian operator with infinity norm smaller than
1
.
Now, let us proceed with the upper bound.

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}\tr^{2}(P\psi)\tr^{2}(Q\psi)\tr^{4}(PQ\psi)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}\tr^{2}(P\psi)\tr^{2}(PQ\psi)\tr^{2}(Q\psi)\tr^{2}(PQ\psi)

\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{4}(P\psi)\tr^{4}(PQ\psi)}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\tr^{4}(Q\psi)\tr^{4}(PQ\psi)}

(281)

which concludes the proof.

∎

The above theorem confirms our intuition: stabilizer entropies tightly bound Bell magic from above and below, effectively an intermediate between
\Delta_{4}^{2}
and
\Delta_{6}^{2}
.
Bell magic gained significant attention upon its introduction because of its efficient measurability via Bell difference sampling, while the efficient measurability of stabilizer entropies has initially been unclear. However, as shown, odd stabilizer entropies are related (through the non-linear function
-\log
) to the expectation values of unitary primitive Pauli monomials, which can be directly measured as we know that Pauli monomials factorize on qubits (see
Lemma

31
).

VII.2.3
The triple purity

So far, we have shown that any magic measure is a Pauli polynomial and, therefore, a linear combination of generalized stabilizer purities. These generalized stabilizer purities provide a meaningful extension of stabilizer purities (entropies), as they can be expressed as the expectation value of an operator obtained from the product of
\Omega_{2\alpha}
, whose expectation value yields
\Delta_{2\alpha}
(see
Definition

67
). The term ”entropy” in stabilizer entropy arises from the fact that these quantities serve as entropy measures for the Pauli distribution of a pure quantum state. Specifically, for any pure state
\ket{\psi}
, one can define a normalized distribution over Pauli operators given by
\Xi_{\psi}(P)\coloneqq\frac{\tr^{2}(P\psi)}{d}
, known as the
characteristic distribution
. The Rényi entropies of
\Xi_{\psi}
correspond, up to an offset, to stabilizer entropies. Since stabilizer entropies are magic monotones
Leone and Bittel 2024a
, the property of magic can be understood purely as a function of the Pauli distribution
\Xi_{\psi}
. However, not every magic measure depends solely on the Pauli distribution. This distinction becomes evident when considering generalized stabilizer purities. In particular, for
k=9
, we encounter the first measurable generalization of stabilizer purities—one that extends beyond being a mere function of the Pauli distribution.

Definition 78

(Triple purity)
.

\Delta_{\text{triple}}
