From the definition of triple purity it becomes evident that
\Delta_{\text{triple}}
is not a mere function of the Pauli distribution, as not only the absolute value of expectation values of Pauli operators
|\tr(P\psi)|
matters but also their signs.

VII.3
Property testing of stabilizer states

In this subsection, we revisit the well-studied problem of property testing for stabilizer states
Montanaro and de Wolf 2018
;
Gross et al. 2021
;
Bu et al. 2023
;
Grewal et al. 2023
;
Arunachalam and Dutt 2024
;
Chen et al. 2024b
;
Hinsche and Helsen 2024
;
Bao et al. 2024
, connecting it with the commutant structure of the Clifford group. The idea of connecting property testing with the commutant—or the invariant symmetries of the problem—is well established in the literature (see, e.g.,
Montanaro and de Wolf 2018
;
Gross et al. 2021
;
Hinsche and Helsen 2024
). Our aim here is not to introduce new methods, but to emphasize how the characterization of the Clifford group commutant constrains the design of optimal measurement strategies in this context. In particular, we show that
generalized stabilizer purities
emerge as essentially the only viable measurements for stabilizer property testing when the number of available copies is fixed.

We begin by briefly introducing the problem. Property testing of stabilizer states involves determining whether an unknown quantum state is close to or far from the stabilizer set, based on measurements on multiple copies of the state. Formally, we define the problem as follows.

Problem 79

(Property testing of stabilizer states)
.

Let
1\geq\varepsilon_{B}\geq\varepsilon_{A}>0
. Given access to
k
copies of an unknown quantum state
\rho
, assume that
\rho
satisfies one of the following conditions:

•

\rho
is
\varepsilon_{A}
-close to some stabilizer state, i.e., there exists
\phi\in\stab(n)
such that
\|\rho-\phi\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon_{A}
.

•

\rho
is at least
\varepsilon_{B}
-far from all stabilizer states, that is,
\min_{\phi\in\stab(n)}\|\rho-\phi\|_{1}\geq\varepsilon_{B}
.

The goal is to design a measurement strategy that acts on
k
copies of
\rho
that distinguishes these two cases with probability at least
2/3
.

Equivalently, the task is to find a two-outcome POVM
\{E,I-E\}
such that

\displaystyle\text{if }\rho\text{ is }\varepsilon_{A}\text{-close to a stabilizer state, then }\tr(E \rho^{\otimes k})\geq a,

(283)

\displaystyle\text{if }\rho\text{ is }\varepsilon_{B}\text{-far from all stabilizer states, then }\tr(E \rho^{\otimes k})\leq b.

(284)

We note that the threshold values
a
and
b
are arbitrary, and any constants satisfying
a\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}+\Theta(1)
and
b\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}-\Theta(1)
suffice to solve the property testing problem. Moreover, if an tester is given
k
-copies of a stabilizer state or
k
-copies of a non-stabilizer state with
1/2
probability, the probability of success of the property testing algorithm associated with the POVM
E
is given by

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptp_{\text{succ}}=\frac{1}{2}(a+(1-b))\,.

(285)

We observe that a natural figure of merit for the
k
-copy testing problem is the maximal success probability achievable over all possible POVMs acting on
k
copies.
We now show that the optimal POVM must lie in the commutant. This follows from the observation that any optimal measurement strategy must respect the symmetry constraints imposed by the problem. Since the commutant consists of operators that commute with the symmetry group, it forms the natural space in which the optimal POVM resides.

Proposition 80

(Characterization of the optimal two-outcome POVM)
.

An optimal two-outcome POVM
E
solving the property testing problem (
79
) acting on
k
-copies of the unknown state must lie in the commutant.

Proof.

To prove this, we show that for any POVM
E
satisfying
Eq.

283
, the POVM given by

\displaystyle E^{\prime}=\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(E)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{n}|}\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}C^{\otimes k}EC^{\dagger\otimes k}

(286)

performs at least as well as
E
in the testing problem.

First, if
\rho
is
\varepsilon_{A}
-close to a stabilizer state
\phi
, then for any Clifford
C
, the state
C\rho C^{\dagger}
is also
\varepsilon_{A}
-close to a stabilizer state (i.e.,
C^{\dagger}\phi C
), due to the unitary invariance of the trace distance. This gives:

\tr(E' \rho^{\otimes k})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{n}|}\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}\tr(E (C \rho C^\dagger)^{\otimes k})\geq\frac{2}{3}.

(287)

Similarly, if
\rho
is
\varepsilon_{B}
-far from all stabilizer states, then
C\rho C^{\dagger}
is
\varepsilon_{B}
-far from all stabilizer states for any Clifford
C
. This gives:

\tr(E' \rho^{\otimes k})\leq\frac{1}{3}.

(288)

Therefore, we conclude that
E^{\prime}
satisfies the property testing criteria and performs as well as
E
, which implies that the optimal POVM must lie in the commutant of the Clifford group.
∎

VII.3.1
No efficient testing algorithm with
\leq 5
copies

We now prove that no stabilizer property testing algorithm can succeed using at most five copies of the unknown state. This follows from the fact that the commutant of the Clifford group up to
k=5
contains only primitives proportional to projectors.

Proposition 81
.

No quantum algorithm can solve the stabilizer property testing problem (
79
) using at most five copies of the unknown state.

Proof.

To prove the statement and thus the hardness of stabilizer testing using
k=5
copies, we can focus on showing the hardness, for the less hard case for which
\varepsilon_{A}=0
and the unknown state is assumed to be pure.

Suppose, towards contradiction, that there exists a two-outcome POVM tester
\{E,I-E\}
satisfying
Eq.

283
, capable of testing stabilizer states. First, let us show that the existence of such POVM also implies the existence of a POVM capable of separating Haar random states from uniformly random stabilizer states. First, by definition of stabilizer tester we have

\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\tr(E \psi^{\otimes k})\geq\min_{\phi\in\stab(n)}\tr(E\psi^{\otimes k})\geq\frac{2}{3}.

(289)

On the other hand, we also have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\tr((I - E) \psi^{\otimes k})

\displaystyle\geq\frac{2}{3}\cdot\Pr_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\left(\min_{\phi\in\text{STAB}}\|\psi-\phi\|_{1}\geq\varepsilon_{B}\right)

(290)

\displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\Pr_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\left(2\min_{\phi\in\text{STAB}}\sqrt{1-|\innerproduct{\psi}{\phi}|^{2}}\geq\varepsilon_{B}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\left(1-\Pr_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\left(\max_{\phi\in\text{STAB}}|\innerproduct{\psi}{\phi}|^{2}\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon_{B}^{2}}{4}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\geq\frac{2}{3}\left(1-\exp\left(0.52n^{2}-(2^{n}-1)\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon_{B}^{2}}{4}\right)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\Omega(1),

where in the first step we have used that
1-\tr(E \psi^{\otimes k})\geq\frac{2}{3}
if
\psi
is
\varepsilon_{B}
-far from all stabilizer states, while the fourth step follows from the union bound and Lévy’s lemma (as done explicitly in Ref.
Liu and Winter 2022
).
Therefore, we have

\displaystyle\tr\left(E\left(\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\psi^{\otimes k}-\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\psi^{\otimes k}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\tr(E \psi^{\otimes k})+\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\tr((I - E) \psi^{\otimes k})-1

(291)

\displaystyle=\Omega(1).

However, this provides a contradiction, since the one-norm distance between the moment operators satisfies:

\sup_{E:0<\|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\left|\tr\left(E\left(\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\psi^{\otimes k}-\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\psi^{\otimes k}\right)\right)\right|=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\psi^{\otimes k}-\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\psi^{\otimes k}\right\|_{1}=\exp(-\Omega(n))\,,

(292)

i.e., it is exponentially small in
n
for
k\leq 5
, as we show in
Example

6
.
∎

VII.3.2
Optimal testing by measuring the unitaries in the commutant basis

In the previous section, we established that there is no strategy to solve the stabilizer testing problem when strictly fewer than six copies of the unknown state are available. This result has been derived by reducing the problem of testing stabilizer states to a simpler problem: testing Haar-random states against random stabilizer states, for which we showed hardness.

In this section, we first demonstrate that testing Haar-random states from random stabilizer states becomes feasible when six copies of the unknown state are provided.
Specifically, we show that the two-outcome POVM element
E=\frac{1+\Omega_{6}}{2}
, where
\Omega_{6}\coloneqq\frac{1}{d}\sum P^{\otimes 6}
, enables the testing of Haar-random states against random stabilizer states.

First, note that
E
is a valid POVM element since
\Omega_{6}
is a unitary operator, and its operator norm is equal to one (see
Lemma

45
). Moreover, we have

\displaystyle\tr\left(E\left(\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\psi^{\otimes 6}-\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\psi^{\otimes 6}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\tr\left(\Omega_{6}\psi^{\otimes 6}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\tr\left(\Omega_{6}\psi^{\otimes 6}\right)

(293)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}-\exp(\Omega(-n))=\Omega(1),

where in the second line we have used
Example

7
. Thus, we conclude that
\Omega_{6}
allows for efficient testing of Haar-random states against random stabilizer states, i.e.,
\left\|\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{STAB}}\psi^{\otimes 6}-\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\text{Haar}}\psi^{\otimes 6}\right\|_{1}=\Omega(1)
.

In general, we can state the following.

Proposition 82

(Best POVM for testing given any
k=O(n^{2-c})
for
c>0
copies must be in the span of the unitary basis elements of the commutant)
.

For any
k=O(1)
copies of the unknown state, the best POVM which solves the property testing problem must lie in the span of the unitary elements in the commutant basis. If we have the additional assumption that the unknown state is pure, the best POVM is a linear combination of basis elements of the commutant, projected onto the symmetric subspace that are also unitary.

Proof.

This follows directly from
Lemma

62
by expressing the POVM element as
E\in\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
. Indeed, we can express it as
\hat{M}=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}\alpha_{\Omega}(E)\Omega
with
\Omega
being a Pauli monomial. Using
Lemma

62
, and using that
\|E\|_{\infty}\leq 1
, we know

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\alpha_{\Omega}(E)\leq O(2^{\frac{3}{2}k^{2}-n})

(294)

Therefore, we can express the expectation value of
E
on
\rho
as
\tr(E\rho^{\otimes k})=\sum_{\Omega}\alpha_{\Omega}(E)\tr(\Omega\rho)
.
Since
\tr(\Omega\rho)\leq 1
(see
Theorem

72
), then it immediately follows that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(E\psi^{\otimes k})=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}}\alpha_{\Omega}(E)\tr(\Omega\rho)+O(2^{2k^{2}-n}),

(295)

where we have used the fact the dimension of the
k
-th order commutant in this regime is
O(2^{k^{2}/2})

Nebe et al. 2000
.
Therefore, the operator
E=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}_{U}}\alpha_{\Omega}(E)\Omega
performs as well as the POVM
E
up to an exponentially small error in
n
(in the hypothesis that
k^{2}=o(n^{2-c})
for
c>0
. This proves the statement.
∎

Corollary 83

(Best POVM for testing given
k=6
copies must be given by
\Omega_{6}
)
.

For
k=6
copies of the unknown pure state, the best POVM which solves the property testing problem (even in the possibly general tolerant scenario) must be given by
E=\alpha_{1}\mathbb{1}+\alpha_{2}\Omega_{6}
.

Proof.

This follows directly from the previous proposition and the fact that
\Omega_{6}
is the only unitary residing in the
k=6
order commutant of the Clifford group, when projected onto the symmetric subspace. For an explicit construction of the
k=6
order commutant, see
Section

VII.5.3
.
∎

In fact, Ref.
Gross et al. 2021
has shown that
\Omega_{6}
enables testing using only
6
copies. Using the same argument and our computation of the
k=8
commutant, it follows that an optimal algorithm with access to
8
copies can essentially only use
\Omega_{6}
and the
\Omega
associated to Bell magic.

VII.3.3
An operational meaning for stabilizer entropies

In this section, we build on the results of the previous section to show that stabilizer property testing provides a simple and powerful operational interpretation of the
(\alpha=3)
stabilizer entropy.

Specifically, we formulate the stabilizer testing problem as follows. A tester is given
k=6
copies of an unknown pure quantum state, which is either a stabilizer state
\sigma
with probability
1/2
, or a pure (non-stabilizer) state
\ket{\psi}
with probability
1/2
. The task of the tester is to determine which of the two cases applies. From
Corollary

83
, we know that the optimal POVM is of the form
E=\alpha_{1}\mathbb{1}+\alpha_{2}\Omega_{6}
. The condition
E\geq 0
for a valid POVM implies
\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}
, since
\Omega_{6}
is a unitary operator (cf.
Lemma

29
).

Using
Eq.

285
, the success probability for correctly identifying the state in this scenario is given by

\displaystyle p_{\text{succ}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\tr(E \sigma^{\otimes 6})+\frac{1}{2}\tr((\mathbb{1} - E) \psi^{\otimes 6})

(296)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}[(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})+(1-\alpha_{1})-\alpha_{2}\Delta_{6}(\psi)]

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}[1+\alpha_{2}(1-\Delta_{6}(\psi))],

where we recall the definition of the stabilizer purity
\Delta_{6}(\psi)
from
Definition

67
, and the fact that
\Delta_{6}(\sigma)=1
for all stabilizer states
\sigma
.

Maximizing over
\alpha_{2}
under the constraint
\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}
, we obtain the optimal success probability for the
k=6
property testing problem:

p_{\text{succ}}^{\text{optimal}}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}(1-2^{-2M_{3}(\psi)}),

(297)

and the optimal property testing algorithm (i.e., the one with the highest success probability) is given by
\frac{\mathbb{1}+\Omega_{6}}{2}
.
Eq.

297
endows the
(k=3)
stabilizer entropy with a clear operational meaning, revealing a deep connection between magic-state resource theory and stabilizer property testing.

VII.4
Clifford-symmetric quantum states

The findings here immediately translate into a framework of symmetric states. Group-symmetric states play an important role in quantum information
theory, prominently in entanglement theory, where states that are
U\otimes U
-symmetric go under the name of
Werner states
. The commutant
\com(U\otimes U:U\in{\cal U}(2^{n}))
is spanned by the identity
\mathbb{1}
and the swap operator
T

Werner 1989
. Hence,
the set of Werner states is a one-dimensional set of quantum states. In fact, many interesting research questions can be decided on this set, such as their entanglement distillability. Being able to precisely characterize the commutant of symmetry groups is also instrumental for computing asymptotic entanglement measures under symmetry
Audenaert et al. 2001
. The importance of
being able to characterize sets of group
symmetric
quantum states for the field of quantum information
theory can hardly be overestimated.

Similar statements can also be made for Clifford-symmetric states that are invariant under
{\cal C}_{n}
, again with

\displaystyle\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})\coloneqq\{O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}):C^{\dagger\otimes k}OC^{\otimes k}=O\,\text{ for all }C\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\}.

(298)

The set of symmetric quantum states is then nothing but the intersection of the commutant with the quantum mechanical state space,

\displaystyle{\cal D}_{\cl}({\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}})\coloneq\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})\cap{\cal D}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}),

(299)

which in turn is the positive semi-definite cone intersected with unit trace operators.
Since the commutant is spanned by Pauli monomials
\Omega\in\mathcal{P}
, membership to
the
set
{\cal D}_{\cl}({\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}})
of
Clifford-symmetric quantum states is characterized by the semi-definite feasibility problem

Boyd and Vanderberghe 2004

\displaystyle\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}}c_{\Omega}\Omega\geq 0,

(300)

\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}d^{k-m}\sum_{\Omega\,:\,m(\Omega)=m}c_{\Omega}=1,

(301)

which can be solved for relatively small
k
, with interior point
methods, given the dimension

\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))=\exp(\Theta(k^2))
(see
Theorem

26
)
of
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k})
.

VII.5
Explicit
characterization of the commutant up to
k=8

In this section, we explicitly construct the commutant of the Clifford group for low values of
k
. Specifically, we begin with
k=4
, which represents the first non-trivial case, and extend our analysis up to
k=8
. We provide explicit constructions of the Clifford-Weingarten functions (when restricted to pure quantum states), as introduced in
Section

VII.1.2
, and illustrate their applications with concrete examples.

VII.5.1
k=4

Let us start from the first non-trivial case, i.e.,
k=4
. There are two possible types of Pauli monomials to be defined. One class corresponds to permutations
S_{4}
. The second non-trivial element are generated by
\Omega_{4}
equal to

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega_{4}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 4}

(302)

which is proportional to a projector
(\Omega_{4})^{2}=d\Omega_{4}
. The dimension of the commutant is
\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes 4}))=30
. As such, Weingarten calculus is straightforward. Through graphical calculus, one can verify the following identities

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega_{4}=\Omega_{4}T_{(12)(34)}=\Omega_{4}T_{(13)(24)}=\Omega_{4}T_{(14)(23)}

(303)

For example, the
first identity is verified via the following diagrammatic calculation

=

=

(304)

and the others follow identically. It follows that, in addition to permutations, there are only
6
additional elements, that is,
\Omega_{4}
,
\Omega_{4}T_{(12)}
,
\Omega_{4}T_{(13)}
,
\Omega_{4}T_{(14)}
,
\Omega_{4}T_{(123)}
,
\Omega_{4}T_{(132)}
.
The Gram-Schmidt matrix is a
30\times 30
matrix, which in a compact notation reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{W}^{(4)}=\begin{pmatrix}\tr(T_{\pi}T_{\sigma})&\tr(T_{\kappa}\Omega_4)\\
\tr(T_{\kappa}\Omega_4)&\tr(T_{\kappa}T_{\kappa'}\Omega_4)\end{pmatrix}

(305)

where
\pi,\sigma\in S_{4}
runs over all the permutation group
S_{4}
, while
\kappa,\kappa^{\prime}\in\{(),(12),(13),(14),(123),(132)\}
, for a total of
30
elements. While in Ref.
Bittel et al. 2025
we explicitly provide
the Gram-Schmidt matrix and its inverse for readers interested in utilizing them, here we apply this framework to derive the Clifford orbit of a pure quantum state.
Following
Lemma

59
, we can now simply compute the Clifford twirling operator
\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}
, by computing the Clifford-Weingarten functions
(\mathcal{W}^{-1})_{\Omega,\Omega^{\prime}}
. As such, one
can express
the Clifford twirling of any
operator
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 4})
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(O)=\begin{pmatrix}\tr(T_{\pi}T_{\sigma})&\tr(T_{\kappa}\Omega_4)\\
\tr(T_{\kappa}\Omega_4)&\tr(T_{\kappa}T_{\kappa'}\Omega_4)\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\tr(T_{\pi}O)\\
\tr(T_{\kappa}\Omega_4O)\end{pmatrix}.

(306)

One can express the Clifford orbit of a pure quantum state
\psi^{\otimes 4}=\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}^{\otimes 4}
as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})=p(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}+(1-p(\psi))\frac{\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})}

(307)

where the (quasi)-probability is equal to

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptp(\psi)=\frac{(d+3)(d-\tr(\Omega_4\psi^{\otimes 4}))}{(d+4)(d-1)}.

(308)

Example 4

(Purity fluctuations of Clifford orbit states
Leone et al. 2021
;
Oliviero et al. 2021
)
.

In
Example

8
, we computed starting from the average purity in a subsystem; we computed the average entropy in a subsystem. Let us now focus on the average purity fluctuations. Let us show the example for both the unitary and Clifford cases to also show the relevant differences.
Starting from the unitary case, we have seen in the previous section how the
4
-fold channel is built; let us use these tools to compute the average purity fluctuations. Let us start from the definition of purity fluctuations for a state
\psi
.

\displaystyle\Delta_{\psi\sim\operatorname{Haar}}\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A})\coloneqq\int\de\psi\mathrm{Pur}^{2}(\psi_{A})-\left(\int\de\psi\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A}\right)^{2}.

(309)

That can also be rewritten in a more convenient form as

\displaystyle\Delta_{\psi\sim\operatorname{Haar}}(\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A}))

\displaystyle=\tr(T_{(12)(34)}^{A}\Phi_{\haar}(\psi^{\otimes 4}))-\frac{d_{A}^{2}+d_{B}^{2}+2d_{A}d_{B}}{(d_{A}d_{B}+1)^{2}}

(310)

\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\pi}T^{A}_{(12)(34)}T_{\pi}^{A}T_{\pi}^{B}}{d_{A}d_{B}(d_{A}d_{B}+1)(d_{A}d_{B}+2)(d_{A}d_{B}+3)}-\frac{d_{A}^{2}+d_{B}^{2}+2d_{A}d_{B}}{(d_{A}d_{B}+1)^{2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{2\left(d_{A}^{2}-1\right)\left(d_{B}^{2}-1\right)}{\left(d_{A}d_{B}+1\right)^{2}\left(d_{A}d_{B}+2\right)\left(d_{A}d_{B}+3\right)}

where we have used
the results of
Example

8
.
Shown, as an example, are the
purity fluctuations with respect to the unitary group; we are now able to show what happens when we instead consider the Clifford group.
The purity fluctuations read

\displaystyle\Delta_{\psi\sim\stab_{n}}(\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A}))

\displaystyle=\tr(T_{(12)(34)}^{A}\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4}))-\frac{d_{A}^{2}+d_{B}^{2}+2d_{A}d_{B}}{(d_{A}d_{B}+1)^{2}}

(311)

\displaystyle+\tr(T_{(12)(34)}^{A}\left(p(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}+(1-p(\psi))(\psi)\frac{\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})}\right))-\frac{d_{A}^{2}+d_{B}^{2}+2d_{A}d_{B}}{(d_{A}d_{B}+1)^{2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\left(d_{A}^{2}-1\right)\left(d_{B}^{2}-1\right)\left(\left(d_{A}d_{B}+1\right)\tr( \Omega_4 \psi^{\otimes 4})-2\right)}{\left(d_{A}d_{B}+1\right){}^{2}\left(d_{A}^{2}d_{B}^{2}+d_{A}d_{B}-2\right)}.

As a last application, we compute the trace norm between the Clifford twirling of a pure state and a Haar random state, which is exponentially vanishing.

Example 5

(Trace distance of random Clifford orbit)
.

Let us compute
\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})\|_{1}
.
Let us start by recalling that the twirling over the whole unitary group of a pure quantum state is equivalent to
Proposition

23

\displaystyle\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})=\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}.

(312)

Now by using
Eq.

307
we have that the
1
-norm can be rewritten as follows

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\norm{\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})-\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4}) }_{1}=|1-p(\psi)|\norm{\frac{\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr( \Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}) }-\frac{\Pi_{\sym} }{\tr\Pi_{\sym} }}_{1}.

(313)

To proceed, let us
notice that given an operator in its spectral decomposition
A=\sum_{i}a_{i}\outerproduct{a_i}{a_i}
its
1
-norm is equal to
\norm{A}_{1}=\sum_{i}|a_{i}|
. Then, note the following: (i)
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}/\tr( \Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})
is a mixed quantum state of
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 4}
with purity
\tr^{-1}(\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym})
. (ii)
\Pi_{\sym}/\tr\Pi_{\sym}
and
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}^{(4)}/\tr( \Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})
commute
[\Pi_{\sym},\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}]=0
and thus admit a common basis in the Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 4}
. (iii) The product of
\Pi_{\sym}
and
\Omega_{1}\Pi_{\sym}
is proportional to
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}
as we have
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}\Pi_{\sym}=\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}
. (iv) Both
\Pi_{\sym}
and
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}
are proportional to projectors and therefore have flat spectra.

Therefore, the eigenvalues
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}
of
\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(4)(\psi^{\otimes 4})}
are

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\lambda_{1}=\frac{1}{\tr\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}-\frac{1}{\tr\Pi_{\sym}}

(314)

with multiplicity given by the rank of
\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}
, i.e.,
m_{\lambda_{1}}=\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})
and

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\lambda_{2}=-\frac{1}{\tr\Pi_{\sym}}

(315)

with multiplicity given by the difference of the ranks, i.e.,
m_{\lambda_{2}}=\tr(\Pi_{\sym})-\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})
. Therefore, we get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\norm{\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})-\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})}_{1}

\displaystyle=(1-p(\psi))(m_{\lambda_{1}}\lambda_{1}+m_{\lambda_{2}}|\lambda_{2}|)

(316)

\displaystyle=(1-p(\psi))\left(2-2\frac{\tr\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr\Pi_{\sym}}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{2}{d(d+1)}\left|\Delta_{4}(\psi)-4\right|

and for large
d
, we obtain
\norm{\Phi_{\cl}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})-\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\psi^{\otimes 4})}_{1}\simeq 2\Delta_{4}(\psi)/d
.

VII.5.2
k=5

Let us analyze the commutant for the Clifford group for
k=5
. The cardinality of the commutant is given by
|\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes 5})|=270
. According to
Theorem

55
, the commutant of the Clifford group is generated by permutations and
\Omega_{4}
. It turns out that, other than permutations, there are only
5
more additional elements that, on top of left and right multiplication for permutations, generate the entire commutant, which are
T_{\pi}\Omega_{4}T_{\pi}
. While
\Omega_{4}
is the only one with
m(\Omega)=1
, we can ask if there are others with a higher weight.

{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@fill\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 6.89 -82.68 h 13.78 v 13.78 h -13.78 Z}{stroke:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}{}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {{{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\quad\textbf{=}T_{(15)}\Omega_{4}

(317)

This tells us that the product of any two adjoint permutations of
\Omega_{4}
for
i\in[5]
, regardless of whether a phase is included, results in another instance of
\Omega_{4}
, up to permutations.

Therefore, the
5
order commutant looks very similar to the
4
order commutant embedded in a larger space. The reason is that there is no additional register in which to embed the unitary
\Omega_{6}
that, together with
\Omega_{4}
and permutations, generates the commutant for any
k
.

Exploiting the fact that we do not really have a different non-trivial object in the commutant for
k=5
, but only
\Omega_{4}
embedded in
k=5
copies of the Hilbert space, it is easy to see that there are
30
independent elements for each non-trivial
\Omega
generated by right multiplication for permutations. This can be seen by the fact that any permutation in
S_{5}
can be written as a permutation
\pi\in S_{4}
times a permutation in the set
S_{5/4}\coloneqq\{e,(15),(25),(35),(45)\}
, thus generating a total of
30\times 5+5!=270
, recovering the dimension of the full Clifford group.

We can thus express the Clifford twirling operator
\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(O)
for any
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 5})
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(O)=\sum_{\pi\sigma\in S_{5}}\alpha_{\sigma,\pi}T_{\sigma}\Omega_{4}T_{\sigma^{-1}}T_{\pi}+\beta_{\pi}T_{\pi}

(318)

where the coefficients can be determined by computing the Gram-Schmidt matrix and inverting it to get the Clifford-Weingarten functions. Although we omit the explicit computation of the Clifford-Weingarten functions in this case, we focus again on the computation of the Clifford twirling applied on
5
tensor copies of a pure quantum state, giving explicit details for its computation.

Note that, from
Section

VII.1.3
, we can write

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(\psi)=p(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}+(1-p({\psi}))\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})}

(319)

which is very similar to the one for the case
k=4
, but not exactly. Indeed note that while for
k=4

[\Omega_{4},\Pi_{\sym}]=0
, for
k=5
we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}\propto\sum_{\sigma}(T_{\sigma}\Omega_{4}T_{\sigma^{-1}})\Pi_{\sym}

(320)

and thus clearly
[\Omega_{4},\Pi_{\sym}]\neq 0
. To find the probabilities, we proceed in the way sketched in
Section

VII.1.3
and write the matrix
\mathcal{S}
down as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\
1&\frac{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})^{2}}\\
\end{pmatrix}.

(321)

Let us compute the matrix elements.
First of all,

\tr(\Pi_{\sym})=d(d+1)(d+2)(d+3)(d+4)/120
. Then, because of the structure of the symmetric group, one can write the projector onto the symmetric subspace as
\Pi_{\sym}=\frac{1}{5!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{4},\sigma\in S_{5/4}}T_{\pi}T_{\sigma}
, which allows us to compute the trace right away as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})=\frac{1}{5!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{4},\sigma\in S_{5/4}}\tr(\Omega_4T_{\pi}T_{\sigma})=\frac{1}{5!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{4},\sigma\in S_{5/4}}\tr(\Omega_4T_{\pi}\tr_5T_{\sigma})=\frac{(d+4)}{5}\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}),

(322)

where we have used the fact that

\tr_{5}T_{4,5}=d^{-1}\sum_{P}\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 3}\otimes P\otimes\tr(P)=\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 4}
. Thus, we have
\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})=\frac{d+4}{5}\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})
. Similarly

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{5!}\sum_{\pi,i}\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Omega_4T_{\pi})

(323)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{5}\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4(d\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 5}+T_{(15)}+T_{(25)}+T_{(35)}+T_{(45)}))

\displaystyle=\frac{(d+4)}{5}\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}),

where we have used the identity
\Omega_{4}T_{\pi}\Omega_{4}T_{\pi}=\Omega_{4}T_{(i5)}
for any
i\in[2,\ldots,5]
, which we showed by the graphical calculus in
Eq.

317
. Finally, we can express the matrix
\mathcal{S}
, and its inverse

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\
1&\frac{(d+4)(d+3)}{5}\\
\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\mathcal{S}^{-1}=\frac{d(d+1)(d+2)(d+3)(d+4)}{6(d+8)(d-1)}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{(d+4)(d+3)}{20}&-1\\
-1&1\\
\end{pmatrix}.

(324)

Therefore, according to
Section

VII.1.3
, we can compute the quasi-probabilities as

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p(\psi)\\
1-p(\psi)\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{S}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\psi^{\otimes 5})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\\
\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\psi^{\otimes 5})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{(d+3)(d+4-5\Delta_{4}(\psi)))}{(d+8)(d-1)}\\
\frac{5[(d+3)\Delta_{4}(\psi))-4]}{(d+8)(d-1)}\end{pmatrix}

(325)

where
\Delta_{4}(\psi)
is the stabilizer purity, see
Definition

67
.

As an application, let us compute the trace distance between
\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})
and
\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})
and show that
5
copies of a stabilizer state cannot be distinguished by
5
copies of a Haar random state.

Example 6

(Trace distance of random Clifford orbit)
.

Let us compute
\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})\|_{1}
. Using
Eq.

319
, we can immediately write

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\left\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})\right\|_{1}

\displaystyle=\left(1-p(\psi)\right)\left\|\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}-\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)}\right\|

(326)

\displaystyle\left(1-p(\psi)\right)\left(\left\|\frac{\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\right\|+\left\|\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4}\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)}\right\|\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2(1-p(\psi))

where we have used the fact that
p(\psi)\geq 0
. Using
Eq.

325
, we get

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\left\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(5)}(\psi^{\otimes 5})\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{10[(d+3)\Delta_{4}(\psi))-4]}{(d+8)(d-1)}=O(d^{-1}).

(327)

VII.5.3
k=6

k=6

m
, i.e., the number of primitives in the matrix
V
. For
m=0
, we only have the identity.
m=1

(330)

This concludes the possible terms, since it is not difficult to see that adding an additional
\Omega_{1}
term would return us still
\Omega_{3}
up to permutations.
Hence, the commutant, other than permutations, is spanned by the following operators, up to left and right action of permutations

\displaystyle\Omega_{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 6}

\displaystyle\Omega_{4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 4}\otimes\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 4},

\displaystyle\Omega_{6}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 6}\otimes\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 2},

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes(PQ)^{\otimes 2}\otimes Q^{\otimes 2}.

(331)

While it is clear that multiplying the different
\Omega
among themselves does not generate new elements of the commutant, the same is not true when considering permutations. To generate all possible elements of the commutant, we must
permute
the representative elements. Thus, the most general element of the commutant for
k=6

is
T_{\pi}\Omega^{(6)}T_{\sigma}
, where
T_{\pi}
and
T_{\sigma}
are permutation matrices. In
Table

1
, we show the cardinality of the different classes generated.

\Omega

\#(T_{\pi}\Omega T_{\sigma})

\Omega_{2}

720

\Omega_{4}

2700

\Omega_{6}

720

\Omega_{4,4}

450

Table 1:
Cardinality of the independent class forming the basis for
\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes 6})
.

Once we have given the Clifford commutant for
k=6
, we can then introduce the action of the twirling operator. By noticing that all the terms are given by
T_{\pi}\Omega T_{\sigma}
, the twirling operator for
k=6
can be written as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(O)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Omega\in\mathcal{P}\\
\pi\sigma\in S_{6}\end{subarray}}T_{\pi}\left(\alpha_{\pi,\sigma}^{(\Omega)}\Omega\right)T_{\sigma}

(332)

where each of the coefficients can be computed through the inverse of the Gram-Schmidt matrix through the rules introduced in
Section

VII.1.2
.

As done before, instead of directly computing the Clifford Weingarten functions, let us focus our attention on the twirling of a pure quantum state. We can write

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega,\in\mathcal{P}/S_{6}}p_{\Omega}(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega)}

(333)

where the
p_{\Omega}
s are equal to

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptp_{\Omega}(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}/S_{6}}(\mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\Omega\Omega^{\prime}}\frac{\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega)}.

(334)

One can then use the definition of
\mathcal{S}
from
Section

VII.1.3
with
k=6
, leading to the computation of

\displaystyle S=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&1\\
1&\frac{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym} )\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})^{2}}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_6 \Pi_{\sym})}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_{4,4} \Pi_{\sym})}\\
1&\frac{\tr(\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym} )\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_6 \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_6 \Pi_{\sym})^{2}}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_6 \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_{4,4} \Pi_{\sym})}\\
1&\frac{\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym} )\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_{4,4} \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_4 \Pi_{\sym})}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_{4,4} \Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Omega_6 \Pi_{\sym})}&\frac{\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym})\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}{\tr(\Omega_{4,4} \Pi_{\sym})^{2}}\end{pmatrix}.

(335)

The computation of
\mathcal{S}
reduces to the computation of a few elements, and then combines them. So we have, by brute force computation, the result

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{180}d(d+5)(d+4)(d+2)(d+1),

(336)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{30}d(d+4)(d+2)(d+1),

(337)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{6!}d(d+23)(d+4)(d+2)(d+1),

(338)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2700}d(d+1)(d+2)(d+4)(76+13d+d^{2}),

(339)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)

\displaystyle=\frac{(d+4)}{5}\tr(\Pi_{\sym} \Omega_{4,4}),

(340)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4)

\displaystyle=\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4),

(341)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{450}d(d+4)^{2}(d+2)^{2}(d+1),

(342)

\displaystyle\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4})

\displaystyle=\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}).

(343)

Consequently, the matrix
\mathcal{S}
can be written as

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&1\\
1&\frac{(d^{2}+13d+76)(d+3)}{60(d+5)}&\frac{(4+d)(d+3)}{20}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}\\
1&\frac{(d+3)(4+d)}{20}&\frac{(d+5)(d+4)(d+3)(d+2)}{360}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}\\
1&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}&\frac{(5+d)^{2}(d+3)^{2}}{(23+d)^{2}}\end{pmatrix}.

(344)

Therefore, according to
Section

VII.1.3
we get that the quasi-probabilities are

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p_{2}\\
p_{4}\\
p_{6}\\
p_{4,4}\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&1\\
1&\frac{(d^{2}+13d+76)(d+3)}{60(d+5)}&\frac{(4+d)(d+3)}{20}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}\\
1&\frac{(d+3)(4+d)}{20}&\frac{(d+5)(d+4)(d+3)(d+2)}{360}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}\\
1&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}&\frac{(5+d)(d+3)}{23+d}&\frac{(5+d)^{2}(d+3)^{2}}{(23+d)^{2}}\end{pmatrix}\right]^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\psi^{\otimes 6})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\\
\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_4\Pi_{sym}^{(6)}\psi^{\otimes 6})}{\tr(\Omega_4\Pi_{\sym})}\\
\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_6\Pi_{sym}^{(6)}\psi^{\otimes 6})}{\tr(\Omega_6\Pi_{\sym})}\\
\frac{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{sym}^{(6)}\psi^{\otimes 6})}{\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\Pi_{\sym})}\end{pmatrix}

(345)

\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{(d+5)(d+3)[(d^{2}+13d)-\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\psi^{\otimes 6})(d-32)-(15d+60)\tr(\Omega_4\psi^{\otimes 4})+30\tr(\Omega_6\psi^{\otimes 6})]}{(d+16)(d+8)(d-1)(d-2)}\\
\frac{15(d+5)[-4(d+4)-4(d+4)\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\psi^{\otimes 6})-(d^{2}+8d+52)\tr(\Omega_4\psi^{\otimes 4})-3(d+6)\tr(\Omega_6\psi^{\otimes 6})]}{(d+16)(d+8)(d-1)(d-2)}\\
\frac{720+720\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\psi^{\otimes 6})+270(d+6)\tr(\Omega_4\psi^{\otimes 4})+15(d+14)(d+1)\tr(\Omega_6\psi^{\otimes 6})}{(d+16)(d+8)(d-1)(d-2)}\\
\frac{(d+23)[-(d-32)+d(d+13)\tr(\Omega_{4,4}\psi^{\otimes 6})-(15d+60)\tr(\Omega_4\psi^{\otimes 4})+30\tr(\Omega_6\psi^{\otimes 6})]}{(d+16)(d+8)(d-1)(d-2)}\end{pmatrix},

where we are adopting the lighter notation of
p_{x}\coloneqq p_{\Omega_{x}}
.
Let us point out that, for the sake of completeness, the inverse matrix of
\mathcal{S}
is given in Ref.
Bittel et al. 2025
.

In
Examples

5
and
6
, we showed that the trace distance between five coherent copies of Haar-random states and random stabilizer states is exponentially small. In the following, we show that for
k=6
, the trace distance becomes large. This occurs because the commutant supports the first non-trivial unitary primitive,
\Omega_{6}
.

Example 7

(Trace distance of random Clifford orbit)
.

Let us compute the lower bound
\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})\|_{1}
. To do it, let us start by considering the unitary primitive
\Omega_{6}
. The expectation value over
\psi^{\otimes 6}
corresponds to the stabilizer purity
\Delta_{6}(\psi)=\tr(\Omega_6\psi^{\otimes 6})
, see
Definition

67
. If
\psi
is a pure quantum state vector it follows

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Delta_{6}(\psi)-\tr(\Phi_{\haar}^{(6)}\Omega_6)=\tr(\Omega_6(\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})-\Phi_{\haar}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})))\leq\|\Omega_{6}\|_{\infty}\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})\|_{1}

(346)

which implies that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\|\Phi_{\cl}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(6)}(\psi^{\otimes 6})\|_{1}\geq\Delta_{6}(\psi)-O(d^{-1}).

(347)

For the case of
\sigma\in\stab(n)
, since
\Delta_{6}(\sigma)=1
(see
Definition

67
), then
\|\Phi_{\cl}(\sigma^{\otimes 6})-\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(6)}(\sigma^{\otimes 6})\|_{1}\geq 1-O(d^{-1})
.

VII.5.4
k=8

In this section, we construct the commutant for
k=8
. We want to construct all the Pauli monomials that are independent up to left and right multiplication for permutations. The analysis is quite similar to the one done for
k=6
, and previously for
k=5
and
k=4
. We do it iteratively, by iterating over
m
, i.e., the number of primitives in the matrix
V
. For
m=0
, we only have the identity.

Section

V.1
, we know that two even primitives overlapping evenly with a phase are equivalent to an odd primitive up to right multiplication for permutations. Therefore, the fourth and the sixth monomial in

349
are permutationally equivalent to
\Omega_{6}

(352)

We can now start adding primitives to
\Omega_{2}^{(8)}
. However, we have already exhausted all the possibilities allowed by analyzing
\Omega_{4}
by
Eq.

351
and
\Omega_{4,6}
.

Now, we can construct Pauli monomials with
m=3
from
\Omega_{4,4},\cdots,\Omega_{6,6}
. We observe that it is only sufficient to add the weight four primitives. Indeed, adding a weight
8
primitive would necessarily make the Pauli monomial not reducible anymore, and adding a weight
6
primitive would necessarily result in a Pauli monomial corresponding to a
V
equivalent to one with weight 2 vectors in the span. Therefore, we can add weight 2 vectors only to
\Omega_{4}^{(8)},\Omega_{5}^{(8)},\Omega_{6}^{(8)}
. However, it will be sufficient to add all the possible weight 2 primitives to
\Omega_{4}^{(8)}
to exhaust all possibilities. Let us first write all the possibilities as

(353)

Notice that we did not consider any phases yet, as it turns out that all the Pauli monomials with phases are dependent on all the others that we already defined. Indeed, since in
\Omega_{4,4,4}
and
\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 1}}
all primitives commute, by virtue of
Section

V.1
, we know that any commuting weight 2 primitive with a phase can be reduced to a weight
6
primitive up to permutation, which has already been covered by the Pauli monomials defined above with
m=2
. However, for
\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 2}}
, the argument is even simpler: the third and the second primitive anticommute with each other, and therefore any phases put between them can be canceled by a trivial swapping, cf.
Section

V.1
.

We are now left with the last case, that is,
m=4
. Following the reasoning above, the only possibility is to add a weight 4 primitive to
\Omega_{4,4,4},\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 1}},\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 2}}
. However, by the same argument as before, it will be sufficient to add it to just the first one. In particular, for
\Omega_{4,4,4}
and
\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 1}}
there is one possibility in each case that would result in the same Pauli monomial with

(354)

whereas, it is not possible to add anything to
\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 2}}
as it would result in a vector space with a weight 2 vector in it. By the same argument as in the case
m=3
, adding any phase would result in a lower
m
Pauli monomial, since two weight 4 primitives sharing a phase are permutationally equivalent to a weight 6 primitive. At this point, it is easy to get convinced that no more primitive can be added to
\Omega_{4,4,4,4}
without violating our
3
above principles. Hence, the commutant with
k=8
is spanned by the following operators, up to left and right action for permutations

\displaystyle\Omega_{2}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{1},

(355)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 4}\otimes\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 4},

(356)

\displaystyle\Omega_{6}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 6}\otimes\mathbb{1}^{\otimes 2},

(357)

\displaystyle\Omega_{8}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P}P^{\otimes 8},

(358)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes(PQ)^{\otimes 2}\otimes Q^{\otimes 2}\otimes I^{\otimes 2},

(359)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 3}\otimes(PQ)\otimes Q^{\otimes 3},

(360)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 4}\otimes Q^{\otimes 4},

(361)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,6}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes(PQ)^{\otimes 2}\otimes Q^{\otimes 4},

(362)

\displaystyle\Omega_{6,6}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{P,Q}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes(PQ)^{\otimes 4}\otimes Q^{\otimes 2},

(363)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4,4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{3}}\sum_{P,Q,K}P^{\otimes 2}\otimes(PK)^{\otimes 2}\otimes(QK)^{\otimes 2}\otimes Q^{\otimes 2},

(364)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{3}}\sum_{P,Q,K}P\otimes(PK)\otimes(PQ)\otimes(PQK)\otimes(QK)\otimes Q\otimes K\otimes\mathbb{1},

(365)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4,4^{\scriptscriptstyle 2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{3}}\sum_{P,Q,K}(PK)\otimes P\otimes(PQK)\otimes(PQ)\otimes Q^{\otimes 2}\otimes K^{\otimes 2},

(366)

\displaystyle\Omega_{4,4,4,4}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{4}}\sum_{P,Q,K,L}(PL)\otimes P\otimes(PQKL)\otimes(PQK)\otimes(QL)\otimes Q\otimes(KL)\otimes K.

(367)

Extending the logic from the
k=6
case, the commutant for
k=8
is generated by permuting its representative elements,
\Omega
. Specifically, any element can be expressed as
T_{\pi}\Omega T_{\sigma}
, where
T_{\pi}
and
T_{\sigma}
are permutation matrices. The cardinality of the resulting classes is presented in

2
.

.

Once built the commutant for
k=8
, we can also write the general equation for the twirling of an operator
O
as

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(8)}(O)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Omega\in\mathcal{P}\\
\pi\sigma\in S_{8}\end{subarray}}T_{\pi}(\alpha_{\pi,\sigma}^{(\Omega)}\Omega)T_{\sigma}

(368)

where each of the coefficients can be computed through the inverse of the Gram-Schmidt matrix through the rules introduced in
Section

VII.1.2
. As done before, instead of directly computing the Clifford Weingarten functions, let us focus our attention on the twirling of a pure quantum state. We can write

\displaystyle\Phi_{\cl}^{(8)}(\psi^{\otimes 8})=\sum_{\Omega\in\mathcal{P}/S_{8}}p_{\Omega}(\psi)\frac{\Pi_{\sym}\Omega\Pi_{\sym}}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega)}

(369)

where the
p_{\Omega}
s are equal to

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0ptp_{\Omega}(\psi)=\sum_{\Omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}/S_{8}}(\mathcal{S}^{-1})_{\Omega\Omega^{\prime}}\frac{\tr(\Omega\psi^{\otimes k})}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym}\Omega)}.

(370)

VIII
Clifford commutant in the multi-qudit scenario

Preliminaries:

We consider a system of
n
qudits with local dimension
q
, being a prime number. It is crucial for
q
to be a prime number, so that the generalized Pauli operators have the same eigenvalues and the Clifford group can be defined analogously to the qubit case, as those unitary operators that map Pauli operators to Pauli operators. In the reminder of the section, we adopt the same notation that we have used for the qubit case, and
\mathbb{P}_{n}
,
\mathcal{C}_{n}
denotes the Pauli group and the Clifford group on
n
qudits. Similarly, the dimension of the Hilbert space is denoted as
d\equiv q^{n}
. The generalized Pauli operators on
n
qudits, that in the following will be called as
Weyl operators
to adapt better to the current literature, are generated by the following
X
- and
Z
-like operators:

\displaystyle X\ket{i}=\ket{i+1}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad Z\ket{i}=\omega^{i}\ket{i}

(371)

where
\omega=e^{-2\pi i/q}
. We also define
\tau=\sqrt{\omega}=e^{i\pi(q^{2}+1)/q}
. Notice that for
q>2
, the square root can be uniquely defined as a power of
\omega
.
The single qudit Weyl operators are given by

\displaystyle P=\tau^{ac}X^{a}Z^{c}\,.

(372)

for
a,c\in\mathbb{F}_{q}
. Analogously to the qubit case, we can encode each Weyl operator
P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}
into a string
b(P)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2n}
, which gives the rule

\displaystyle PQ

\displaystyle=\tau^{b(P)^{T}Jb(Q)}K,

(373)

\displaystyle PQ

\displaystyle=\omega^{b(P)^{T}Jb(Q)}QP

(374)

of the product between Weyl operators.
In the above

\displaystyle J\coloneqq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},

(375)

while
b(K)=b(P)+b(Q)\pmod{q}
. By recalling
Eq.

59
, and from the equations above, it follows that one can identify

\displaystyle\chi(P,Q)=\omega^{b(P)^{T}Jb(Q)}.

(376)

Since the branch of the square root is fixed by demanding that it remains a
q
-th root of unity, we can define

\displaystyle\sqrt{\chi(P,Q)}\coloneqq\tau^{b(P)^{T}Jb(Q)}\,.

(377)

Orthogonal basis for the commutant and its dimension:

Let us now outline a proof analogous to that of
Theorem

25
. The key step in the proof of
Theorem

25
is the definition of the equivalence class
[V,G]
. We begin by identifying the analog of
V
. Observe that for
k
tensor copies and any
Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\otimes k}
, we have
b(Q)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2nk}
, which allows us to construct
B(Q)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k\times 2n}
via the vectorization isomorphism. One can also prove an analog of
Lemma

13
. Specifically, we can decompose
B(Q)
as
B(Q)=VB_{\boldsymbol{P}}^{T}
, where
V\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k\times m}
and
B_{\boldsymbol{P}}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2n\times m}
, with
m
denoting the minimal rank. This means we can write

\displaystyle Q\propto P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\,,

(378)

where
V=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{m})
and
P_{1},\ldots,P_{m}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}
. As in
Lemma

13
, all such decompositions are related by multiplication with an invertible matrix
A\in\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times m})
.

We also define the
weighted anticommutation
graph
G
, with associated matrix
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}
, via the relation

\displaystyle P_{i}P_{j}-\omega^{\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}}P_{j}P_{i}=0\,,\quad P_{i},P_{j}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}\,.

(379)

From this, it follows that
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})
is anti-symmetric, i.e.,
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})^{T}=-\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})
, and
\chi(P_{i},P_{j})=\omega^{\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}}
.

We define the phase
\varphi(P)
(as in the statement of
Theorem

25
) for Weyl operators analogously to be

\displaystyle\varphi(P)=\frac{\tr(P T_{(k \cdots 2\ 1)})}{d}\,.

(380)

The condition
\varphi(P)\neq 0
is necessary and sufficient for
\Phi_{\cl}^{(k)}(P)\neq 0
. For
\varphi(P)\neq 0
, we require
\sum_{i}v_{i}=0\pmod{q}
. For each
v\in\mathbb{F}_{q}
, this condition determines the last entry, effectively yielding a
(k-1)
-dimensional vector space.

Clifford operators on qudits can likewise map any list of Weyl operators to any other, provided the algebraic and anticommutation relations are preserved, as one can similarly prove an analog of
Lemma

17
. Hence, the equivalence class
[V,G]
is defined identically.

This procedure defines the independent-based graph monomials
\mho_{I}([V,G])
, which form a basis for any
n
and
k
, analogous to the qubit case as

\mho_{I}(V,G)\coloneqq\frac{1}{S_{[V,G]}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\\
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\\
\boldsymbol{P}\text{ is alg. indep.}\end{subarray}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}},

(381)

where
S_{[V,G]}
denotes the set of all such Weyl operators, which forms the Weyl orbit under Clifford operations.

We now consider which graphs are admissible. The strategy used in
Theorem

25
—constructing pairwise noncommuting and otherwise commuting Weyl operators by multiplication—works also for
\mathbb{F}_{q}
. Therefore, we can replicate the same argument from
Theorem

25
, sketched below. Any matrix
G
can be brought by invertible transformations to the canonical (anti-symmetric) form:

\displaystyle G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
-1&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus 0_{m-2r,m-2r}.

(382)

We can describe a noncommutation graph on
m-r
qudits by choosing appropriate Weyl operators for each noncommuting pair. Since any two algebraically independent Weyl operators on a single qudit do not commute, we get
\mathrm{rank}_{q}(G)\geq 2(m-n)
. Consequently, in analogy with
Theorem

26
, the dimension of the commutant is given by

\displaystyle\dim(\com(\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\otimes k}))

\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{r=\max(m-n,0)}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\binom{k-1}{m}_{q}N_{q}(m,r)

(383)

\displaystyle\simeq\begin{cases}q^{\frac{k^{2}-3k}{2}+1}&\text{if }2n\geq k-1,\\
q^{2kn-2n^{2}-3n}&\text{if }2n<k-1,\end{cases}

where
N_{q}(m,r)
(see, e.g., Ref.
Carlitz 1954
) denotes the number of
m\times m
anti-symmetric matrices over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
with rank
2r
, and the Gaussian binomial coefficient
\binom{k-1}{m}_{q}
count the number of even vector subspaces of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
of dimension
m
. The approximation in
Eq.

383
follows identically to the one in
Theorem

26
, since the structure of the expressions remains the same apart from the base of the exponentials. The bounds should also become increasingly accurate with increasing
q
.

Weyl monomials
(\Omega)
:

Similarly to the qubit case, alternative bases—beyond the one formed by independent graph-based monomials—can be defined. These alternative bases often offer more manageable or insightful representations. The strategy to define such bases is to directly generalize the linear transformations that connect them in the qubit setting, as explored in
Section

V.3.2
.

Starting from
Eq.

381
, we extend the definition to include ordered lists of Pauli operators that are not necessarily algebraically independent:

\mho(V,G)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\\
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\end{subarray}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}.

(384)

These are precisely the qudit analogues of the “
\mho
” basis introduced in
Section

V.3
. Following the approach of
Section

V.3.2
, we employ a Fourier-like transform over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
to define Weyl monomials. Starting from the definition above, we proceed as follows:

\displaystyle\mho(V,G)

\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}\\
\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})=G\end{subarray}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}

(385)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}\prod_{i<j}\delta_{\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}=G_{i,j}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}q^{m(m-1)/2}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}\prod_{i<j}\sum_{M_{i,j}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}\omega^{M_{i,j}(\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}-G_{i,j})}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{m}q^{m(m-1)/2}}\sum_{M\in\operatorname{Asym}(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times m})}\omega^{-\sum_{i<j}M_{i,j}G_{i,j}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{\times m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_{j}^{\otimes v_{j}}\prod_{i<j}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}

\displaystyle\eqqcolon\frac{1}{q^{m(m-1)/2}}\sum_{M\in\operatorname{Asym}(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times m})}\omega^{-\sum_{i<j}M_{i,j}G_{i,j}}\Omega(V,M),

where we have used the identity
\frac{1}{q}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\omega^{qi}=\delta_{i0}
, and the fact that
\chi(P_{i},P_{j})=\omega^{\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{P})_{i,j}}
. Since the Fourier-like transform is invertible, it follows that the monomials
\Omega(V,M)
form a well-defined basis of the commutant for
n\geq k-1
. From
Section

VIII
, they are defined as

\displaystyle\Omega(V,M)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d^{m}}\sum_{\boldsymbol{P}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{m}}P_{1}^{\otimes v_{1}}P_{2}^{\otimes v_{2}}\cdots P_{m}^{\otimes v_{m}}\times\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[m]\\
i<j\end{subarray}}\chi(P_{i},P_{j})^{M_{i,j}}\right).

(386)

Primitive monomials:

Among the Weyl monomials, some are particularly simple and fundamental: the
primitive Weyl monomials
, defined as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Omega(v)\coloneqq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P^{\otimes v},

(387)

where
v\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}
satisfies the constraint
\sum_{i}v_{i}=0\pmod{q}
.

Analogously to
Lemma

29
, we can determine when these primitives are unitary or proportional to projectors. Specifically, by using the identity

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}\chi(P,Q)=d^{2}\delta_{P=\mathbb{1}},

(388)

we obtain the following classification:

•

If
\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2}=0
, then
\Omega(v)
is proportional to a projector of rank
d^{k-2}
, i.e.,
\Omega^{2}(v)=d\Omega(v)
;

•

Otherwise,
\Omega(v)
is a unitary operator.

Substitution rules:

In
Section

V
, we introduced the graphical calculus—an intuitive method for manipulating Pauli monomials, which are generated as products of primitive Pauli monomials. At the core of this calculus lies the substitution rule for Pauli monomials, formalized in
Theorem

38
.

While it is possible to extend this framework to a
colored
graphical calculus for qudits, such an extension can become increasingly intricate as the local dimension grows. Therefore, in this section we restrict ourselves to sketching the
algebraic
version of the substitution rule, which serves as a generalization of
Theorem

37
.
The relations

\displaystyle P^{\otimes v}Q^{\otimes w}

\displaystyle=\left(\sqrt{\chi(K,Q)}\,KQ\right)^{\otimes v}Q^{\otimes w}=\left(\sqrt{\chi(K,Q)}\right)^{\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2}}K^{\otimes v}Q^{\otimes(v+w)},

(389)

\displaystyle\chi(P,L)

\displaystyle=\chi\left(\sqrt{\chi(K,Q)}\,KQ,L\right)=\chi(KQ,L)=\chi(K,L)\chi(Q,L),

(390)

hold,
where
P=\sqrt{\chi(K,Q)}\,KQ
. Then, the substitution rules result in the mapping:

\displaystyle v_{i+1}\mapsto v_{i+1}+v_{i},\qquad M_{\cdot,i+1}\mapsto M_{\cdot,i+1}+M_{\cdot,i}+\frac{\sum_{\alpha}(v_{i})_{\alpha}^{2}}{2}\vec{e}_{i},\qquad M_{i+1,\cdot}\mapsto M_{i+1,\cdot}+M_{i,\cdot}-\frac{\sum_{\alpha}(v_{i})_{\alpha}^{2}}{2}\vec{e}_{i}.

(391)

This operation mirrors the substitution rule used in the qubit case. Consequently, one can employ the same algebraic expressions to compute equivalences and define the matrix
\Lambda
, as introduced in
Theorem

37

\displaystyle H^{1/2}_{i,j}

\displaystyle\coloneqq\begin{cases}(V^{T}V)_{i,j}&\text{if }i<j,\\
(V^{T}V)_{i,i}/2&\text{if }i=j,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

(392)

\displaystyle\Lambda

\displaystyle\coloneqq H^{1/2}+M.

(393)

Normal form and generators:

The final aspect to address is the structure of the multi-qudit Clifford commutant from the perspective of algebra. In
Section

VI
, we demonstrated that primitive monomials generate the full commutant in the qubit case. In line with other generalizations, we now discuss how this result extends to the multi-qudit setting.

The reduced form, as introduced in
Definition

39
, is inherently preserved in the qudit generalization and remains well-defined. Similarly, the notion of a normal form (see
Lemma

46
) carries over naturally. The proof of
Lemma

46
relies solely on the substitution rules established in
Theorem

38
, which can be replicated in the qudit case with analogous arguments. This is because these rules depend only on the underlying algebraic transformations, and as shown in the preceding paragraphs, the matrix
\Lambda
governing these transformations behaves identically in the qudit setting.

In particular, a primitive corresponding to a unitary can be shifted to the right, effectively absorbing any global phases. Additionally, two projectors that do not commute can be rewritten as a combination of a unitary and a projector. Commuting projectors with non-trivial relative phases can also be rewritten as a product of unitary primitives via conjugation with a commuting unitary.
Consequently, we can define a
normal form
for Weyl monomials

\displaystyle\Omega=\Omega_{P}\times\Omega_{U},

(394)

where
\Omega_{P}
is a product of commuting projective primitives and
\Omega_{U}
is a product of unitary primitives. This implies that the entire commutant in the multi-qudit setting can also be generated by products of primitive Weyl monomials.

Applications:

In
Section

VII
, we employed the framework developed in the previous sections to explore scenarios in which the Clifford commutant plays a central role—most notably, in magic-state resource theory and stabilizer property testing. Just as in the qubit case, these two topics are of significant interest in the qudit setting as well. In particular, the results of
Section

VII.2
can be generalized to qudits, allowing for the definition of a measurable family of magic measures that meaningfully extend stabilizer entropies to multi-qudit quantum states.

We note that parts of this generalization have already been explored in Ref.
Turkeshi et al. 2025
, where the authors showed that generalized stabilizer entropies for qutrits (
q=3
), defined via the expectation values of primitive Weyl monomials, are not only valid magic measures (according to our definition in
Section

VII.2
) but also satisfy the stronger condition of being magic monotones.

For stabilizer property testing, similar conclusions to those presented in
Section

VII.3
can be drawn in the qudit context. In particular, we can determine, as a function of the local dimension
q
, the minimal number of copies required to achieve a non-exponentially vanishing success probability for testing stabilizerness. This critical threshold depends on whether the commutant—beyond the permutation operators—is spanned by unitary or projective Weyl monomials, just as discussed in
Section

VII.3
.

As an example, we can see why qudit Cliffords are not
3
-designs. This follows as non-trivial Weyl monomials exist

\Omega(1,1,-2)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{P\in\mathbb{P}_{n}}P\otimes P\otimes P^{\dagger 2},

(395)

For qutrits (
q=3
), we only have this
\Omega(1,1,-2)=\Omega(1,1,1)
and permutations. As
\Omega(1,1,1)
is a projector, testing stabilizer properties using only
k=3
copies is not possible for qutrits, meaning stabilizer states form an approximate state
3
-design. In contrast, for local dimension
q=5
, the same monomial
\Omega(1,1,-2)
becomes unitary, making testing feasible with just three copies.

Appendix

Appendix A.1
Examples of Haar average over the unitary group step by step

In this section, we are going to show an example for relatively small order
k
of the
k
-fold twirling in
Eq.

23
. For a more comprehensive reference and tutorial, see also Refs.
Zhang 2024
;
Mele 2024
. Let us start with the following definition

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Gamma^{(k)}_{\operatorname{Haar}}\coloneqq\int\de UU^{\otimes k}\otimes U^{{\dagger}\otimes k}

(A1)

It is useful to write down the relation between the
k
-fold channel
\Phi^{(k)}_{\operatorname{Haar}}(\cdot)
and the
\Gamma^{(k)}_{\operatorname{Haar}}
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(O)=\tr_{1,\ldots,k}(\hat{T}\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}O\otimes\mathbb{1}).

(A2)

Note, indeed, that
\Gamma_{\mathcal{E}}^{(k)}
is an operator on
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2k}
. Let us compute the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2k})
. Let us recall that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(k)}(O)=\sum_{\pi,\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\sigma}\tr(T_{\pi}O)T_{\sigma}=\sum_{\pi,\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\sigma}\tr_{1,\ldots,k}(T_{\pi}\otimes T_{\sigma}O\otimes\mathbb{1}).

(A3)

By comparing
Eqs.

A3
and
A2
which are valid for every
O\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k})
, it is easy to be convinced that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Gamma^{(k)}_{\operatorname{Haar}}=\hat{T}\sum_{\pi,\sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1})_{\pi,\sigma}T_{\pi}\otimes T_{\sigma}

(A4)

where
\hat{T}
has been defined above as a product of elementary swaps
\hat{T}=\prod_{j=1}^{k}T_{k,k+j}
. To check the validity of
Eq.

A4
, it suffices to note that
\hat{T}^{2}=\mathbb{1}
.

As a useful application, let us begin by considering the Haar
1
-fold channel in
Eq.

23
. The symmetric group
S_{1}=\{e\}
is filled by just the identity. Therefore, the matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
is just a number equal to
\Omega=\tr(\mathbb{1})=d
; consequently, we only have one Weingarten function
W=d^{-1}
and thus it is straightforward to write the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(1)}
, defined below in
Eq.

A4
, as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}=T\left(\frac{\mathbb{1}\otimes\mathbb{1}}{d}\right)=\frac{T}{d}

(A5)

where
T
is the swap operator between the two copies of
\mathcal{H}
. Now, consider the operator
A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
. The
1
-fold channel applied in
A
reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(1)}(A)=\frac{\tr(A)}{d}\mathbb{1}.

(A6)

The
2
-fold channel, i.e.,
k=2
, is the first non-trivial example of a Haar channel that has found an enormous number of applications. In this section, we will explore just a couple of those.

The symmetric group
S_{2}=\{e,(12)\}
is given by the identity
\mathbb{1}
and the swap operator
T
on
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2}
. The matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\begin{pmatrix}\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T)\\
\tr(T)&\tr(TT)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}d^{2}&d\\
d&d^{2}\end{pmatrix}

(A7)

and the inverse, whose components are the Weingarten functions, reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}=\frac{1}{d^{2}-1}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\frac{1}{d}\\
-\frac{1}{d}&1\end{pmatrix}.

(A8)

Thus, the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}
, defined later on in
Eq.

A4
, reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}=\frac{T_{(13)(24)}}{d^{2}-1}\left(\mathbb{1}\otimes\mathbb{1}+T\otimes T-\frac{\mathbb{1}\otimes\mathbb{1}+T\otimes T}{d}\right)

(A9)

where
T_{(13)(24)}
is the permutation unitary operator corresponding to the cycle
(13)(24)\in S_{4}
. Recall in fact that the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 4})
. Multiplying permutations one gets
T_{(13)(24)}T_{(12)}T_{(34)}=T_{(14)(23)}
and thus

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}=\frac{1}{d^{2}-1}\left(T_{(13)(24)}+T_{(14)(23)}-\frac{T_{(13)(24)}+T_{(14)(23)}}{d}\right)

(A10)

while the
2
-fold channel applied on an operator
A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2})
reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}(A)=\frac{1}{d^{2}-1}\left(\tr(A)\mathbb{1}-\frac{\tr(A)}{d}T-\frac{\tr(TA)}{d}\mathbb{1}+\tr(AT)T\right).

(A11)

Example 8

(Average subsystem entropy)
.

Over many application of the Haar orbit of pure states, we find the computation of average entropy on subsystem of typical states. With the tool of the Weingarten calculus (cf.
Lemma

21
), we can compute it right away. Let
A|B
be a bipartition of the system of
n
qubits, with
n_{A},n_{B}
qubits respectively. Let
\ket{\psi}
an
n
-qubit state vector, then the purity of the reduced density matrix
\rho_{A}\coloneqq\tr_{B}\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}
is defined as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A})\coloneqq\tr(\psi_A^{2 })=\tr(T_{A}\psi^{\otimes 2})

(A12)

Let us compute the average purity by integrating over
\de\psi

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A})=\frac{1}{\tr(\mathbb{1}+T)}\tr(T_{A}\Pi_{\sym})=\frac{1}{\tr(\Pi_{\sym})}\tr(T_{A}+T_{B})=\frac{d_{A}^{2}d_{B}+d_{A}d_{B}^{2}}{d(d+1)}

(A13)

where we have denoted
d_{A(B)}=2^{n_{A(B)}}
. Note that we have used the fact that permutation operators are factorized on qubits, i.e.,
T=T_{A}T_{B}
, where
T_{A(B)}
acts non-identically on
A(B)
. If one considers the subsystem
A
to be much smaller than
B
, i.e.,
d_{A}\ll d_{B}
, one has

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de\psi\mathrm{Pur}(\psi_{A})=\frac{1}{d_{A}}+O(d^{-1})

(A14)

which tells us that, on average, states are maximally entangled, up to an error exponentially small in the total number of qubits
n
.

Example 9

(Twirling of a quantum channel)
.

An interesting and non-trivial application of the
2
-fold channel is the following: consider a completely positive trace preserving map
\mathcal{K}
with kraus operators
A_{k}
, i.e.,
\mathcal{K}(\cdot)=\sum_{k}A_{k}(\cdot)A_{k}^{{\dagger}}
. In the same fashion as the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(1)}
, we can define

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tilde{\mathcal{K}}=\sum_{k}A_{k}\otimes A_{k}^{{\dagger}}

(A15)

and let
\tilde{\mathcal{K}}
act on states
\rho\in\mathcal{H}
via the following isomorphism

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{K}(\rho)\mapsto\tr_{1}(T\tilde{\mathcal{K}}\rho\otimes\mathbb{1}).

(A16)

Note that
\tilde{\mathcal{K}}
is an operator on
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2}
, thus we can apply the
2
-fold Haar channel
\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}(\cdot)

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})=\frac{1}{d^{2}-1}\left(\tr(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})[\mathbb{1}-T/d]-\mathbb{1}+Td\right)

(A17)

where we have used the fact that
\tr(T\tilde{\mathcal{K}})=\sum_{k}\tr(A_{k}^{\dag}A_{k})=\tr(\mathbb{1})=d
for every CPTP map. Let us act with
\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})
on a state
\rho
as in
Eq.

A16

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr_{1}(T\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(2)}(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})\rho\otimes\mathbb{1})=\frac{\tr(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})-1}{d^{2}-1}\rho+\left(1-\frac{\tr(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})-1}{d^{2}-1}\right)\frac{\mathbb{1}}{d}

(A18)

that is a depolarizing channel
\mathcal{D}(\rho)=p\rho+(1-p)\mathbb{1}/d
with
p=\frac{\tr(\tilde{\mathcal{K}})-1}{d^{2}-1}
. We just found out that, on average, over Kraus operators
A_{k}\mapsto UA_{k}U^{{\dagger}}
every channel is a depolarizing channel with probability depending on the trace of
\tilde{\mathcal{K}}
in
Eq.

A15
.

Let us now go a step further and consider the
3
-fold channel. The symmetric group
S_{3}
contains
3!=6
permutation operators
S_{3}=\{e,(12),(23),(13),(123),(132)\}
. Denote
T_{\sigma}
the unitary representation of
\sigma
on
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 3}
and let us compute the matrix
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\scalebox{0.8}{
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\begin{pmatrix}\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T_{(12)})&\tr(T_{(23)})&\tr(T_{(13)})&\tr(T_{(123)})&\tr(T_{(132)})\\
\tr(T_{(12)})&\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T_{(132)})&\tr(T_{(123)})&\tr(T_{(13)})&\tr(T_{(23)})\\
\tr(T_{(23)})&\tr(T_{(123)})&\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T_{(132)})&\tr(T_{(12)})&\tr(T_{(13)})\\
\tr(T_{(13)})&\tr(T_{(132)})&\tr(T_{(123)})&\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T_{(23)})&\tr(T_{(12)})\\
\tr(T_{(123)})&\tr(T_{(23)})&\tr(T_{(13)})&\tr(T_{(12)})&\tr(T_{(132)})&\tr(\mathbb{1})\\
\tr(T_{(132)})&\tr(T_{(13)})&\tr(T_{(12)})&\tr(T_{(23)})&\tr(\mathbb{1})&\tr(T_{(123)})\\
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}d^{3}&d^{2}&d^{2}&d^{2}&d&d\\
d^{2}&d^{3}&d&d&d^{2}&d^{2}\\
d^{2}&d&d^{3}&d&d^{2}&d^{2}\\
d^{2}&d&d&d^{3}&d^{2}&d^{2}\\
d&d^{2}&d^{2}&d^{2}&d&d^{3}\\
d&d^{2}&d^{2}&d^{2}&d^{3}&d\\
\end{pmatrix}$},

(A19)

where we have computed the above matrix
following the rule sketched in
Lemma

22
, i.e.,
\tr(T_{\sigma})=d^{|\sigma|}
for
\sigma\in S_{3}
where
|\sigma|
is the length of
\sigma
, the number of cycles in the cycle-representation. For example, we have
|e|=|(1)(2)(3)|=3
or
|(123)|=|(132)|=2
because
(123)=(12)(23)
and
(132)=(23)(12)
. The inverse reads

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}=\frac{1}{d(d^{3}-4)(d^{2}-1)}\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}d^{2}-2&-d&-d&-d&2&2\\
-d&d^{2}-2&2&2&-d&-d\\
-d&2&d^{2}-2&2&-d&-d\\
-d&2&2&d^{2}-2&-d&-d\\
2&-d&-d&-d&2&d^{2}-2\\
2&-d&-d&-d&d^{2}-2&2\\
\end{array}\right).

(A20)

We avoid explicitly writing the operator
\Gamma_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(3)}
and the twirling
\Phi_{\operatorname{Haar}}^{(3)}
. We instead show an application by computing the average value of a
6
-point OTOC.

Example 10

(Average
6
-point OTOC)
.

Consider
P,Q\in\mathbb{P}_{n}

2
non-identity Pauli operator and the following correlation function

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\otoc_{6}(U)=\frac{1}{d}\tr(P(U)QQ(U)PQ(U)P(U)PQ)

(A21)

where
P(U)=U^{{\dagger}}PU
. Note that for
U=\mathbb{1}
one has
\otoc_{6}(U)=1
. Let us use the following trick
\tr(ABC)=\tr(T_{(132)}A\otimes B\otimes C)=\tr(T_{(123)}A\otimes C\otimes B)
and write
\otoc_{6}(U)
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\otoc_{6}(U)=\frac{1}{d}\tr(T_{(132)}U^{\dag\otimes 3}[P\otimes Q\otimes QP ]U^{\otimes 3}[Q\otimes P\otimes PQ]).

(A22)

Let us average over the realizations of the unitary operator
U
according to the Haar distribution

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de U\otoc_{6}(U)=\frac{1}{d}\tr(T_{(132)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(3)}(P\otimes Q\otimes QP )Q\otimes P\otimes PQ ).

(A23)

In order to compute the above twirling using the matrix formalism, and thus
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}
, let us compute the following
6
-components vectors
v_{\sigma}=\tr(T_{\sigma}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)
and
w_{\sigma}=\tr(T_{\sigma}Q\otimes P\otimes PQ)
. First note that
v_{\sigma}=w_{\sigma}
for two non-identity Pauli operators. Thus

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{v}=\begin{pmatrix}\tr(P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\\
\tr(T_{(12)}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\\
\tr(T_{(23)}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\\
\tr(T_{(13)}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\\
\tr(T_{(123)}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\\
\tr(T_{(132)}P\otimes Q\otimes QP)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
0\\
0\\
d\chi(P,Q)\\
d\chi(P,Q)\end{pmatrix}

(A24)

where
\chi(P,Q)=\frac{1}{d}\tr(PQPQ)
and
\chi(P,Q)=1
for commuting Pauli operators
[P,Q]=0
and
-1
for anticommuting Pauli operators
\{P,Q\}=0
. We can write the average
\otoc_{6}
as

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\int\de U\otoc_{6}(U)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\pi,\sigma}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}_{\pi,\sigma}v_{\sigma}v_{\pi}=\frac{2d^{2}}{(d^{2}-4)(d^{2}-1)}

(A25)

cf. also the results in Ref.
Roberts and Yoshida 2017
.

We now consider the
4
-fold channel, i.e.,
k=4
. Being the symmetric group of
4
objects of
4!
elements, calculations with the
4
-fold channel are long and tedious. However, in this section, we outline a systematic and general method to conduct such calculation by reducing the possibility of making typos around. First, let us list the permutations in
S_{4}
ordered by conjugacy class

\displaystyle\text{1-cycle:}\quad

\displaystyle e

(A26)

\displaystyle\text{2-cycle:}

\displaystyle(12),(13),(14),(23),(24),(34)

\displaystyle\text{3-cycle:}

\displaystyle(123),(132),(142),(234),(243),(132),(124),(143)

\displaystyle\text{4-cycle:}

\displaystyle(1234),(1324),(1423),(1342),(1243),(1432)

\displaystyle\text{22-cycle:}

\displaystyle(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(32)

For clarity, we omit to report the
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}
matrices for
k=4
due to their size, but it is possible to find them in the
.nb
file attached to the manuscript together with its inverse.
Let us apply the above formalism to see in what conditions a channel can be well approximated with a depolarizing channel.

Example 11

(Approximating a channel with the depolarizing channel)
.

In
Example

9
, we showed that on average every channel is a depolarizing channel with probability depending on the trace of
\tilde{\mathcal{K}}=\sum_{k}A_{k}\otimes A_{k}^{{\dagger}}
. Let us compute the fluctuations around the average evaluated for an expectation value of a Hermitian operator
A
with null trace (for simplicity). We need to evaluate the following average square distance from the average (variance)

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(T_{(12)(34)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2})(\rho\otimes A)^{\otimes 2})-\tr(T_{(12)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\mathcal{K})\rho\otimes A)^{2}

(A27)

where
\tilde{\mathcal{K}}
is defined in
Example

9
, see
Eq.

A15
. Let us specialize the discussion to a specific, although quite general, quantum channel referred to as Pauli channel
Flammia and Wallman 2020

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{K}(\rho)=\sum_{P}k_{P}P\rho P

(A28)

where
P
are Pauli operators
\sum_{P}k_{P}=1
to preserve the trace. Although the second term in
Eq.

A27
has already been computed in
Eq.

A18
, let us consider the first term and define the vectors
\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}
with components in
S_{4}
defined as
v_{\sigma}=\tr(\tilde{\mathcal{K}}^{\otimes 2}T_{\sigma})
and
w_{\sigma}=\tr(T_{(12)(34)}T_{\sigma}(\rho\otimes\mathbb{1})^{\otimes 2}A^{\otimes 2})
. In terms of
\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}
we have

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(T_{(12)(34)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2})(\rho\otimes\mathbb{1})^{\otimes 2}A^{\otimes 2})=\sum_{\pi,\sigma}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}_{\pi,\sigma}v_{\sigma}w_{\pi}.

(A29)

Let us compute the first vector

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{v}

\displaystyle=(d^{4}k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2},d^{3}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},

(A30)

\displaystyle d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},d^{2}k_{\mathbb{1}},s,s,s,d,d,d,d^{2},d^{2}\mathrm{Pur}(k),d^{2}\mathrm{Pur}(k)),

where
s=\sum_{P,Q}k_{P}k_{Q}\tr(PQPQ)
, and
\mathrm{Pur}(k)=\sum_{P}k_{P}^{2}
is the purity of the probability distribution
k
.

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\boldsymbol{w}=(

\displaystyle\tr^{2}(\rho A),0,\tr^{2}(\rho A),\tr(\rho A^2),\tr(\rho A^2),\tr^{2}(\rho A),0,0,\tr(\rho A^2),\tr(\rho A^2),0,\tr(\rho A^2),\tr(\rho A^2),0,\tr(\rho A^2),

(A31)

\displaystyle 0,\tr(\rho A^2),\tr(\rho A^2),0,0,\tr(A^2),0,\tr^{2}(\rho A),\tr(A^2)),

where we have taken into account that
\rho^{2}=\rho
and
\tr(A)=0
. We obtain

\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\tr(T_{(12)(34)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\mathcal{K}^{\otimes 2})(\rho\otimes A)^{\otimes 2})-\tr(T_{(12)}\Phi_{\haar}^{(4)}(\mathcal{K})\rho\otimes A)^{2}=\tr^{2}(A\rho)(k_{\mathbb{1}}-k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2})+O(d^{-1}).

(A32)

We thus conclude that, on average, every channel behaves like a depolarizing channel and the fluctuations around the average are small in two cases:
(i)
in the case of an almost unitary channel
k_{\mathbb{1}}-k_{\mathbb{1}}^{2}\ll 1
or
(ii)
for noisy channels
k_{\mathbb{1}}\ll 1
.
